His slider, an 85-88 mph mixed bag of some true sliders and lots that have more cutter-y shape, is his most-used pitch. Joseph's delivery isn't violent or messy, he simply lacks tactile feel for release. If he can find even 40-grade control, he's going to be a great weapon. He'll likely begin his major league career in an up/down capacity and root himself into a more consistent role if he can throw strikes in front of the big league manager.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During the 2019-20 international signing period, the Braves weren’t allowed to sign any amateur free agents for more than $10,000 as part of the penalty for previous signing infractions on the market. That doesn’t mean they weren’t able to find any talent. They nabbed Joseph in November 2019 when he was already closing in on his 19th birthday, and he wasn’t able to make his pro debut until 2021. He spent three years either in the Florida Complex League or with Single-A Augusta until 2024, when he managed to pitch his way from High-A Rome to Double-A Mississippi. It’s not difficult to figure out what Joseph, 24 for all of the 2025 season, is all about. He’s a two-pitch-only reliever who offers power and more power. His fastball sat at 98 mph in 2024 and touched triple digits, missing bats at a 36 percent clip thanks to good ride up in the zone. He unfurled his slider, topping out at 89 mph, more than his fastball and it’s easy to see why: The nasty breaking ball produced a 45 percent miss rate last year, according to Synergy. The one thing that has held Joseph back has been his control, and he enters 2025 with a career 5.9 BB/9 walk rate to go along with his 12.2 K/9 rate. He found the zone a bit more consistently to start the year, which enabled him to reach Double-A for the first time, but there’s a reason why the Braves didn’t put him on the 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft and why he wasn’t taken. It’s clear his stuff would be good for the backend of a bullpen, but he won’t see any high leverage situations unless he can improve his command.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Langevin hasn't yet pitched in a pro game due to a shoulder injury. He was a Canadian high schooler, then a two-season JUCO guy at Wabash Valley in Illinois before transferring to University of Louisiana-Lafayette for his draft year. He threw 80% fastballs in 2024, humming along at 94-97 in a relief capacity and generating a whopping 40% miss rate on his heater from its rise/run action. His changeup's tail gives it bat-missing potential, but his slider is very inconsistent (and if it's consistent, it's consistently bad), though it flashes once in a long while. That said, he hasn't thrown it much. Langevin needs to find a second good pitch to work out of a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Quebec native, Langevin came to the United States for college ball at Wabash Valley (Ill.) Community College before transferring to Louisiana-Lafayette his junior year. He struck out the world there, maintaining a nearly 40 percent strikeout rate. The metrics on his fastball in particular were part of the reason the Royals took Langevin in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft, signing him for $597,500. It’s no secret that Langevin’s fastball is what makes him stand out. It’s a unique pitch that has baffled hitters so far, although not because of velocity -- it sits 92-96 mph. The pitch has extremely high spin rates and features plenty of ride and run from a lower vertical approach angle. Langevin’s deceptive delivery definitely helps the pitch play up too, as does his quick arm. His secondaries are fringe average at best, as he didn’t really need or use them in college, so that will be a focus for him in his first pro season. The slider has some sweeping action to it, but it varies in speed and he needs to work on landing it in the zone. He has a feel for a changeup but needs to develop it more. If it translates to results in pro ball, Langevin’s fastball could dominate, and he could move quickly as a reliever. Officials love his makeup and fiery competitiveness on the mound. He’s a one-trick pitcher right now, though, and needs to improve his secondaries and control to reach his ceiling as a potential back-end bullpen arm. Langevin will likely begin his pro career at High-A in 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Venezuela natives Brayan Rocchio (Guardians) and Ezequiel Tovar (Rockies) have taken their slick-fielding ways at shortstop to the Majors in recent years with varying levels of effectiveness. Cortesia is several years behind his countrymen at the position but could very well follow in their footsteps in time. The 17-year-old was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 14 prospect in the 2025 class and became Washington’s top international signing at the start of the 2025 period when he joined the organization for $1.92 million. Nationals officials said they targeted hit tools at the top of this year’s international group, and Cortesia has a solid one with a level right-handed swing that can send the ball all over the diamond. It’s been hit-over-power at this early stage, but he’s been growing into his frame, adding to the hope that average pop could be in the tank by the time he fully matures. Cortesia earned his best amateur grades on the defensive side. His hands, footwork and arm strength all look above-average at this early stage, and as the brother of a member of the Venezuelan national track-and-field team, he’ll flash plus-plus run times in the 60-yard dash right now. Even if he slows down as he fills out, he should still be good for above-average wheels. The Nationals will take that defensive profile and hope to build a stronger and sustainable hitter in Cortesia, starting with their Dominican Summer League program.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Cortesia signed for $1.92 million in 2025 and was generally considered more of a skills-over-tools utility type prospect. His DSL debut reinforced those notions, as he slashed .317/.440/.358 with just four extra-base hits. Cortesia tracks the baseball well and moves the barrel around. He's a competent shortstop with a medium frame and modest projection. He has a realistic utility infield ceiling barring continued improvement of his bat-to-ball ability to an elite level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rajcic worked as both a closer and starter for UCLA before joining the Cardinals as a Draft-eligible sophomore in the sixth round in 2022. He was St. Louis’ Minor League Pitcher of the Year a year later after posting a 2.48 ERA and a 1.01 WHIP with 123 strikeouts in 123 1/3 innings between Single-A and High-A and moved onto Double-A for the duration of his second full season. His 131 K’s were third-most in the Texas League for 2024, but his other results (4.33 ERA, 1.35 WHIP) took a step back. The 6-foot hurler sits 92-94 mph with his fastball, touching 95, giving him average velocity. There isn’t great movement on the pitch, and Double-A hitters saw it well out of his high three-quarters release, hitting .306 with a .521 slugging percentage off the heater alone. Rajcic’s best pitch in terms of whiff and chase was his 83-85 mph changeup, a promising armside fader that could fool batters from both sides. His 82-84 mph slider was his most-used secondary against righties, but it’s a 79-82 mph curveball that shows more promise with sharp 12-to-6 break. Known for his fastball command coming out of college, Rajcic has seen his walk rates slowly climb in pro ball as more experienced hitters have laid off his secondaries outside the zone. He could use a touch more velocity or more overall deception heading into year three, but a deep arsenal and average control should keep him in the future backend rotation conversations.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Rajcic was Garrett Mitchell's teammate at Orange Lutheran and then again at UCLA, where he began his college career as the closer before transitioning into the Friday night starter role as a sophomore. Since then, Rajcic has mostly been remarkably durable and consistent. He's worked at least 123 innings each of the last two seasons and is on pace to do so again, this time hopefully closing out the season at Memphis (he's repeating Springfield currently) and fighting for a 40-man spot. Physically dense but limber, Rajcic repeats his delivery, which features late arm acceleration that stymies hitters the first time they see him. He works with five different pitches — two fastball variants, a downhill tailing changeup, the occasional slider and curveball — and commands them with starter-quality feel. The changeup, which Rajcic uses a lot against righties, is easily his best pure pitch and the lone above-average piece of his toolkit. He could be needed in a spot start capacity as soon as next year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Manon is originally from the same city that brought the baseball world Elly De La Cruz -- Sabana Grande de Boya in the Dominican Republic. He moved to Santo Domingo to train with the MLB Trainer Partnership Program's Amaurys Nina and was No. 15 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list when the Braves signed him for right around $1.5 million when the signing period opened in mid-January of this year. Strong and physical, Manon is a right-handed hitter who makes a ton of contact with an aggressive approach at the plate. There’s a definite feel for hitting, which he showed off in places like the Amateur Scouting League in 2024, batting .308 over nine games. He uses a small leg kick to stay on time and has shown the ability to drive the ball to all fields, with most of the juice showing up to his pull side. He’s reminded some of a young Aaron Hicks in terms of his swing and projected impact as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame. Manon is a solid defender with good lateral movement and the ability to get to all the balls he should at shortstop. He might not have the arm to stick there, but work can be done to build up strength so he can stay at the premium position. He’s an above-average runner who maximizes his speed with strong instincts on the basepaths.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Manon stood out for his bat speed and physical projection on Dominicana's U-18 PanAm qualifier roster late in 2024, but also struggled with his timing at the dish and often looked out of control. He has the athleticism and arm strength to develop at shortstop, but his size puts him on the 3B/SS line for the long haul. His contact puzzle piece made him a high-variance $1.5 million bet by Atlanta in the 2026 international class.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally recruited by Auburn as a left-handed pitcher, Snell redshirted there while injured in 2021 before transferring to Wallace-Dothan (Ala.) CC and becoming the national junior college player of the year in 2023. He played both ways on Alabama in 2024 before becoming a full-time left fielder in his final college season. As a Southeastern Conference performer with intriguing data and no college eligibility remaining, he was one of the better discount hitters available in the 2025 Draft and went in the fifth round. After displaying one of the best combinations of swing decisions, contact and exit velocities in the 2025 college crop, Snell continued to stand out in those areas even while slashing just .167/.268/.219 at High-A during his 27-game pro debut. He drives the ball to all fields and handles all types of pitches with a quality left-handed swing. His biggest need is to learn to launch balls in the air more regularly, or else he'll be a hit-over-power corner outfielder who will top out at 15 homers per season. Snell can show close to average speed at his top end but he's more of a below-average runner with limited outfield range. He reached 93 mph with his fastball as a redshirt junior and the Cubs deployed him on both outfield corners after Alabama utilized him solely in left field. Most of his value will come from his bat, though he also receives high marks for his leadership skills and competitiveness.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Snell began his college career at Auburn but didn't play as a freshman and left for Wallace Community College in 2022. He spent two years as a two-way player there and then transferred to Alabama, where he both pitched and hit in 2024 before he was named team captain and exclusively played the outfield in 2025. The Cubs gave the fifth-year senior $200,000 in the draft's fifth round, an indication that they considered him one of the priority senior players in the class. Snell was aggressively assigned to High-A and is back there to start 2026, and is starting to get some traction. He can run and throw, and he swings hard for a player his size, tools that didn't always shine through in college (Snell stole zero bases at 'Bama even though he's a plus runner). It's possible that's simply because he has only focused on hitting for one year. Snell's feel for defense isn't great, and his swing path results in a lot of groundball contact. These are things that could be manicured with the reps and development that Snell has only just begun to get consistently. He's a toolsy late-bloomer sleeper.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text:
Ahuna spent his first two college seasons at Kansas and had one of the hottest 2022's in college baseball. He slashed .396/.479/.634 and put himself in the first round mix before transferring to Tennessee for his draft year. That next season was rocky. He was ineligible to play at the start of the season because Tennessee didn't properly handle some clerical aspects of his transfer, and then Ahuna played through a stress reaction in his back all year and K'd at a daming 31% clip. He fell to the fourth round. Hopes for a bounce back were dashed as Ahuna dealt with more injuries in 2024, playing in just 23 non-rehab games and eventually needing mid-season Tommy John surgery. 
Ahuna's long, low-ball swing makes it tough for him to pull the baseball, and he'll probably swing underneath a lot of fastballs as he climbs the minors, unless a truly healthy return means new things for his swing. Amid all these injuries, Ahuna has always looked good playing defense. His hands, acrobatic actions, and big time arm are all fits at short. When Ahuna returns, he'll be 23 and yet to play a game above Low-A. He's purely a bounce-back candidate entering 2025.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A projected 2023 first-rounder after transferring from Kansas to Tennessee, Ahuna fell to the fourth round after trying to do too much at the plate while dealing with a stress reaction in his back. The Giants saw a lot of parallels between him and another slick-fielding college shortstop who had fallen to them in the fourth round 15 years earlier: Brandon Crawford. Ahuna has had a difficult time making good on that comparison because he injured his elbow early in his 2024 pro debut, requiring Tommy John surgery, and played just 97 games in his first two seasons. Crawford earned four Gold Gloves with San Francisco and Ahuna has the talent to do the same. He has fluid actions, a quick first step, plenty of range and fast hands. He also possesses a strong arm, though it graded more as solid than its usual plus in his first year back from elbow reconstruction. Ahuna has sneaky pop for a 6-foot-1, 170-pounder and could provide 15-20 homers per season, but it comes at a price. He swings for the fences with a big leg kick and a left-handed stroke that gets too long and uphill, leading to too many empty swings on strikes and too many grounders when he does make contact, and he particularly struggles against southpaws. He has solid speed and some basestealing aptitude but needs to focus on reaching base more often to take advantage of them.

fangraphs.label: 2024updated
fangraphs.text: Owen slid to the fourth round of the 2023 draft after some health issues overshadowed his final season at Vanderbilt. The Royals assigned Owen to Quad Cities for his first season of pro ball, and he’s been effective at limiting his walks (7.7% BB) but his strikeouts have also been limited (17.5% K). He has a five-pitch mix and an XL frame that has already fully matured. His 89-94 mph fastball has downhill angle created by Owen’s 6-foot-6 height and over-the-top release point. It lacks above-average movement and life, and is an underwhelming pitch overall. His curveball is a deep vertical breaker in the mid-to-upper 70s, while his two-plane slider comes in at 82-86 mph with nastier break. His mid-80s changeup is playing against lower level hitters, though more because of his ability to sell the offering with arm speed than the depth the pitch tends to show. He'll also use a little cutter as another way to stay off the barrels of right-handers. Owen's arsenal lacks big upside and has limited swing-and-miss potential, but there’s obvious feel for command and pitchability here, which will give him up/down starter value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Three seasons at Vanderbilt both starting and relieving as well as a strong MLB Draft Combine showing led the Royals to take Owen in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft, signing him for $631,700, He might have gone higher if not for injury concerns in his final season at Vandy. Owen put those aside by throwing 102 innings across 23 games (22 starts) for High-A Quad Cities in his first pro season. He had a 4.20 ERA with a 1.20 WHIP, an 18.9% strikeout rate and a 7.5% walk rate. Owen is a presence on the mound at 6-foot-6 and 260 pounds. His fastball is 90-94 mph with solid carry and vert to it and uses the top of the zone well. His 86-89 mph slider is smaller, almost cutter-like, misses bats and has potential to be his out pitch, while his 75-76 mph curveball is still developing after he wasn't able to land it much in 2024. His 83-85 mph changeup is near average with sink and gets some chase on it. Owen’s delivery is simple but does have some effort because of his bigger frame, although he likes using that strong presence to his advantage on the mound. Owen looks the part of a big-bodied rotation guy who’s built like a workhorse, so it was good to see him stay healthy across a full season with a lot of innings and a jump from what he had in ‘23. He’ll head to Double-A in 2025 and projects as a back-end starter if he can keep developing his secondaries, but that stuff might tick up in a bullpen, especially against lefties.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Slender, slight, and speedy, Jaworsky got almost half a million dollars over his fifth round slot value to sign out of his Colorado high school in 2023, but he hasn't grown meaningfully stronger since. He has the range and hands to cover both middle infield positions and push a glove-dependent utility profile. But he lacks the power to thrive with the 20% or so K-rate he’s run across both levels of A-ball, which a mark driven both by excessive two-strike chase and worrisome trouble with velocity. The defensive floor is high enough to drive a sixth infielder projection, but Jaworsky will need to add strength to stabilize his offense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Jaworsky impressed with his athleticism at the 2023 MLB Draft Combine, the Astros spent a fifth-round pick and an over-slot $847,500 bonus to lure the Colorado prepster away from a commitment to Utah Valley State. His top priority was to add muscle to his skinny 6-foot-1 frame and he has added about 15 pounds since turning pro. He showed steady improvement as a 19-year-old in Single-A last year and made the jump to High-A in 2025 before Houston sent him to the Marlins in a trade for Jesus Sanchez in July. A left-handed hitter, Jaworsky has good bat-to-ball skills but needs to improve his selectivity while continuing to gain strength. While he shows the ability to make adjustments and uses the entire field well, he currently makes a lot of soft groundball contact. Added physical development could result in 12-15 homers per year, though he'll always be a hit-over-power guy. Jaworsky's most obvious tool is his plus speed, which he used to steal 28 bases in 78 games last season. He has nice actions and range to both sides at shortstop, though there are questions as to whether his average arm will be enough to remain at the position. His quick release and good internal clock will help him, but some scouts think second base and center field are more realistic destinations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Weston had an accomplished college career at Michigan before the Orioles made him an eighth-round pick in 2022, and he’s been one of their systems most consistent performers since debuting that summer. He spent most of his full season debut at High-A Aberdeen and had his most impressive year yet in 2024, pitching to a 2.97 ERA and 1.01 WHIP across 109 innings, mostly at Double-A. The 6-foot-2, 215-pound Weston is a sinker/slider righty with a three-quarters arm slot, a four-pitch mix and some polish. He operates off a low-90s two-seamer that generates weak contact and high ground-ball rates, and uses a high-70s sweeping slider to miss bats when he needs to. He also uses a splitter against righties and a changeup against lefties, throwing both with a deceptive delivery that makes his low arm slot difficult to pick up. Paired with above -average control and the ability to locate all of his pitches, Weston is able to miss bats without breaking the radar gun. He walked only 2.4 batters per nine at Double-A. If Weston maintains his level of performance, he has a chance to fulfill his ceiling as a durable back-end starter. But there is a chance the stuff proves less vexing for more advanced hitters, particularly the second and third time through a lineup. If that’s the case, Weston could profile as the type of valuable multi-inning reliever that tends to always be in demand and consequently enjoy lengthy careers.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Weston is a low-slot, nearly sidearm kitchen-sinker working in a length role at Norfolk. He succeeds in part by distributing his mix relatively evenly. His two-seamer sits in the low 90s and can generate grounders when used judiciously, but it doesn't have the kind of movement that lets him lean on it. The cutter and particularly the slider are his best bat-missers. His sweeper is pretty slow, down to the mid-70s, and has a strike-stealing, disarming effect. The split and change are pure chase pitches, with the former generating more whiffs. No one pitch carries the mail on its own, but like so many other guys in this system, the well-rounded movement profile has a more-than-the-sum-of-its-parts effect. 
Deception wise, there’s some push and pull here. Weston’s deep arsenal comes with an unusual combination of good extension and a low slot. Hitters seem to find his open stride and slow arm path pretty comfortable, though, and his results at Triple-A hint that this could be a real problem. The jump from Double- to Triple-A generally isn't large, but Weston’s walk rate has nearly doubled at Norfolk and his home run rate surged once he hit the upper minors, suggesting that experienced opponents are picking up the ball pretty well. The Orioles have already moved him from a pure starting role to more of a hybrid assignment, and it’s in that sort of lower-leverage length capacity that he figures to work at the highest level.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: The Bronx native and former second round pick has filled out his 6-foot-4 frame and cultivated a downer bat-missing low-80s slider, with a cutter that ably protects it. That’s enough to hold together a relief projection without lingering too much on the disappointment that more hasn't developed around it. Santos is sitting in the low-90s again with middling results, but he has flashed 96 and can miss bats when he locates his heater at the letters. But his lack of fastball command holds back both his current efforts of starting at Double-A and the relief future we’re projecting. Santos prominently drags his back foot across the pitching rubber right as he’s releasing the ball, which is the messiest element of an involved lower-half move he struggles to repeat. It was driving a nearly 18% walk rate at the time Santos hit the IL again in June, thus the relief projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros lost their first two picks in the 2020 Draft as part of their punishment for sign stealing, and they spent their top selection (supplemental second round) and an over-slot $1.25 million bonus on Santos. Though he was one of the best high school arms to come out of New York City in the last decade, his conditioning, stuff and control all regressed in the early years of his pro career. He got hammered for a 7.83 ERA in Double-A during the first month of the season before getting sidelined by an elbow strain, but he looked like a different pitcher when he returned to tie for the Arizona Fall League lead with 26 strikeouts in 17 2/3 innings. Small sample size aside, Santos' AFL performance provided cause for optimism as he averaged 95 mph and touched 98 with his fastball, getting good carry on his four-seamer and effective sink and run on his two-seamer. His low-80s slider was unhittable at times with two-plane depth and he mixed it with a tighter upper-80s cutter. His upper-70s curveball wasn't as reliable as his other offerings, and he didn't throw a single changeup. Houston had Santos lower his arm slot a bit, and he looks more comfortable while throwing with greater velocity and spin. He also demonstrated better control in the Fall League than he had in the Minors. If he can sustain that stuff and strike-throwing, he still might be a big league starter if he can find a way to get lefties out reliably.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Montalvo came to Detroit as part of the 2024 Andrew Chafin deal. He had a torn ligament in his foot at the time, which limited him to a handful of starts at West Michigan. He was promoted to Double-A last season, appearing 11 times and struggling to miss bats across 44 mediocre innings. His velo was down a couple ticks — his average fastball was 90-93, similar to 2024, but he was unable to rear back for more like he has in the past — and then he began to deal with elbow inflammation in June, which ended his season. 
Montalvo is very lean, which makes these injuries both a little less surprising and more worrying than they would be for the average bear, er, Tiger. On paper, he looks like a backend starter: He has a low-maintenance delivery and the athleticism to repeat it well, along with projectable, if inconsistent, secondaries. But thus far, Montalvo hasn't shown the health or the length that makes us especially confident he'll be able to handle that kind of workload.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in Puerto Rico before moving to Florida as a teenager, Montalvo was a shortstop prospect until he took up pitching as a high school senior. He rose from a 20th-round pick in the 2021 Draft to a ranked prospect in the Rangers' system on the strength of swing-and-miss stuff, which held after converting from reliever to starter in 2023. The Tigers liked the pitch shapes and command enough to include him in the return package for Andrew Chafin at the 2024 Trade Deadline. Montalvo shows good command and instincts for someone still relatively new to pitching, reading and reacting to hitters’ swings. His extension out of a relatively low arm angle allows his low to mid-90s fastball to play up, and he can spot it in different parts of the zone. His low-80s slider is his main swing-and-miss pitch, looking like a fastball out of his hand before moving late with sweeping action. He has improved his command on his mid-80s changeup, which he uses to generate weak contact, but might need more deception to handle left-handed hitters. Montalvo fits the profile of pitcher that the Tigers’ player development group has had success polishing in the last few years. If he fills out his frame, polishes his changeup and adds another tick or two of velocity to his fastball, he could become an intriguing prospect for the Tigers to push.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Spikerman is a plus-running switch-hitter who plays great outfield defense. He's a decisive outfielder with plus range and arm strength. Spikerman has a gap-to-gap line drive approach as a left-handed hitter and is more opposite-field oriented as a righty, though both swings tend to be vulnerable to fastballs at the top of the zone. Speed and defense should allow Spikerman to play a marginal role down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since Spikerman showed up on the University of Oklahoma's campus for his freshman season in 2022, he's shown off explosive speed and athleticism. But injuries have gotten in the way of his progress, missing two months as a freshman, then breaking his right hamate in March 2024, his junior season. That's continued as a pro since the Phillies took him in the third round of that summer's Draft, with a shoulder injury limiting him to just 62 games in an uneven first full season of pro ball. The Phillies were optimistic that the switch-hitting Spikerman was figuring things out thanks to a lot of work he put in during the offseason. While he should be all about making contact, getting on base and using his speed, he used to have way too big of a swing for someone with his size and offensive profile. He made some adjustments over the winter, showing a better understanding of how to use his elite athleticism in the box and engage his hands better when he hits. There have never been any questions about Spikerman's ability to use his speed to steal bags and play plus outfield defense. He's shown he can handle all three spots, and can play an outstanding center field long-term, with a plus arm only adding to his profile. That helps give him a decent floor as a backup outfielder, with a greater role if the bat comes along.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
It's starting to feel like the Rockies have cornered the market on pitchers named "Herrera." This Herrera had something of a breakout 2024. The gigantic righty began the season in Milwaukee’s Low-A bullpen, but by the end of May, he was in the High-A rotation. He was then traded to Colorado as part of the Nick Mears deal and finished the season in Spokane. Overall, he threw 100.2 innings, allowed 85 hits, struck out 110 with 34 walks, and posted a 3.04 ERA. Unfortunately, he blew out at the end of the season and missed almost all of 2025. He returned for instructs and then made a dozen appearances in the Venezuelan Winter League, where he was effectively wild. 
Herrera is listed at 175 pounds, but he looks more like 250. He’s a slow-twitch, below-average athlete who has struggled to throw strikes at various points during his career. Even though he has mostly started, his effort level and the way he falls and spins off the mound have made him scattered in a way that’s almost always better suited for the bullpen. His stuff looks down a tick or two this spring, but in shorter stints, he could have two 60’s in the holster, as he touched the upper 90s and his slider missed a ton of bats back in 2024, even though visually it looks more average or 55 than plus. He has experimented with a change but hasn't used it a ton, and neither the action nor the arm speed scream “projectable.” He’s a middle relief prospect who could move quickly if he’s moved to the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers’ international scouting department did an excellent job finding Herrera and signing him for just $10,000 in August of 2019. It wasn’t until 2023 that he gained any real traction, pitching well in his second go-round in the Single-A Carolina League. Things clicked more the following year as he made his way to High-A ball when he was sent to the Rockies in the Nick Mears trade that July. He threw very well upon his arrival, but got shut down after six starts and he needed Tommy John surgery, so he missed all of the 2025 season. Herrera did return in time for instructional league play and was providing some optimism by dialing his fastball up to 97-98 mph in shorter stints. Before the injury, he was usually in the 92-94 mph range, getting groundball outs when he sinks it, but relying on his hard slider as his main out pitch. His feel to spin also helps him land a slightly slower curve and he has a changeup that he hadn’t committed to before he got hurt. The new pitching group with the Rockies are excited about working with Herrera because of his ability to shape different pitches, all coming out of the same slot. He got in some competitive innings in winter ball and he’ll pitch most of the 2026 season at age 22, trying to show he has the stuff and command to stick in a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starting his college career at Southern Mississippi as a two-way player in 2023, Monistere focused on hitting and played six different positions as a sophomore. He became a full-time second baseman in 2025 and won Sun Belt Conference player of the year honors after slashing .323/.410/.623 with a league-best 21 homers. The Astros made him a fourth-round pick because they liked his athleticism and versatility, though he looked less refined than expected on both sides of the ball during his introduction to pro ball. Monistere uses an aggressive right-handed swing to produce high exit velocities, though he needs to tone down his approach. He rolls over on too many fastballs and comes up empty while chasing too many breaking balls and changeups. His solid-to-plus raw power could translate into 20 homers per season if he can become more selective and less pull happy. Monistere features average quickness and solid arm strength that produced fastballs up to 94 mph when he pitched as a freshman. The game sped up on him when he spent most of his pro debut at shortstop and third base, and he began 2026 by mainly playing second base. That's his best position and he projects as an average defender there.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: After ditching his two-way player pursuit as a sophomore, Monistere had a draft year offensive breakout at Southern Miss, launching 21 bombs and slashing .323/.410/.623 against Sun Belt pitching. It looked more like fringe average raw power with a long swing in a tough post-draft look at Low-A, where he ran a 74% contact rate but continued to look vulnerable and chase-prone against spin. Primarily a second baseman while being a defensive nomad who has done everything but catch over the last three years, Monistere obviously has a plus throwing arm but shaky hands. It’s a non-shortstop utility profile that depends on some more pop showing up.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: While generally seen as more of a late-first-round talent, the Royals popped Mozzicato with the seventh overall pick in the 2021 draft. He took a haircut on his bonus, which helped facilitate a number of other big-dollar signings, including Carter Jensen. Mozzicato himself has progressed slowly. His long, high-spin curve has missed bats and barrels up and down the minor league ladder, but the pitch is arguably his only weapon. His change looks and plays fringy, and while the lefty was drafted in part on his physical projection, his velocity has stubbornly remained in the same range throughout his career. His feel for the zone and ability to locate look better when you're watching him than the numbers imply, but his stuff is so soft that he has to nibble; essentially, he can get strike one, but strike three is a real problem. It’s the skill set of an up-down spot starter or long reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals surprised many by selecting Mozzicato at No. 7 overall in the 2021 Draft, taking the Connecticut prep pitcher higher than some thought but also leaving flexibility to draft Ben Kudrna and Carter Jensen after the first round. It hasn’t been the smoothest of journeys for Mozzicato since the Draft, plagued by command issues and inconsistent results. He returned to High-A Quad Cities to begin 2025 and was excellent there, posting a 1.24 ERA in seven starts. Mozzicato faced more challenges in Double-A, where he recorded a 7.46 ERA in 17 games (13 starts), saw his walk rate balloon to 19.4 percent and strikeout rate dip to 17.6 percent, while batters hit .278 against him. Mozzicato has yet to find the velocity that many thought would come in his development, averaging around 90 mph in 2025 and getting hit hard. His 86 mph circle changeup is fringe-average. His curveball, though, has never let him down. It’s a plus pitch, has tons of spin and misses bats. Mozzicato introduced a 90 mph cutter this past offseason, which gives him more confidence in the zone and misses the barrel, although how he uses it in games and how it opens up his arsenal remains to be seen. What has hurt Mozzicato the most, though, is his delivery, and it’s what the Royals have worked extensively on with him. His long stroke never allowed him to sync up, and while he doesn’t have a short arm stroke now, it has tightened and timed up better. The Royals want to continue to see Mozzicato as a starter for now, but there’s clear reliever potential here. Some say the curveball is ready for the Majors; Mozzicato just needs to be able to get his fastball to a place where he can trust it up there, too.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Kennedy has advanced command of two good offspeed pitches and well-below-average fastball velocity, sitting 88-91. He was a 2022 over-slot fourth rounder who signed for $1 million rather than go to LSU. In 2024, he pitched his way to High-A in the Pirates org, then was traded to the Guardians as part of the Spencer Horwitz deal during the offseason. A short-levered 6-foot-1, Kennedy’s physical traits combine with his low-to-the-ground delivery to help his fastball have shallow angle toward the top of the zone, but his utter lack of velocity still makes it a vulnerable pitch. He needs to pitch off his secondary stuff in order to succeed. The vertical snap and 11-to-5 movement of Kennedy’s 77-83 mph breaking ball play nicely off of his fastball, and his feel for locating his 82-84 mph changeup improved in 2024; that pitch has generated above-average chase and miss throughout the last year and change. Kennedy also likes to alter his leg kick to mess with hitters’ timing. He's a pitchability spot starter with more ceiling if, despite lacking obvious physical projection, he can somehow find more velocity as he gets deeper into his 20s.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: New York's best prep prospect in 2022, Kennedy worried clubs with his commitment to Louisiana State but turned pro for a well-over-slot $1 million when the Pirates drafted him in the fourth round. Pittsburgh handled him with care and he compiled a 3.11 ERA with a 158/44 K/BB ratio in 130 1/3 innings at the lower levels of the Minors in his first two pro seasons. After acquiring Spencer Horwitz from the Blue Jays in the Andrés Giménez trade at the Winter Meetings in December, the Guardians immediately spun Horwitz to the Pirates for Luis Ortiz, Kennedy and lefty pitching prospect Josh Hartle. Kennedy's fastball averaged just under 90 mph and peaked at 93 last season, though it was effective because he creates deception and carry with a flat approach angle. Hitters also can't sit on his heater because he has a pair of solid secondary pitches that elicit a lot of chases. His sweeping low-80s slider keeps left-handers in check and his sinking low-80s changeup keeps right-handers at bay. Kennedy's lack of overpowering stuff leaves him with little margin for error, but he rarely makes mistakes. More athletic than physical, he ranked third among teenagers in the full-season Minors (minimum: 80 innings) with a 6 percent walk rate last year, but his control has regressed in 2025. His floor stands out more than his ceiling, and he'll have to prove he can get higher-level hitters out without huge velocity, but his feel for pitching is impressive.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: As much as it’s not working for the former 21st overall pick right now, it’s no mystery why someone would spend $3.6 million on this type of talent. Davis swings very hard to produce big-time left-handed juice (106 mph 90th-percentile EV), and even with an approach that leans passive, a 17% chase rate is typically a good pairing with that kind of pop. He has below-average range for a center fielder, but he has the athleticism to be plus in a corner and certainly the hose for it to be right. Even with those enticing raw ingredients, Davis slugged just .353 in Double-A, two years after posting a figure more than twice that in his final season at Arizona. It takes effort to rotate as hard as Davis does, and his late barrel tilt seems to fuel a lot of in-zone misses on fastballs. While his overall chase is under control, Davis doesn't seem to track spin well, and two-strike whiffs on dirted breakers are the biggest culprit for the 29.6% strikeout rate he ran at Springfield, which also does not bode well for maintaining his burly walks rates at higher levels. To add to the warning signs heading into Davis’ 40-man platform year, he also isn't elevating the ball (48.1% groundball rate), but there are enough physical tools and just enough defensive utility to hold out hope for a fourth outfielder future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis showed off monster power numbers in his final two seasons on campus at the University of Arizona, including a .742 slugging percentage and a 1.231 OPS as a Pac-12 All-Conference honoree in 2023. The Cardinals selected him 21st overall that July and signed him for slot at $3,618,200. St. Louis played it fairly passively with Davis out of the gate in 2024 with an assignment to Single-A Palm Beach, and he didn’t crack out of the level for 74 games, hitting .232/.337/.401 with eight homers in that span. He was much better after a late July promotion to High-A Peoria (.301/.388/.451 in 30 games) and even finished things out with a quick trip to Double-A Springfield. The left-handed slugger worked through numerous swing and approach changes in his first full season but appears to be at his best with a swing that often draws comparisons to Carlos Gonzalez with his hands starting high near his head, his stance open and his front leg kicking to generate forward momentum. His raw power numbers are still clearly above average and he can pull the ball well, especially heaters. But soft stuff tailing away from him can be an issue when it comes to whiffs or quality contact. Even during the good times at High-A, he ran a 55.6 percent ground-ball rate, and he's continued to miss on a ton of offspeed pitches in 2025. Davis gets most of his reps in center field, but with average speed and plus arm strength, he figures to land in a corner full time as he closes in on St. Louis. That puts added pressure on the raw power to come through in games, and with his whiff rates with Springfield, that's becoming a tall order.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Feliz is a stiffer-bodied athlete who plays baseball with a high center of gravity and funky-looking actions. His swing is also odd, as he cuts downward at the baseball in the extreme and sprays almost exclusively opposite-field contact. But Feliz is also a heady, crafty, high baseball IQ player who always seems to find a way to put the ball in play or make plays on defense. He is a versatile defender (2B/3B/SS) and has the same creative zest at each position. While Feliz has tended to be an above-average contact hitter, the nature of his swing and spray chart are bizarre enough to be skeptical that will continue. He projects as a skills-y extra infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feliz was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 24 international prospect in the 2024 class and signed with the Nationals for $1.8 million that January. Only outfielder Victor Hurtado ($2.7 million) signed for more. Feliz was a Dominican Summer League mid-season All-Star in his first taste of the pros after hitting .310/.381/.468 with four homers and 27 steals in 49 games and handled himself decently well with his move stateside for his age-18 season in 2025. The infielder produced a .264/.366/.358 line in 53 games in the Florida Complex League and produced a 96 wRC+ with Single-A Fredericksburg following a late July promotion. It was notable that Feliz was one of only 30 age-18 prospects to get more than 100 plate appearances in Single-A last season and the only Washington player to meet that criteria. Already standing at 6-foot-3, there’s hope that he can add some strength to that frame and get to at least average power, but to do that, he’ll have to lift the ball at a much better rate. He doesn’t chase pitches outside the zone much for his age, but when he does, it’s often with an empty swing, especially against soft stuff. Starting with his hands held above his head, he can yank over breaking pitches beyond the outer third of the plate right now, but it’s still plenty early in his development cycle. Feliz will flash decent home-to-first times when he’s really pushing it out of the box, but many expect him to land at fringy speed at best by the time he fills out. He isn’t the twitchiest defender, though Nats officials have praised him for his hands on the dirt and arm strength. With Eli Willits likely in his path, Feliz remains a priority infielder, albeit one likely to move to third long-term.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Mobley is an XL-framed, 6-foot-5 righty who brings big heat in the 93-98 mph range. He signed for $1.8 million in 2024 rather than head to Florida State and spent most of 2025 on the complex in Arizona before a brief stint in Lynchburg to end the year. Mobley's has a super short arm action in an effort to make his release more consistent, but he still struggles with his feel for location, and he walked a batter per inning in 2025. His lack of control made it tough for either of his secondary pitches to shine from a pitch performance standpoint, but his slider still flashes plus and often freezes hitters even when it backs up on him. Mobley looks like a relief-only prospect who is rather far from the bigs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mobley established himself as one of the best prep pitchers in the 2024 Draft early in his career at Durant HS (Plant City, Fla.) and stood out last spring as one of the youngest, most projectable and hardest-throwing high school hurlers available. Armed with the largest bonus pool ($18,334,000) since those rules came into play in 2012, the Guardians floated Mobley all the way down to the 295th overall pick, where they signed him for $1.8 million. That obliterated the 10th-round bonus record Cleveland set two years earlier by paying Jacob Zibin $1.2 million. Mobley already reaches 92-95 mph and reaches 99 with armside run and carry on his fastball, which gains deception coming out of a low three-quarters arm slot and low release height. Because he could overmatch most high schoolers simply by using his heaters, he didn't need to rely on or develop his secondary pitches very much. His slider and tumbling changeup both park in the low 80s and have solid upside, while his mid-70s curveball needs more power. There still plenty of projection remaining in Mobley's 6-foot-5, 205-pound frame, so he could add even more velocity as he gets stronger. He's still in the process of learning how to keep his long limbs in sync, maintain a consistent regular point and land his secondary pitches in the zone. He comes with some reliever risk and will need time to add polish but could develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hamm looked like a Draft steal in his first full pro season, earning Midwest League Pitcher of the Year and Tigers Minor League Pitcher of the Year honors in an impressive 2024 season that included a 2.64 ERA and 11.1 strikeouts per nine innings. Still, his second-half fade that year had some curious whether he could keep it up. Those concerns were realized in 2025, when Hamm struggled to make the jump to the more hitter-friendly surroundings of Double-A Erie and the Eastern League. He regressed in virtually every statistic, and looked no better after missing more than a month at midseason with injury. Hamm has always been a unique pitcher as a pro with an over-the-top delivery, and part of his struggles in 2025 came from an alarming drop in velocity on his fastball. What had been firmly in the low 90s and approaching 94-95 mph at times dropped into the upper 80s for a stretch. That loss of heat had a trickle-down impact on his changeup. Without the base pitches to pound the strike zone and get ahead in counts, Hamm’s 12-to-6 curveball and sweepish slider became less of a worry for hitters. He could still get strikeouts with lesser stuff, particularly against right-handed hitters, but it took more work to get them. Hamm still has the potential to be a Major League pitcher, but he’ll need to add strength and durability to regain and maintain his velocity, especially if he wants to be a starter. If his struggles carry into 2026, his best fit might be in the bullpen, where shorter outings could help bring his fastball back.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Hamm entered 2025 as something of a pop-up prospect who had taken well to pro ball after the Tigers selected him from Middle Tennessee State. The big story for him last year was that he lost two ticks on everything, dropping from 91-93 mph with the fastball to either side of 90, with a corresponding dip in sharpness on everything else. Though he still survived Double-A, practically every number went the wrong direction. Hamm didn’t see a meaningful innings increase nor any kind of velo shift on either side of a midsummer injury that knocked him out for a month, which means we don't really have the kind of satisfying explanation for the loss that would lead us to project a bounce-back. Instead, the softening of the curve in particular (which was graded plus last year) limited his ability to miss bats. Oddly, he’d have outings where it sat 79-80 and looked quite sharp, and others in which it stayed in the mid-70s and rolled like a 40. Hamm has always managed to throw strikes despite a high-effort delivery, but less wiggle room also exposed fringy command. It’s always possible that he gets that arm strength back, and with it the backend starter ceiling we forecast last year, but at this point, Hamm looks more like a depth arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Regarded as one of the top infielders of the 2025 international signing period, Johnson, a Nassau, Bahamas native, received a $1.5 million signing bonus from the A’s. His arrival to the organization comes with considerable hype, with some talent evaluators labeling him as arguably the Caribbean nation’s most polished prospect to ever enter pro ball. Johnson is fully bilingual and has been training with Jose Fortuna, which afforded him the opportunity to play in the United States and the Dominican Republic. Joining his brother, Paris -- a current member of the Dodgers organization -- in the pro ranks, Johnson will get his career started in 2025. Johnson is a bat-first prospect. He has a clean setup at the plate from the right side and utilizes a quick and crisp bat path, which leads to spraying the ball to all fields. He hunts for his pitch and looks to do extra damage, and the power should start to show up as he continues to grow into his 6-foot-2 frame. Johnson is not a burner but his speed is solid. While some evaluators see him as an eventual third baseman, the A’s will get him plenty of reps at shortstop, where he is considered a steady defender up the middle, to begin his journey as a professional.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Johnson was the best Bahamian prospect in the 2025 international class, a powerfully built youngster with the look of a D-I running back prospect who signed for $1.5 million. He worked out for teams at shortstop, but at his size he was a pretty good bet to move to third base, and indeed Johnson spent most of his DSL debut at the hot corner. He slashed .257/.414/.321 last year and K'd at a 27.1% clip, too much for the A's to bring him to the States in 2026. Johnson's bat speed and power projection are still exciting, but he needs to cut his strikeouts this season to retain prospect status for next cycle.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Marquis Grissom was a two-time All-Star and four-time Gold Glover across his 17 seasons in the Majors. His son headed to Georgia Tech to make it as a starting pitcher but didn’t produce high-quality results, leading to him being taken by the Nationals (the same organized that selected his dad as an Expo in 1988) in the 13th round as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2022. He’s been a reliever in the Washington system ever since and a dominant one at that. Grissom split 2024 between High-A Wilmington and Double-A Harrisburg, finishing with a 2.21 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 56 strikeouts in 53 innings. The 6-foot-2 right-hander’s best pitch is easily his 82-85 mph changeup. It gets roughly 10 mph separation off Grissom’s 92-95 mph fastball and also fades incredibly well to the armside, holding lefties at bat. Even right-handed hitters whiff on 49 percent of their swings against the changeup last season, per Synergy Sports. The fastball has just average life but can touch 96 when Grissom really needs it. A mid-80s slider gives him a breaker with gloveside action. Grissom struggled with strikes over longer outings as a collegiate starter but has reined that in as a pro. He can use the fastball to steal early strikes and then put batters away by getting them to chase over and over with the changeup. More fastball velocity would help his case to be a high-leverage reliever, but the cambio alone should help him punch his ticket to working out of an MLB bullpen. Considering when he was drafted, he might have more runway of development than a typical college relief arm anyways.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Grissom's dad played 17 big league seasons and was one of the steadiest big league hitters throughout the 1990s and early 2000s. He's still the most recent of just six total alumni of Florida A&M to play major league baseball, a short list that's unreal, pound-for-pound: Mudcat Grant, Hal McRae, Andre Dawson, Vince Coleman, Jimmy Everett, and Grissom. Young Marquis was the class of 2020 as a high school prospect at a Montessori school south of Atlanta and then an age-eligible sophomore after two years in Georgia Tech's rotation. He was moved into the bullpen as soon as he turned pro and ascended to Triple-A early this season on the strength of his changeup, which he hides in part because his delivery is funky for a guy with a pretty typical overhand arm slot. Grissom pitches off his changeup first and mixes in slightly below-average fastballs and sliders. His strikeout and walk performance has slipped as he's reached the upper levels, but he should be able to ride his changeup to a near-term up/down relief role.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Ozuna signed for $850,000 in 2025 as one of the more projectable righty-hitting power bats in the international class. He struggled in his DSL debut, slashing .211/.301/.311 and posting a sub-70% contact rate. But Ozuna's size — he's 6-foot-3 and has room for big strength on his frame — and explosive swing are too exciting to move off of him entirely after a bad debut. He will repeat the DSL in 2026 and needs to improve as a contact bat to remain on the list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ozuna was the latest standout to train at the Niche Baseball Academy in Santo Domingo North, Dominican Republic, where stars such as Juan Soto, Elly De La Cruz and others have trained at under Cristian Batista. Drawing rave reviews by those who watched him closely there, he came in at No. 16 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 50 International Prospects list for 2025 and signed with the A’s for $850,000 when the signing period opened in January. He got his feet wet in pro ball with 35 games in the Dominican Summer League but was limited production-wise because of a hamate injury. Listed at 6-foot-3 and 185 pounds, Ozuna is a presence that is hard to miss when walking through the A’s Dominican complex. He reminds some within the organization of a young Vladimir Guerrero Sr. in terms of how he looks standing in the box for batting practice. His physical attributes lend to impressive power as a right-handed hitter that could reach plus-plus levels as he continues growing into his body. Ozuna’s cannon of an arm and natural athleticism gives him a shot at being a decent defensive right fielder. The obvious question here is whether he will make enough contact to fully unleash that tremendous raw power. The A’s are hopeful that he will come back this year in a healthier form and continue his valuable development time as a teenager.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hainline spent two seasons at Washington State before transferring to Oregon State, where he formed a double-play combination with No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana in 2024. A below-slot seventh-rounder that July, he played at all four levels of the Dodgers system in 2025, counting the Double-A Texas League playoffs. He earned All-Star honors in the High-A California League and played well enough during an emergency Triple-A assignment in June that the Oklahoma City coaching staff wanted to keep him. A right-handed hitter, Hainline has a good eye at the plate but swings and misses at strikes more than he should, especially against non-fastballs. His sneaky raw power and ability to turn on pitches could translate into 15 or more homers per season, though he produces more groundballs than are desirable. He hits the ball consistently hard but needs to improve his quantity and quality of contact. Hainline has average speed and good instincts on the bases, and he swiped 31 bases in 39 attempts (79 percent) last year. He played shortstop, second base and third base and his glovework earned differing reviews from inside and outside the organization. The Dodgers see him as a solid defender with arm strength to match, while other scouts grade him as more average in both regards.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: The duality of man is a universal concept, but Hainline embodies it better than most. He was the double play partner of 2024 first overall pick Travis Bazzana at Oregon State, but largely slid under the radar and signed with the Dodgers for $50,000 less than his seventh round slot value. Despite a medium build, he has at least average raw power and posted a 44% hard-hit rate in his first full year, but his swing plane doesn't lift the ball (eight homers in 111 games). Hainline’s swing is level but grooved, and he works around a below-average contact rate by almost never chasing — just 21% (!!) in two-strike counts — which shook out to a .288/.417/.418 line across two levels of A-ball and a brief Triple-A cameo last season. It’s rare to turn below-average hit and power into a regular, and the Dodgers have already begun bouncing Hainline all over the diamond, but his range and arm portend a shaky fit outside of second base (though Hainline's defensive metrics are nuts). There’s some genuine ability here, as Hainline's approach is real and not just passivity against wild low-level pitchers, but his defensive foibles make him an atypical utilityman fit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonzagni worked just 23 1/3 innings in two seasons at Weatherford (Texas) JC after coming back from Tommy John surgery, then operated mostly out of the bullpen after transferring to Southern Illinois in 2023. The Rangers thought he had one of the best sinkers in that Draft and selected him in the 12th round. In his first full pro season, he compiled a 3.64 ERA with 95 strikeouts in 89 innings between two Class A stops. Bonzagni’s two-seam fastball operates at 92-94 mph and tops out at 96 while burrowing at the plate, and its heavy sink is the reason why he posted an excellent 2.0 groundout/airout ratio in his first two pro seasons. He also throws a four-seamer that reaches 98 mph with more armside run and carry. He gets good depth on a sweeping low-80s slider, giving him a solid second offering. A good athlete, Bonzagni repeats his simple side-step delivery and provides a steady stream of strikes. He has yet to show much feel for his too-firm changeup in the mid-80s and almost never uses it. He’ll project more as a sinker/slider multi-inning reliever unless he can refine his cambio, but he might advance quickly in that role.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: A 12th-rounder in 2023, Bonzagni was an arrow-up arm heading into 2025 but missed most of the season with elbow inflammation. That’s scary for anyone, particularly a guy who missed significant time in college recovering from Tommy John surgery. When he’s on the bump, Bonzagni is primarily a sinker-slider guy. He touches 98 and has generated a ton of grounders at the lower levels. He’s a slow-twitch guy and not especially deceptive, and between that and the injuries, I'm skeptical he'll be able to start. He projects as a groundball specialist reliever, and has the ceiling of the 22nd or 23rd guy on the roster.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Palmquist’s deceptive, low-slot attack didn’t translate in his first big league stint. He both nibbled (25 walks in 34.1 innings), and surrendered a ton of hard contact when he did find the zone (45 hits, 10 homers). His fastball and cutter in particular got walloped to the point that it’s hard to project him as more than a low-leverage option. His sweeper and change are both above average, though, which gives him a way to attack both lefties and righties in some sort of role if he leans on them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palmquist threw well as a reliever in his first two years at the University of Miami, and when his move to the rotation in 2022 was successful, his name ran up Draft boards. The Rockies took the left-hander in the third round of the Draft that July, and he pitched his way to Triple-A exclusively as a starter in 2024. He made his big league debut in 2025, making seven starts (nine outings total), then had a not-so-smooth transition to a relief role back at Triple-A for most of the year. The left-hander's key attributes are still his deception, funky delivery and extension. His fastball continues to sit around 91 mph, maxing out at 94, and while it was effective at the lower levels at missing bats coming from his low arm slot, it got pounded in the big leagues. His 74-75 mph sweeper has the chance to be an out pitch, especially if he can find a little more velocity for it, perhaps becoming a kind of slider-monster-type reliever. Then he could mix in his harder cutter more effectively. Palmquist also hasn't been able to be around the strike zone as consistently as he was early on in his pro career. The Rockies had hoped they could give him time to adjust to a relief role, learning how to bounce back in consecutive games and pitching in close contests. That never really transpired, so he'll give it another go in 2026, with perhaps a multi-inning role the best option in the future.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Naylor had a lackluster offensive season in 2024, posting an OPS of just .643 while punching out at a 35% rate. Even more of a red flag, Naylor also carried a 35% in-zone swing-and-miss rate on the year, which speaks to his inability to manipulate the barrel to cover multiple quadrants. Naylor’s bat speed still warrants above-average marks, but a stiff lower half hinders his ability to rotate explosively and forces him to use only his hands to move the barrel around. On the defensive side, Naylor has been playing shortstop. His hands are soft, but again, stiffness in Naylor's lower body hinders his mobility and range; ideally, he'll improve in this area while he's still feasibly young enough to do so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest Naylor to join the professional ranks, Myles is hoping to follow the Major League path of older brothers Bo and Josh. He signed for $2.2 million with the A’s as a Competitive Balance Round A pick (39th) out of St. Joan of Arc Catholic Secondary School (Mississauga, Ontario) in the 2023 Draft and was aggressively moved to Single-A Stockton after just two games in the Arizona Complex League to begin his pro career. After struggling a bit more than the A’s were expecting, he spent the entire 2024 season at Stockton and hit .192 with a .643 OPS, 11 homers, 17 doubles and 58 RBIs in 116 games. Naylor’s legitimate raw power stood out through the scouting process, though his bat was considered less polished than Josh and Bo at the time they were drafted. While his bat speed is impressive with a smooth extension and follow-through, the A’s believe he may have been too caught up in seeking outside advice when it came to hitting last year. He still drew a fair amount of walks, but the overall result was a tendency to sell out for power to the pull side and continued swing-and-miss issues, especially with breaking balls. This offseason, they remained in close contact with Naylor to discuss a change in approach and believe the two sides are now on the same page in terms of who he needs to be as a hitter. What was once considered average speed is starting to slow down as Naylor grows into his 6-foot-2 frame. While he was drafted as a shortstop and has played mostly short and some second base as a pro, the A’s acknowledge he will likely be moving to third base in 2025. He has a strong arm, but his 27 errors last year highlight the need to improve as a defender. Time is certainly still on his side as are the Major League bloodlines, though he will have to put that hopefully improved approach to use this upcoming season.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Gordon began his draft year in Clemson's rotation but was moved to the closer role toward the end of March. He stretched out to five innings (and struck out 10) again at the very end of the season for a postseason game against Florida, and at his size (a wispy, loose 6-foot-5), there's a chance he can be stretched out again in pro ball. Gordon sat 95 as a reliever and 92 as a starter in 2024, and his mid-80s slider is his secondary weapon of choice, with a slower curveball occupying most of the rest of his repertoire. He has a collection of average pitches, with great long-term physical projection for a college prospect. There are many developmental avenues that Gordon's career might take, but he's pretty likely to wind up a lower-leverage member of a pitching staff pretty quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A South Carolina high school standout who stayed nearby to go to Clemson for college ball, Gordon was an outstanding reliever for the Tigers as a freshman, then spent his sophomore year in their weekend rotation. He lost his starting gig as a junior, though he did get into a bit of a groove closing games, finishing with 11 saves. The Angels sent him out as a starter in his first full season after taking him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft and he missed bats and limited walks, but he got hit over the course of the year with High-A Tri-City. Gordon has a potential four-pitch mix coming from a 6-foot-5 frame, ingredients to be a starter long-term if things click. Nothing in his repertoire is better than average at present, limiting his ceiling. He’ll typically throw his fastball in the 92-93 mph range, occasionally touching 96-97. He still has two breaking balls -- a mid-80s slider and upper-70s curve -- and both can miss bats but don’t profile as true out pitches. He still doesn’t throw the mid-80s changeup he has very often. Gordon can fill up the strike zone, walking just 2.9 per nine during his pro debut. It’s definitely control over command, and he often got too much of the zone, with Northwest League hitters combining for a .260 average against him. There’s a starter profile in there, but he’ll have to improve his secondary offerings to get to the big leagues as a back end of a rotation type.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Even after holding his own against SEC competition his junior year at Oklahoma and during an effective, if sloppy, pro debut season, Davis doesn't wow you with his raw ingredients. He’s a compactly built lefty who sits 90-94 from a higher slot, doesn’t produce a lot of raw spin, and has one of the shortest strides in the minors. Even the action on his signature changeup doesn't stand out, though the level to which it perfectly mirrors his rise-and-run heater with 11 ticks of separation might be the key to its bonkers 60% miss rate. The angle that his slot and stride create for his slider allows it to perform like an average pitch and has kept his reverse splits from growing too severe. It was definitely too sophisticated for low minors hitters last year, as Davis toyed with Low- and High-A opponents alike to the tune of 153 strikeouts in 110.1 innings in his debut season. But while his fastball played just fine in the zone, he was surprisingly bad at locating it. The 44.6% in-zone rate on his two-seamer is something you really only see from relievers at this level, and Davis really struggled to get anything to the glove side while running a 16.6% walk rate. The polish on his secondaries makes Davis a good option to continue developing as a depth starter, but it won't really work if the 30-grade control persists.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis worked out of the Sam Houston State bullpen for two years, got a taste for starting in the Cape Cod League in 2023 and transferred to Oklahoma for the '24 season. He posted a 4.30 ERA with 117 strikeouts in 92 innings during his time in Norman, and the Cardinals took him in the fifth round that summer before signing him for $485,700. He led all Cardinals farmhands with 153 strikeouts and finished with a 2.85 ERA over 110 1/3 innings between Single-A Palm Beach and High-A Peoria last season. The 5-foot-11 southpaw picked up velo from his days as a Sooner and sat 90-94 mph with his fastball, touching as high as 96.9 in the Florida State League. There was a ton of ride and run on the pitch that lower-level hitters just couldn’t handle. But its below-average velo also comes with below-average extension, and it’s likely that more experienced bats will read it better. Davis’ best pitch is a killer 80-82 mph changeup that had a 61 percent whiff rate across both levels. It moves much like the heater and has only a smidge less spin, but the velo differential fooled batters and led to dominance against righties. A low-80s slider also showed some depth as an option moving gloveside, and a mid-80s cutter bridged the repertoire. As untouchable as he could be in terms of hits and strikeouts, Davis struggled to stay in the strike zone consistently, and his 16.6 percent walk rate was the highest among any Minor League full-season qualifier. He can pitch like he’s trying to be fine at the corners, only to miss with uncompetitive pitches. The reverse splits and nasty changeup still make him intriguing, but the lack of control could shorten his leash as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: All of the Giants' best prospects from their 2023 international class were bargains: Keyner Martinez ($10,000), Carlos Gutierrez ($32,500), Luis de la Torre ($10,000) and Diaz ($50,000). The Cuban-born Diaz made the jump to Single-A at age 18 in 2024 and returned there last season to help San Jose win the California League championship. He batted .269/.320/.405 and topped the circuit in hits (139) and doubles (32). Diaz tries to do too much at the plate, chasing all types of pitches out of the zone and trying to yank them all to left field. The right-handed hitter somewhat makes up for those flaws with his ability to put the bat on the ball and generate high exit velocities when he makes contact, and he could develop 20-homer power if he tones down his approach. He crushes fastballs but flails against breaking balls, so he's going to have to make adjustments. A solid runner, Diaz enhanced his value by improving his basestealing aptitude and proving he could play center field in 2025. Mostly a corner outfielder in the past, he has good instincts and can remain in center going forward. His strong arm helped him notch 25 assists in 212 outfield starts during his first three pro seasons.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Diaz is a fairly projectable 19-year-old outfielder with good spreadsheet stats — 13% swinging strike rate, 84% in-zone contact, 74% overall, 109 mph max exit velo — for a hitter his age. He raked his way from the Arizona complex to the Cal League in the second half of 2024 and held his own, with a 103 wRC+ across 55 games at San Jose. The combination of Diaz's tendency to chase and his bat path (which I think will leave him very vulnerable to soft stuff in the bottom of the zone) is what's stopping him from ranking higher on this list, as I fear a strikeout uptick looms. But for a relatively projectable 6-foot-2, he's on time to pull fairly often and he has a great arm. There's enough to like here to consider Diaz a prospect, but aspects of his swing and underlying chase data serve as a warning not to take his other stats at face value.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Martin is an athletic, undersized five-pitch righty with a vertical low-90s fastball and a panoply of breaking balls. He'll sit 94-95 early in outings, then settle into the 92-95 mph range throughout the bulk of his starts. Though this pitch has nearly perfect vertical shape, it lacks explosive movement and has been vulnerable to contact throughout Martin's career. He can vary the shape of his breaking balls across a roughly 15-mph range, with an upper-70s curveball, mid-80s slider, and upper-80s cutter all playing a role in his mix. None of them are plus, but they're all distinct in both shape and velo. The cutter and curveball induce weak contact, while the slider is Martin's best bat-misser. He's just about to turn 21 and looks like a spot starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A North Carolina prep product, Martin planned on going to East Carolina to play shortstop until Los Angeles spotted him on the mound at the end of his 2022 senior season, drafted him in the 17th round and signed him for $125,000. His stuff made a jump in his pro debut after he focused on pitching full-time, but an offseason car accident and other outside factors led him to regress physically in 2024. He got off to a poor start in High-A last April, necessitating a month to recalibrate at the Dodgers' training facility in Arizona, Martin's best pitch is a tight upper-80s slider that elicits plenty of chases and empty swings, and he trusts it and uses it more than a fastball that parked at 92-94 mph last year and peaked at 99. His heater has some carry but is fairly straight and gets pounded when he doesn't locate it well. He's still developing feel for a mid-80s changeup with some depth and has mostly shelved an upper-70s curveball. Martin has a quick arm and works with an up-tempo delivery that creates some deception. Though he's just 6 feet tall, he has the athleticism and strike-throwing to succeed as a starter if he can refine his fastball command and changeup quality. Added strength and durability would help as well.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Recruited by Georgia Tech to play football but committed to Mississippi State for baseball, it took $2.75 million for the Mets to coax Houck to pro ball. In his first full season, he struggled badly at Low-A St. Lucie, where he struck out 36.3% of the time and hit .206. Tasked with repeating the level in 2025, he hit for power early in the year and cut his strikeouts enough (28.7%) to force a promotion to Brooklyn, where his strikeouts again spiked and he hit .198 during the second half. Houck is allergic to spin, and whiffs at roughly 50% of the breaking pitches he offers at, which nerfed his overall contact rate to 65% in 2025, down in Gabriel Arias territory. That's the sort of player Houck projects to be. He's still fairly projectable at 21 years old, he has roughly average raw power and should grow into more, and his pull-oriented approach allows him to get to power when he makes contact. Still, Houck probably can't make enough of it to be a consequential player and is looking at a fringe 40-man future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Houck was a two-way star at Parkview HS in Liburn, Ga., the same school that produced Matt Olson and Jeff Francouer. He threw for 2,189 yards as a senior quarterback, earning Power 5 football offers along the way, and was named Gatorade’s Georgia Player of the Year for baseball. The Mets selected the Mississippi State commit with the 32nd overall pick in 2023 and signed for him above slot at $2.75 million. Houck spent his entire first full season with Single-A St. Lucie but struggled with the jump to full-season ball, hitting just .206/.304/.306 with five homers and 171 strikeouts in 112 games. Houck’s 171 K’s were tied for third-most among Single-A batters, and his 36.3 percent K rate was fourth-highest among qualifiers at the level. The punchouts came in a variety of ways. On one hand, the right-handed hitter couldn’t handle breaking and offspeed pitches, whiffing on 53.9 percent of his swings against secondaries. On the other, he had 59 called third strikes because of his passivity; no one else in the FSL had more than 42. When he did make contact, there was still decent pop in there for his age and experience level. An average runner, Houck has plus arm strength, and that helps him on the left side of the dirt. He remains a work in progress defensively, however, and saw time at third base earlier than expected. He can rush plays at the corner, either forcing him to bobble on a transfer or throw inaccurately.
