Houck will be 20 for the entire 2025 Minor League season, making him the age of a college sophomore, but he needs to prove he can adjust off these early issues to get anything close to the potential he showed heading into the 2023 Draft.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Plus-plus raw power gives Bitonti a puncher’s chance to profile as a dangerous bat off the bench, though his propensity to swing and miss may expose him well before that point. He’s a slower twitch guy with a long swing, a tough blend for a stiffer athlete with limited ability to adjust his bat path and front side leak that pulls him well off the plate. He’s a good example of a player whose measurable bat speed (max velocity, which is high in Bitonti’s case) differs considerably from his bat speed in the way scouts have traditionally used the term (more like time from first move to contact point, which is slow). The data is alarming as well. Bitonti's swing-and-miss rate on fastballs up is sky high for a big leaguer, much less someone facing A-ball velocity, and he also struggles to read soft stuff out of the hand. He’s young and his prodigious pop gives him runway, but this isn't going to work if he can’t make considerably more contact. Bitonti will really need to hit, too, as he’s basically first base-only now and not especially spry around the bag.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 35 | Power: 60 | Run: 40 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 The Brewers took Bitonti out of the California prep ranks in the third round in 2023 when he was only 17 years old, signing him away from an Oregon commitment for $1.75 million, more than double slot value. He showed promise out of the gate with 16 homers (the second-most by a Minor Leaguer age 18 or younger) and a 147 wRC+ in 79 games between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Carolina in 2024 but came back to down to earth with a return to the Carolina League a year later. Bitonti hit .238/.341/.421 with 19 homers in 118 games with the Mudcats in ’25; his 33.5 percent strikeout rate was fourth-highest among Single-A qualifiers. Standing 6-foot-5, Bitonti cuts a massive figure from the left side of the box. He uses that size to generate big bat speed that comes primarily from his upper body, considering he only relies on a toe tap for the bottom half of his load. The levers in his swing create a lot of length despite the sheer velocity of his hacks, and he can run late on pitches, even fastballs in the zone. When he does make contact, it’s loud and often in the air to the pull side, giving hope that he could be a future 30-homer slugger. Originally taken as a shortstop, Bitonti has slid down the defensive spectrum since with some time at third base in 2024 and then primary duty at first in ’25. He makes for a big target there and still retains arm strength that will help on throws across the diamond. Bitonti will only be 20 for the duration of the 2026 season, but adjustments will have to come quick if he’s to power his way up the chain.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Rucker's pro career hasn't been able to get off the ground, as the high school draftee only played during 2024 extended spring training and a couple of FCL games before he tore his right labrum sliding into a base. He is a projectable infielder who was signed away from a Tennessee commitment for $772,500 in 2023. Rucker has a strong top hand that generates impressive pull power when his swing is on time, though his lever length may not always allow for that in pro ball. His present power and long-term power projection are his carrying tools, while his relatively grooved swing creates some hit tool risk that will prove more concerning if Rucker outgrows shortstop. For now, he's a raw developmental infielder with a shot to have corner-worthy power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Twins prospect Jake Rucker, Carson was a two-time winner of the Mr. Tennessee award as the state’s top prep baseball player. He seemed poised to stay in the state and play collegiately at Tennessee like his older brother, until the Tigers selected him in the fourth round of the 2023 Draft and signed him above slot for $772,500. Injuries have stalled his career since then, including labrum surgery on his left shoulder last summer that limited him to 13 games at the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. Rucker earned his status on Draft boards with right-handed pull power but has had precious few opportunities to show it as a pro. The pull-heavy approach is still apparent, along with a good eye at the plate. Though Rucker has been primarily a shortstop when he has played, he is expected to eventually shift to third base. The Tigers still believe in Rucker’s potential despite the injuries. He’ll turn 21 in August, but in many ways, 2025 is an introductory season for Rucker to develop an everyday routine as a pro player.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: There’s always been some stiffness to how Hales’ lower half operates in his delivery, as well as some late violence to his low-slot arm action, and those factors seemingly conspired against him across a difficult 2025. Hales was traded to the Cardinals as part of a package for Phil Maton in the middle of a rocky transition to Triple-A that ultimately saw him run an ERA over 8.00 ERA in 27.1 IP at the level, and Memphis was only slightly more kind than Round Rock for his dinger problems. He touched 99 mph and ran up a miss rate north of 30% with his four-seamer thanks to his low slot, but as is often the case from that release point, his secondaries have underperformed despite seemingly average or better ingredients. Hales is operating with mostly just his fastball and slider as a pure one-inning reliever, but the latter lost some drop and effectiveness compared to 2024. It looks more like an up/down profile heading into his 40-man platform year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 40 | Slider: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 The Rangers made Hales the third reliever taken in the 2023 Draft, selecting him in the fourth round out of Santa Clara. He finished his pro debut in the High-A South Atlantic League playoffs, then advanced to Double-A midway through his first full season before getting some extra work in the Arizona Fall League. He could reach the big leagues in 2025 if he can find a reliable pitch to complement his fastball, which can be unhittable at times. Hales turns to his heater about two-thirds of the time, operating at 94-97 mph and reaching 100 with tremendous carry and deception as well as some armside run. His mid-80s slider is his most trusted secondary pitch and features sharp horizontal action at its best, though it doesn’t result in many chases or empty swings. He got roughed up in the AFL while fiddling with a low-80s curveball he couldn’t throw for strikes and an upper-80s cutter that didn’t fool anyone. Hales works from a low slot with a short arm action in back, and his mechanics allow his fastball to get on hitters more quickly than they expect. He has a history of filling the strike zone when he comes out of the bullpen, and his competitiveness contributes to his ceiling as high-leverage option.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Nankil was the A’s seventh round selection out of Cal State Fullerton in 2023. His frame is lean, with room for additional strength in the coming years. He split the season between both A-ball affiliates, posting an .862 OPS with 11 homers and 39 extra-base hits. Nankil’s bat path has loft to it without sacrificing how long his bat stays in the hitting zone, but he has average bat speed. He’s limited to the corner outfield positions, where he projects to be an average defender. Because he lacks a true outlier offensive tool, he projects as an up/down role player in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nankil was a seventh-round selection by the A’s out of Cal State Fullerton in the 2023 MLB Draft as part of a class headlined by No. 6 overall pick Jacob Wilson. After a strong first full professional season, he began 2025 at High-A Lansing and ended with Double-A Midland, combining to hit .278 with a .724 OPS in 124 games. Nankil’s overall approach at the plate is solid, having shown a good ability to draw walks and limit the strikeout totals at a decent rate. His raw power excited the A’s when he entered the organization, but that aspect of his game has yet to fully show through. While he does hit the ball hard, he tends to hit the ball on the ground too often. He also has some trouble picking up on offspeed pitches at times. Nankil is an average defender who can cover a decent amount of range in the outfield with his athleticism, while also bringing a strong arm. He ideally profiles as a corner outfielder, but he will have to hit for more power to continue progressing through the system. The A’s believe he has at least 20-homer power potential, and they plan to work with him on getting the ball in the air more to try to unlock some more of that pop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top high school left-handers in the 2021 Draft, Coppola went undrafted because he was strongly committed to Florida. He struck out 38 percent of the batters he faced with the Gators, but he also worked just 49 1/3 innings in four years because of back and shoulder ailments. After the Cubs made him a seventh-round pick last July, he fanned 14 in eight innings at Single-A. Coppola uses his huge 6-foot-8 frame and a low arm slot to create wide angle on his fastball, which sits in the low 90s and tops out at 96 with carry and armside run. He could have more velocity in the tank if he can stay healthy and add strength. He also operates with an upper-70s slider with sweep that made it unhittable in college, though it may need more power to succeed in pro ball. Though Coppola has toyed with a mid-80s splitter, he's mainly a two-pitch guy. He doesn't have a smooth delivery and doesn't repeat it well, which has led to injuries and below-average control. He'll begin his pro career as a starter to get some much-needed innings, but the likely best-case scenario is that he cleans up his mechanics and adds some power en route to a bullpen role.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Six-foot-eight and exceptionally broad-shouldered and long-levered, Coppola was a significant draft prospect back when he was a New Jersey prep standout, and despite covering less than 50 innings in three years at Florida thanks to back and shoulder injuries, he still got popped in the seventh round by the Cubs last July. His velocity and control have wavered a lot, as he walked nine in eight innings at Myrtle Beach after the draft last summer, sat 91-93 mph, and now has been stuck on the Development List all season. His arm action is long, his stride is a little short considering his size, he’s often late to the firing position, and his feel for his secondaries can abandon him. The fastball has missed bats like a 70-grade pitch even at diminished velocity, and his outlier frame makes him someone to watch, even if tagging his risk level as “extreme” doesn't feel extreme enough.

fangraphs.label: 2024updated
fangraphs.text: Gray got just shy of $1 million in the third round of the 2021 draft, then had TJ in 2022. Back in 2023, he struck out a little more than 33% of opposing hitters as he pitched 34 affiliated innings across 14 starts, working two to three innings per outing. In 2024, he's been more in the three to four inning range and is again missing a ton of bats, but he's also missing the strike zone. Gray has walked nearly 20% of opposing hitters since returning from TJ. His delivery has deception and a late arm stroke that he doesn't really have feel for repeating, and many of his pitches sail nowhere near the zone. He also hasn't quite retained his peak pre-surgery velocity: Gray's fastball has been sitting about 91 mph so far in 2024, a tick or two below the way he looked at his best. That pitch has enough riding life to play despite it's velo, and Gray's upper-70s slurve has plus break. It's reasonable to hope Gray will hone his control as he gets his footing in pro ball but probably not so much that he can start. He's looking more and more like a lefty relief prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray rated as Illinois' top prep prospect until he transferred to IMG Academy (Bradenton, Fla.) for his senior year in 2021, during which control issues and rumors of arm problems plagued him. Signed for an over-slot $900,000 as a third-rounder, he blew out his elbow the following February and required Tommy John surgery that sidelined him until mid-2023. He showcases an interesting arsenal but couldn't harness it last season in High-A, where he limited opponents to a .196 average and logged a 27.6 percent strikeout rate -- but also a 20.8 percent walk rate. While Gray's stuff was down about two mph across the board last year, he still missed bats when he was near the plate. Batters couldn't solve his fastball while it parked at 90-93 mph and topped out at 96 because it features quality carry and the extension in his delivery provides plenty of deception. The sweeping action on his upper-70s slider and mid-70s curveball made them difficult to barrel, though his fading low-80s changeup remains a work in progress. Gray also drew scouting interest as an outfielder in high school, is one of the best athletes in the system and throws without much effort. Yet he struggles to keep all the moving parts of his delivery in sync and when he misses the strike zone, he often does so by such a large margin that hitters aren't tempted to chase. He has the ingredients for mid-rotation starter ceiling, but will be ticketed for the bullpen if he can't improve his control.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text:
Olivar is performing offensively, which has been consistent through the 23-year-old Venezuelan’s professional career. He’s making an above-average amount of contact against Double-A pitching, pairing a strikeout rate around 15% with a solid-average batting eye and raw power. But his deep and late hand load suggests Olivar’s hit tool is less than the sum of its performance metrics, and he's had pockets of whiffing against upper-third fastballs and generally poor performance on velocity 93 mph and above. 
It would still be an intriguing mix of offensive attributes for a catcher, but Olivar’s future there remains murky. He’s continued to fill out into a downright stocky build. And while he’s shown some incremental progress in framing and blocking despite below-average mobility, his footwork is inconsistent and his throwing is frequently inaccurate. The Twins have him manning left field more and more, and though he’s not lost out there, his lack of foot speed will make it hard for Olivar to ever be an average left field defender. If he can’t stay behind the plate, there isn’t a carrying tool here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $20,000 in July 2019 in the same international period that brought Emmanuel Rodriguez into the organization, Olivar skipped over the Dominican Summer League following the long pandemic-related layoff and didn’t make his pro debut until 2021 in the Florida Complex League. That didn’t go well, but a repeat of the level in 2022 led to an MVP award and an OPS north of 1.000 for the summer. He hit well in a full season with Single-A Fort Myers in 2023 then continued to swing the bat well in 2024, reaching Double-A for the first time. A right-handed hitter, Olivar has made excellent progress at the plate over the past two seasons. He has the chance to perhaps be an above-average hitter, one who has kept the strikeouts in check while improving his overall approach and walking at a career 13.4 percent clip heading into 2025. Better swing decisions have continued to enable him to barrel up the baseball and get to his power more consistently. He can drive the ball to all fields, though his home run pop has come mostly to his pull side. His defense hasn’t come along as quickly as his bat, though the Twins do think he has the chance to catch in the big leagues. He’s a tireless worker who is bilingual, works with pitchers well and calls a good game. There’s still work to be done on his arm strength and receiving, but there’s hope it’s trending toward Major League average. He’ll continue getting reps in the outfield, with the versatility giving his bat a better chance of reaching the big leagues.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: After he started just one game as a freshman, Honeyman had a breakout sophomore year when he hit .329/.402/.506 during the college season and .289/.400/.530 on Cape Cod. He followed that up with a .304/.383/.534 line as a junior. Multiple injuries delayed and have slowed Honeyman's career, and even though he's approaching age 24, he only recently left Low-A Palm Beach for Peoria. He has a punchy fifth outfielder's profile featuring gap-to-gap doubles contact and speed. Honeyman's swing is like the SnackWell's version of Yermín Mercedes', with a deep crouch and leg kick that approaches' Honeyman's chest. He swings with a lot of effort and his hands have a fairly long path into the zone. Honeyman's contact rates have been a shade above average throughout his career, but he's always been old for his level. Honeyman isn't a great center fielder right now, but he's barely played there. Only during his sophomore season and again in 2025 has he mostly played center field. He certainly doesn't look comfortable right now, but he runs well enough to be given the opportunity to develop there. If he can, then he'll be a 40 FV type of bench outfielder; if not, he's on the 40-man fringe.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Honeyman enjoyed a breakout sophomore year at Boston College in 2022, one in which he posted a .908 OPS with only 16 strikeouts in 41 games and carried that straight into the Cape Cod League, where he caught additional eyes. He maintained his momentum as a junior with a .304/.383/.534 line through 39 games, but a shoulder injury ended his season early in May. The Cardinals took him in the third round and signed him for around slot at $700,000. Unfortunately, shoulder issues continued to dog Honeyman into pro ball, and he underwent surgery that limited him to 20 games in the Florida Complex and Florida State Leagues in what should have been his first full season. The lost season certainly doesn’t help Honeyman’s growth and development on the pro side, but the scouting report remains much the same until he proves himself more on the field. He bats with an open stance from the right side and swings his front leg forward with a kick to get his momentum moving forward. He can cover most areas of the plate with his bat-to-ball skills, even if he’ll occasionally expand the zone in search of contact. His pop was a work in progress in school but projected as average before the shoulder woes. Honeyman flashed plus home-to-first times during his brief Florida State League stint, and his wheels shouldn’t be affected by the time off. A throwing program was considered his last piece of rehab in his second offseason, and it’ll be worth monitoring how his arm strength holds up after the surgery. The former Eagle seems likely to move around the grass in his return, but the focus will be on getting on the field consistently in the first place.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Acquired as one of three players sent over from the Mets last deadline in exchange for Ryan Helsley, Dohm is a former third rounder who mostly pitched out of the bullpen at Mississippi State, and there’s a reliever-y feel to his 18-IVB four-seamer and short gyro slider combination. Yet he mostly started during his pro debut season, and mostly threw strikes until walking nine in 12.1 innings after the trade. Dohm has a good starter’s build and his 75 innings in 2025 represented a clear career high, so his control wavering down the stretch in a season that saw him post a 27.9% strikeout rate and 9.9% walk rate can mostly be shrugged off. There’s not much changeup feel here, though, and his velocity varied (91-96 mph) from the upper-90s he’s shown in short bursts. It’s a good fastball (27% miss rate) but probably not one that can quite prop up a starter profile without other plus ingredients. Dohm looks like a potential medium-leverage reliever at present.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dohm worked out of the bullpen at both Ball State and Mississippi State as a freshman and sophomore, respectively, before joining the Bulldogs rotation as a junior in 2024. A forearm strain slowed an otherwise hot start, but after re-establishing his health later in the spring and participating in the MLB Draft Combine, he went to the Mets in the third round and signed for below slot at $797,500. He put up solid numbers at Single-A and High-A to begin his first full season in 2025 and was moved to the Cardinals at the Trade Deadline as part of the return for closer Ryan Helsley. Dohm couldn’t find similar results at High-A Peoria after the deal and returned to the Midwest League to begin ’26. The 6-foot-4 right-hander shows a 93-96 mph four-seamer that can zip past batters at the top of the zone with impressive carry. He could reach 99 as a reliever in college in a sign that the pitch could be even more explosive in shorter stints if and when he needs to head back to the bullpen. His 83-86 mph slider can flash hard, late bite to get something move gloveside and similarly generate whiffs. He has much more trouble landing a changeup for strikes, and lefties have become a concern in pro ball without the third pitch. Dohm had started to show improved control as a Mets starter but hasn’t been able to replicate that in either of his Peoria stints so far. He needs batters to chase the high heaters and diving breaking balls to be effective, and that could be a challenge as he climbs. He has the chance for two above-average, bat-missing pitches though and could let them fly to their full potential with a move back to relief, if the control never comes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the younger players and considered one of the most advanced hitters on the 2025 international market, Cedeno received the largest bonus in the Yankees' class. After signing for $2.5 million out of the Dominican Republic, he endured a rough pro debut in the Dominican Summer League. He batted .183/.371/.305 and led the Rookie circuit with 76 strikeouts in 47 games. For someone who struck out 37 percent of the time in his first taste of pro ball, Cedeno has a surprisingly compact right-handed swing and relatively good bat-to-ball skills. His problems last summer stemmed from an overly passive approach that put him behind in too many counts and an extremely pull-happy mentality that leaves him vulnerable to pitches on the outer half. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to reach 15-20 homers per season provided he can overhaul his approach. Cedeno has plus speed and knows how to use it, swiping 21 bases in 23 tries (91 percent) last summer. He has fast hands and solid arm strength at shortstop, though his quickness translates into just average range. It's possible that he'll fit better at second base in the long, which would put more pressure on his bat.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Cedeno is a medium-framed shortstop with maybe the best infield hands in the class. His glove is like a frog's tongue, and he has an unbelievably quick exchange. His range, footwork, arm strength, and overall athleticism are all closer to average. Cedeno has some pull power on middle-in mistakes, but is otherwise more vanilla in terms of his bat speed and physical projection. He signed for $2.5 million in January, but realistically, he's utility fit without an obviously high ceiling.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Alabama transfer who barely played as a freshman then got actual playing time at Florida State in 2024 and 2025. Chase-prone lefty power bat. Much more physical than a typical center fielder and likely moves to a corner in pro ball. Incredibly strong hands. Generates plus raw power with basically no lower half involvement in his swing. Struggles to cover the top of the zone. Traditional low-ball lefty golf stroke. Lack of plate discipline and likely move to corner make Williams risky, but he's just shy of 21 on draft day and didn't play as a freshman. He has a corner platoon shot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams took off after transferring from Alabama to Florida State and hammered 33 homers with a .975 OPS across his sophomore and junior seasons. Known for his massive raw power and free-swinging approach, he was a natural fit for the Marlins in the third round of the 2025 Draft and signed for a below-slot $897,500. He finished the year at Single-A with a .269/.359/.284 slash line across 19 games. The lefty slugger can produce plenty of thump from a crouched stance as he fires his hands with impressive speed. Williams was able to succeed in college with an overly aggressive approach -- he chased all secondary pitches at least 40 percent of the time -- but will have to tighten that up in pro ball. Although the power didn't show up in his brief pro cameo, success in wood bat leagues while in college gives hope that it will come. He did make more contact than usual at Single-A and frequently walked, which will be key to his offensive profile. Despite being a solid athlete, Williams didn't use his average speed much on the bases in college. He'll play all three outfield positions but will be more suited for a corner long term unless he improves his routes. Williams' offense will drive his profile, so sticking in center would merely be a plus, and he could be an above-average defender in right with a strong arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Suárez was a big-time standout in his native Cuba before moving to the Dominican Republic three years ago. He was the youngest member of the silver-medal-winning Cuban roster at the U15 World Cup in Mexico in 2022 and upped his game by hitting .355/.495/.605 in Cuba’s U16 National League in ’23. Ranked as the No. 22 international prospect in the 2026 class by MLB Pipeline, Suárez signed with the Royals for $1,647,500 this past winter; only Angeibel Gomez ($2,797,500) signed for more with Kansas City this cycle. After heading to the D.R., Suárez trained with Javier Rodríguez in Santo Domingo East under the same program that helped develop Cubs outfielder Kevin Alcántara and Mets shortstop Elian Peña. The right-handed slugger, who will be 17 for the duration of his first Minor League season, has shown more pop as he’s matured, and that loud contact layers nicely over the impressive discipline he showed as a teenage amateur, though the latter will be tested against better arms on the pro side. Standing at 6-foot-1 already, Suárez could have an intriguing power-speed combination at full maturity if he holds onto his at least above-average wheels. His plus arm strength is his best defensive asset at this point, and it could help his case to stick at shortstop, where he has solid actions for now. If he needs to move over to third base, his slugging and throwing ability would make him a natural fit at the hot corner.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Another from Eric's 2026 international update: A physically mature Cuban shortstop, Suárez puts up good exit velos for his age, and he runs and throws well. He lacks the physical projection typically associated with a top-of-the-class prospect, and a utility outcome is more realistic for him long-term. He signed for $1.7 million this winter.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Fabian’s backstory and skills are likely familiar to most readers, so we'll recap this quickly: Fabian skipped the draft as a high school senior and put up big numbers as a freshman at Florida. After the COVID season, he swung and missed a ton as a sophomore, enough that he elected to go back to school rather than sign for second-round money. He performed a little better the following year, but was again selected in the second round. 
The concerns stemming from all those strikeouts have proven valid. Fabian swings hard and uphill, and even though he lowered his average launch angle a tick last year, he was still whiffing as often as ever. There’s real juice when he connects, but he looks like a mistake hitter with a grooved swing. Defensively, he’s a plus runner who flies around the outfield with abandon and can go get it in center, enough so that he could be a reliable roster fit even with a one-note offensive profile. Fabian is hitting .226/.377/.403 in Norfolk, with large walk and strikeout totals in line with previous seasons. He’s a ready-made low-variance fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fabian left high school early to enroll at the University of Florida and was a second-round Draft pick by the Red Sox in 2021, but didn’t sign. The Orioles nabbed him in Competitive Balance Round B the following year, signing the toolsy outfielder for a full-slot bonus of $1.03 million. He’s since flashed the exciting combination of power and speed that made him a marquee name in college, mainly by enjoying a 24-homer, 31-steal performance in his first full season. But he has also struggled against better pitching at every level jump and seriously slumped after reaching Triple-A for the first time down the stretch in 2024. Belying Fabian’s enviable tools is all the swing-and-miss in his game, which was once viewed as a stomach-able tradeoff to his power-speed upside. But Fabian’s inability to make consistent contact has severely cut into his upside as he’s reached the higher levels, due to an uppercut right-handed swing that struggles against pitches at the top of the zone. Fabian struck out in 33 percent of his plate appearances at Double-A and in 41 percent at Triple-A. All those whiffs undercut his ability to get on base and get to his power regularly in games. No such glaring holes sabotage Fabian defensively. His plus speed and strong instincts give him excellent range, and his ability to read fly balls and run efficient routes make him a plus defender in center field. He also possesses one of the stronger outfield throwing arms in the O’s system. Given the athleticism, baseball IQ and purse of loud tools, Fabian could be an impact player if he makes enough contact against quality pitching; if not, the swing-and-miss might limit him to a part-time player capable of providing a spark off the bench.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Acquired from Miami as part of the return for David Robertson at the 2023 trade deadline, Hernandez is a skills-oriented third catcher prospect with modest tools. Hernandez's throwing feel and accuracy are fantastic, and make him a threat to hose runners even though he doesn't have rocket arm strength. He starts to exit his crouch as the pitch is in flight, and can throw from weird positions if necessary. His ball blocking can be similarly impressive to the eye, but there's incongruity here between our visual evaluation and what teams' internal metrics say about how he performed as a ball blocker in 2025, which had him nearly 10 runs below average. There is agreement, however, about Hernandez's framing and pitch presentation, which is currently below average. 
Hernandez is a selective hitter who is usually on time to match fastballs from both sides of the dish, but slower breakers elude him. Vanilla bat speed from the left side limits his potential offensive impact to the occasional belt-high pull shot. A 40-hit/40-power combo on a switch-hitting catcher isn't all that bad. None of Hernandez's defensive issues are severe enough to move him out from behind the plate, and the things he needs to improve (framing, blocking) are common warts for catchers this age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez signed with the Marlins for $850,000 out of the catcher-rich nation of Venezuela in January 2021, and he was traded to the Mets in late July for reliever David Robertson while on his third campaign at a Rookie-level circuit in 2023. He closed out that ’23 campaign with a .476 OBP in the Florida Complex League before jumping to Single-A St. Lucie for the first time. He returned to the Minors’ lowest full-season level, where he slashed .271/.362/.359 with five homers in 98 games, and ended his age-20 season with 10 games for High-A Brooklyn. A switch-hitter, Hernandez evened out his splits pretty well in 2024, showing perhaps a tiny bit more slugging ability from his right side after previously displaying the opposite. He still controls the zone better as a lefty hitter, though he expanded the zone a bit too much against breaking pitches. Hernandez enters 2025 with a career .375 OBP in the Minors, and with his catcher’s eye, that will likely be his best offensive asset. He ran into strong 90th-percentile and max exit velocities in the FSL, but he still projects as a hitter who will scrape double-digit homers over a full season. Hernandez continues to draw strong reviews for the way he works with pitching staffs as a bilingual speaker, and early reports indicate he’s already looked much more in shape in order to be better prepared to catch nine innings night in and night out. His receiving can be solid already, and he’ll need to continue to work on his throwing accuracy as his caught-stealing rates have declined. Mets officials view Hernandez as a steady presence, and with his Rule 5 eligibility hitting next offseason, he remains on track as a potential backup MLB catcher.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text:
Morales arrived on Miami's campus with a ton of profile because 6-foot-3 infielders with plus power and arm strength don't typically make it to school. After a somewhat disappointing freshman season, Morales improved in each subsequent year and finished his career in Coral Gables with a god-like .408/.475/.713 line in 2023; he was drafted in the second round and signed for $2.6 million. 
Morales has already reached Triple-A but he's trended down the defensive spectrum and now plays much more first base than third (he isn't unplayable at third, but it isn't great). The length of his swing has made it tough for Morales to tap into any of his BP power in games. He struggles to elevate the baseball and is often late to the contact point, causing him to play pepper with the right field line. His swing length contributes to whiffs against fastballs, too, an issue that might become even more severe against big league arms. We're now going on two years of Morales' contact rate hovering on either side of 70%. His raw juice keeps him alive on the main section of this list in the hope that a swing change can allow him to get to enough of it to play a role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morales was a solid performer in his first two seasons at Miami but broke out even bigger with a .408/.475/.713 line and 20 homers as a junior in 2023. The Nationals were pleased to see him still available in the second round, took him there and signed him for $2.6 million. Morales’ first full season was limited by a serious left thumb injury, and he returned to Double-A Harrisburg briefly to begin 2025. After an early promotion to Triple-A Rochester, he hit .249/.330/.401 with 11 homers in 95 games at the Minors’ top level. A productive stint in the Puerto Rican Winter League (three homers in 15 games) helped buoy his stock heading into 2026. A hulking presence, Morales still brings the plus raw power that made him a college star. His 105.9 90th-percentile exit velocity and 48.8 percent hard-hit rate at Triple-A both rated above the Major League average and speak to his slugging ceiling. But when he did make contact, so much was on the ground or hit the other way because of a long swing that it kept his power from showing up as it should have in games. The same length also made him late on fastballs, leading to heavy whiffs on four-seamers, and he looked at times more ready to swing hard than to swing at good pitches. Morales looked like he was pulling the ball in the air more efficiently in PR this winter, a hopeful sign for his age-24 season. Though he has plus arm strength, he’s been trending toward first base since reaching Rochester. The Nationals plan to get him time at both corners but note that Morales could be more of a defensive asset as a big target at the cold corner, where the offensive bar to slug is even higher.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Signed away from a UC Santa Barbara commitment for a $1.9 million bonus in 2023, Schoenwetter has struggled to develop viable strike-throwing ability and remains in Low-A, where he's walking a batter per inning in the early going of 2025. The aspects of Schoenwetter's prospectdom that made him exciting in high school remain. He has a prototypical 6-foot-3 frame and one hell of a curveball, but the strikes have never been there. Schoenwetter's ability to spin a curveball gives him a shot to develop a great slider/cutter, and he'll occasionally throw a good one, but a lack of control limits that pitch's effectiveness and consistency. He's still just 20 years old, but he has yet to find his footing in pro ball and is now valued as more of a late-blooming flier rather than a high-upside prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds had the No. 7 overall pick and a Competitive Balance Round A pick heading into the 2023 Draft, giving them the sixth largest bonus pool, and they weren’t afraid to spread the money around. They went almost three times over slot in the fourth round to sign Schoenwetter away from his commitment to his hometown Santa Barbara Gauchos. It took a while for the Reds to see what they had on their hands as he headed straight into rehab mode in order to build shoulder strength after the Draft, eventually making his debut in the Arizona Complex League. Numbers aside, the Reds were thrilled he was able to make 18 healthy appearances and spend some time with full-season Daytona at the end of the year. This will be the first year Schoenwetter should be able to show if he can start reaching his potential. He does have three excellent pitches in his arsenal, with a fastball that sat 92-95 mph last year, playing up with good spin rates up in the zone. He has more of a true, hard power curve, thrown anywhere in the 78-84 mph range with good depth, and his 84-87 mph changeup features good fade and he sells it well with arm speed. All three offerings might grade out as average right now, but all three could be plus in time as he physically matures and gets more reps. He struggled a bit finding the zone during his debut, but that might have been the time away from competition as much as it was anything with his delivery, which does have a little effort to it at times. He still has the chance to develop into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Morfe wasn’t a headliner of the Orioles’ 2023 international class, signing for $207,500 out of Venezuela as an undersized right-hander, and he struggled to throw strikes in his Dominican Summer League debut later that year. But he made a big leap forward in 2024, proving quickly he was too good for the DSL in his second go-around there before finishing the year with four starts at Single-A Delmarva as an 18-year-old. He racked up 49 strikeouts over 32 2/3 innings across the two levels, the equivalent of 13.5 strikeouts per nine. Morfe surprised a lot of evaluators with his ascent last summer and has surprisingly high-octane stuff for a pitcher his size. He only stands around 5-foot-8 but can dial his fastball up near triple digits, and it consistently lives in the upper 90s. What Morfe lacks in height he makes up for in athleticism and flexibility, using those qualities in tandem with a whippy arm to generate velocity that belies his size. His two secondary offerings are both hard, too: a mid-80s sweeping slider that can miss bats and a low-90s changeup with fade. The change especially showed big improvement last summer, going from a fringy offering to a potential plus pitch. It’s an advanced arsenal in an unpolished package, as Morfe’s command remains a work in progress. That’s not unusual for a young power pitcher, and Morfe was better at throwing strikes last year than his stats might imply because they were skewed by one ugly blow up start at the very end of the season. His three plus pitches and bulldog mentality remind some evaluators of Carlos Martinez, but to reach that ceiling, Morfe will need to prove he can throw enough strikes and that his body can handle a starter’s workload.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Like fellow farmhand Esteban Mejia, Morfe throws exceptionally hard and has no clue where it’s going. Unlike his teammate, Morfe is a muscular, low-to-the-ground hurler with a comparatively easygoing delivery. His arm swing is short, the effort level isn't anything out of the ordinary, and he actually threw a tolerable number of strikes in the not too distant past; the 12.1% walk rate he posted in the DSL and Low-A in 2024 isn't bad for an 18-year-old with this kind of arm strength. 
Last season was a disaster, though, as Morfe walked or hit 36 batters in 21.2 innings. He made one similarly erratic start this year before hitting the IL with elbow pain. All of that sounds, and is, terrible. Still, Morfe is a 21-year-old with elite arm strength. Even if he needs elbow surgery, this is too good of an arm to drop off the radar entirely.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Liranzo trained with Fernando Tatis Jr. before signing with the Orioles for $500,000 as part of their international class, and raised his stock enough during his first year in the system to the point where he was targeted by clubs in trades the following winter. A solid showing in his pro debut as one of the youngest players in the Dominican Summer League gave him helium heading into 2024, but he lost most of the year to a knee injury. The younger brother of Tigers prospect Thayron Liranzo, Joshua’s tenacious style of play earned him a killer early-career nickname: “Animalito” (“Little Animal”). The bat is Liranzo’s loudest tool. He turned heads after signing by showing the potential for plus raw power, producing high exit velocities and barreling balls consistently for a young player. His bat speed and strength hint at the potential for plus raw power, and he’s drawn comps to Teoscar Hernández at the same age, only with better bat-to-ball and pitch-recognition skills. That package gives Liranzo a chance to develop into an average hitter with more reps and polish. His bat will carry him further than his legs, as Liranzo was a below-average runner before the knee issue. Liranzo signed as a shortstop, outgrew the position quickly and settled at third, where he has adequate arm strength to project as an average defender, assuming the knee problem doesn’t hinder his mobility. He’s still young and inexperienced, but with enough seasoning, Liranzo could still develop into an impact run-producer at the highest level.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Liranzo signed for $500,000 in the 2023 international class. He was very young when he signed, so even though an injury wiped away most of his 2024 season, he’s going to play most of this season as a 19-year-old in Low-A. 
Liranzo is a traits bet. He has big league physicality, with projectable power and enough athleticism to handle the left side of the infield. He takes a big, lofted hack and has the bat speed necessary to stay competitive on fastballs up, but there’s a lot of head movement and he tends to get off balance against soft stuff. Spin in particular presents a challenge, and he misses it a ton when pitchers execute low and away. How he learns to hit that particular pitch could well be the difference between Liranzo reaching the big leagues or sputtering out sooner, because there’s otherwise enough contact feel and power to project on him. Defensively, he’s playing all over the infield, and while we think he’s going to grow off of short, there’s no reason he can't play an average third base at maturity. He projects as a utility infielder with unusual thump for the job and an everyday ceiling at third base if he can find a way to battle the soft stuff to a draw.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing for $350,000 in January 2022, Plaz immediately raised the expectations bar by hitting .382 with a 1.206 OPS in 32 Dominican Summer League games. There were some bumps, both of the production and injury variety, when he came to the United States, though he did start to find his power stroke in 2024 when he homered 15 times in the Florida State League, albeit with a ton of swing-and-miss. The injury bug bit again in 2025 with a fractured finger on his left hand limiting him to just 66 games, though he made up for lost time and swung the bat well in the Arizona Fall League. When Plaz is healthy and squares up the ball, the right-handed batter hits the ball really hard. He was in the upper echelon of Florida State League hitters in terms of data like exit velocity, barrel and hard-hit percentages. In 2025, he even cut down his strikeout rate, which had been an issue, while sticking to a better overall approach. There’s plenty of power to spare and to all fields, but he’s going to have to learn better pitch recognition after a 40 percent chase rate last season. There’s work to be done for Plaz on the defensive side of things as well. He has plenty of arm for the position, but the consistency of his receiving has been lacking. His power bat might profile at first base, but there aren’t too many sub-6-foot right-right players at that infield corner in the big leagues.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Plaz is a strikeout-prone catcher with above-average power and a plus arm. He struggled in limited action on the complex in 2023, and then rebounded in 2024 with a .207/.302/.438 line and 15 bombs at Bradenton. Plaz is a maxed-out 5-foot-11 and isn't likely to grow into any more power, but he already has pretty good pop for a catcher. Whether or not he'll actually be able to get to it as he climbs the minors is another matter. His swing is bottom-hand dominant and pretty long for a guy his size, plus he's fairly chase-prone. He needs to improve as a pitch framer, but Plaz's arm strength is easily plus, and it would probably play better if his exchange were clean more often. He currently looks like a developmental second or third catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coba wouldn’t have popped on many radars as a $10,000 signing out of Venezuela in May 2024, and he was initially used out of the Tigers’ Dominican Summer League bullpen in his first season with rough results (14 ER, 11 BB, 14 K in 12 1/3 innings). He returned to the DSL as a starter in ’25 and was much more in control there. Coba has moved to the Florida Complex League this season for his first taste of affiliated stateside ball, and his early work in the Sunshine State has solidified his standing as one of the more intriguing young arms in the Detroit system. All three of the 6-foot right-hander’s pitches show promise. Coba can run his four-seamer into the mid-90s while generating 18-20 inches of ride, but right now, he can leak some of that velocity over the length of his outings. If he can continue to build strength and sit 94-96 rather than 92-95, the heater would become a true plus pitch. His 79-83 mph slider shows gyro shape, dropping more downward than to the gloveside, but it can play well off the heat running up and in on righties. His 83-86 mph changeup kills spin while showing similar armside run to the four-seamer except it tumbles more, leading to empty swings when it’s on. Coba throws with some energy on the bump -- the arm speed helps sell the changeup -- and when he misses, it’s because he’s yanking the ball a bit too much to his gloveside. Still, it was promising to see him cut his walk rate by more than half between his two DSL stints, and with three potentially above-average pitches in his arsenal, he’ll deserve more starting looks as he climbs the domestic ladder.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: After a walk-prone pro debut in 2024, Coba had a better second season, as he K'd a batter per inning and allowed a 1.38 WHIP and 3.41 FIP in 42 frames. He has a lightning-fast arm that generates good velocity for such a slender young pitcher, with his fastball in the 92-95 mph range. The shape of its movement is inconsistent, and it often features a rise/tail mix even though Coba's arm slot is very vertical on release, a sign he tends to pronate over top of the baseball, but at its best, it has plus life. Coba's gyro-style slider is also inconsistent, but both it and his changeup generated huge miss results in the DSL. His slider has slightly below-average spin and might not be a dominant weapon as he climbs, but Coba's arm speed gives his changeup big long-term ceiling. For now, he's an athletic arm-strength sleeper in the lower minors who is likely headed for the FCL in 2026.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The big splash, headline-grabbing international signings every year tend to happen right when the period opens in January. But sometimes hidden gems are found, and the Reds are hoping Villafana is one of them. Signed in July 2024 for $20,000, Villafana was older than most international prospects, signing at age 21. He made his brief pro debut after joining the Reds in the Dominican Summer League, then came to the U.S. and posted a nifty 42/9 K/BB ratio in the Arizona Complex League, though he also gave up 78 hits over 46 2/3 innings. Villafana has a legitimate three-pitch mix that he’ll throw to hitters on both sides, coming from a projectable 6-foot-4 frame that points to more in the tank to come. Coming from a three-quarters slot and upright delivery, his fastball typically sits in the 92-96 mph range, occasionally touching as high as 98. It doesn’t offer a ton of life, typically offering more horizontal than vertical break, and proving to be hittable in the ACL. He lands his 85-mph changeup for strikes consistently, getting above-average chase and a ton of groundballs with the cambio. His 82-mph gyro slider isn’t a super-high spin breaker, but it has a little sweep because of his arm slot and also elicits a good amount of chase. It’s an interesting package, with solid shapes for his secondary offerings and a clear ability to fill up the zone with all three pitches. The key to his success will be some kind of pitch design for his fastball to keep it away from barrels, especially as he starts to move up the ladder.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Villafana signed in the middle of the summer of 2024 and barely pitched with the Reds' DSL teams that year. Then, as an older rookie baller, he came to the U.S. in 2025 and led the complex roster in innings. Though Villafana's strikeout and walk rates were favorable, he gave up 78 hits in 46.2 innings, an indication that his fastball is hittable even though it's hard. His movement data corroborates this, as his heater has equal parts horizontal and vertical movement much of the time. Villafana is a projectable 6-foot-4 and might have more velo in the tank, especially if he moves to the bullpen eventually. He's an arm strength dev project toward the bottom of this system.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Born in Puerto Rico and raised for a bit stateside, Mercedes eventually settled in the D.R., where he became a prototypical right field prospect with plus potential power and arm strength. The Twins signed him for $1.7 million in January of 2022 and he had a raucous first pro season in the DSL, slashing .355/.420/.555 and swiping 30 bags. But Mercedes has struggled and required time to adjust upon each subsequent promotion, and still hasn't really gotten traction in full season ball. He has roughly average big league raw power right now at age 20 and it plays to all fields. Some of that is out of necessity, as Mercedes' front foot is often late getting down, and he's not on time to the contact point. He does a fair amount of his whiffing for this reason, too. He's tracking more like a short side platoon option with an extreme power-over-hit skill set.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since joining the Twins in January 2022 for $1.7 million as an outfielder ranked in the top 20 of that year’s Top 50 international prospects list, Mercedes has shown off some very impressive tools in fits and bursts. He put up good numbers in the Dominican Summer League after signing, but struggled during his U.S. debut in the Florida Complex League in 2023. A return to the FCL went extremely well a year ago, earning a bump up to full-season Fort Myers, but he struggled there in a very small sample size. When he’s locked in, Mercedes has looked like a very dangerous right-handed hitter. He has excellent bat speed with a ton of raw power to tap into when he sticks to a gameplan. In the DSL and last year in the FCL, he made better swing decisions, limited his swing-and-miss and worked counts well to draw a lot of walks. When he got his feet wet for 10 games in full-season ball, the strikeouts spiked. Mercedes was nursing a quad strain at the end of the year that likely hampered him. Injuries have held back his development, including a minor hamstring issue during his debut and a shoulder injury that plagued him in 2023 and at the start of the 2024 season. He’s slowed down a touch, but he’s going to keep seeing a lot of time in center field while his plus arm would work well in right. For now, the focus will be for him to put in a full, healthy season of at-bats.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hunt never found a full-time spot in the Mississippi State rotation during his four years in school, and after choosing not to sign with the Pirates as a 12th-rounder in 2022, he posted an 8.54 ERA as a reliever the following spring. He boosted his stock with a solid showing as Falmouth’s closer in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2023 and signed with Milwaukee as a nondrafted free agent in July. He broke out in a big way in his first full season of pro ball, moving from Single-A Carolina to starting spots with High-A Wisconsin and Double-A Biloxi. His 2.03 ERA and 0.93 WHIP each ranked fourth best among Minor Leaguers with at least 100 innings, while his 34.7 percent K rate placed fifth. The former Bulldog’s dominance stemmed from heavy slider usage last season. Hunt can wear out the low, armside corner with the 84-86 mph pitch that has gyro shape, dipping below bats at just the right moment. Hunt threw it almost half the time against righties, but the breaker was also effective against lefties, who batted just .163 against the hurler during the season. His 91-93 mph fastball (occasionally touching 96) doesn’t pop for velo but can work well at the top of the zone, especially to set up the slider. Hunt also works with an upper-70s curveball and a firmer mid-80s changeup. Hunt really struggled with control in college but was a control artist last season with a 6.2 percent walk rate. That will likely creep up if hitters can hold off against the sliders outside the zone, but the improvements have helped his case at reaching -- and sticking in -- a pro rotation as a potential future No. 5 in the bigs.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Hunt struggled to find a consistent role during his four seasons at Mississippi State. He was selected by the Pirates after his junior year but chose not to sign, then he really struggled as a senior and went undrafted. He pitched pretty well on Cape Cod that summer and signed with Milwaukee as a undrafted free agent. Hunt had a breakout first full season as a pro, during which he climbed to Double-A and was top five in the minors in K%, WHIP and ERA among pitchers with at least 100 innings. He's had a bit of a velo dip at Biloxi to start 2025 and is only sitting 90-91 mph. Hunt's mid-80s slider is his best pitch and has big vertical depth for an offering that bends in at 85 mph. It's a chase pitch versus righties and a strike-getter against lefties. Hunt can dial things down and throw more of a curveball at 77-79 mph, and his changeup has tailing action, but it lacks sink. It's the four-pitch mix of a deceptive spot starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The biggest acquisition for the Reds on the international market when the 2023 signing period was catcher Alfredo Duno, who received $3.1 million, and the organization gave a seven-figure bonus later in the period to ink Sheng-En Lin. Third on the 2023 bonus list was Alcantara, signed initially as a shortstop out of the Dominican Republic for $640,000 in January of that year. He performed well enough during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League to come stateside in 2024 and struggled with the Arizona Complex League assignment. A return to the level the year after paid dividends, and he earned a bump to full-season Daytona for the first time. The Reds saw enough to move him to High-A Dayton to kick off his age-20 season in 2026. Alcantara, an undersized infielder at 5-foot-9, is a right-handed hitter with an aggressive approach at the plate. After striking out over 36 percent of the time during his U.S. debut, he's worked to refine his approach, cutting down on his swing-and-miss considerably in 2025. He has gap-to-gap power right now, with some ability to impact the ball, and limiting chase and continuing to see pitches and draw walks should help him maximize his offensive potential. While he was signed as a shortstop and saw plenty of time at the premium position over the first three summers of his career, Alcantara doesn't have the range to stick there long-term. He has the arm strength for third, and he's splitting time between the hot corner and second base, which might be the best option for him should he settle into one position permanently in the future.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Alcantara is a 5-foot-9-ish quarter stick of dynamite whose swing is big, elaborate, and very powerful for a hitter of his stature. In his second ACL season, he cut his strikeout rate from a disqualifying 36.1% to a more reasonable 23.3%, which he sustained after a late-season promotion to Daytona. Built like a college running back, Alcantara is a patient hitter whose swing features a ton of movement. It's typical for hitters with these kinds of swings to end up with below-average contact output, and that's likely for Alcantara, but if he's walking a ton and getting to some of his impressive power, it'll be okay if he is striking out at an elevated clip. 
What will be important for Alcantara is to develop on defense. He's seen action all over the infield but was struggling to throw accurately from third base at the end of the season. The likelihood that Alcantara produces enough offense to be an everyday second baseman is low, and for now he projects as a bat-first utility guy whose profile features some risk that his bat-to-ball improvement is a level-repeating mirage.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Humphries is a handful to evaluate. He’s a tall, downhill thrower with a short stride and very high release. It’s an unusual look, but it hasn't helped his fastball, which, despite 19 inches of vertical break and playable velo, got whacked around by High-A hitters last season. Some of that stems from 20 present control and command: Humphries is just a fair athlete, and a violent head whack at release limits his ability to hit a region, much less a spot. While all that sounds untenable, the secondaries are good enough to salvage an otherwise messy profile. Distinct breaking balls both flash above average, and the change is a dandy with late fade and identical arm speed to his heater. 
Still, it won't matter if the Guardians can't find a way to get Humphries in the strike zone significantly more often. The 21-year-old walked 91 hitters in 96.2 innings last season, and even when he inevitably moves to a short-stint role, he'll need to make an adjustment in his delivery to reach competitive locations often enough to profile. We’re less concerned about his fastball issues — plenty of guys live and die with their offspeed these days — but his control isn't viable right now. That said, we're staying on a lefty with good stuff. We think there’s enough athleticism to dream on 40 control, and we still see a path to a middle-relief outcome, but the arrow is pointing down here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the Guardians went under slot to sign their first three selections in the 2022 Draft, they splurged on Humphries in the eighth round, giving him fourth-round money ($600,000) to convince him to forgo his commitment to Campbell. Early returns were positive in his first full season, as he showed his strikeout stuff in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, but the next two years were a wash. An illness caused him to lose significant weight in 2024, and he could not find his control in '25 and walked nearly a batter per inning. Humphries is starting to look like his old self again now that he's diligently grown stronger over the offseason and refined his delivery. While he used to have an extreme over-the-top delivery, he's dropped his release point to a high-three-quarters slot that still enables him to reach nearly 20 inches of induced vertical break on his fastball while also adding more armside run. The southpaw throws his heater about half the time and sits 91-93 mph -- he can reach back and touch 96 mph -- and the hope is that his added strength will help him maintain velocity late into the season. The North Carolina native has a pair of distinct breaking balls -- an upper-80s slider and high-70s curve -- that each have a chance to be plus. His changeup has rare vertical movement and pairs well off the fastball because of 10 mph of velocity separation. However, much of his value will come down to his control. After throwing strikes just 54 percent of the time in 2025, he's been consistently in the zone in 2026, thanks in part to a less effortful delivery and better direction to home plate. Humphries' stuff could play up in relief if the walks don't dissipate, but he has the foundation to be a mid-rotation starter, and Cleveland is likely to keep developing him in that role.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Lanky righty with exciting raw stuff and physical projection. Sat in the low-90s at the Combine, at times with natural cut. Has two 3,000 rpm breakers in an upper-80s cutter and low-80s slider. Slider has two-planed movement in the 82-84 mph range. Size, youth, projection (both skill and body) make Barr one of the best JUCO prospects in the 2025 draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Had things gone differently, Barr might now be a part of the University of Tennessee rotation. But the top junior college player in the 2025 Draft class threw well enough at Niagara County Community College, now known as SUNY Niagara, to catch the attention of the Twins. They went over slot in the fifth round to sign the right-hander for $762,500, making him just the second Thunderwolves player to go in the top five rounds, joining 2023 Brewers fifth-round pick Ryan Birchard. The 20-year-old Barr is a 6-foot-6 poster child for projection with some good now stuff. He can run his fastball up to 97 mph and it features very good life up in the zone. He has a pair of distinct breaking pitches with his slider and curve, and both missed a lot of bats en route to him dominating the NJCAA DIII level. His breaking stuff registers elite-level spin rates and his heater plays up because of spin on that as well. Barr has a loose, easy and athletic delivery, so there’s belief that he can improve what’s been spotty command and control. He’s on the raw side and as good as he is at spinning the ball, he hasn’t always had a feel for consistent grips. There’s a lot of upside here, given that he has plenty of room to fill out both his frame and his repertoire.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 40 | Slider: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 McDaniels only made three outings for Division II Mt. Olive in 2021 before needing Tommy John surgery, but the Dodgers signed him as an undrafted free agent in May 2022 as he was rehabbing on the recommendation of area scout Jonah Rosenthal. They didn’t get a full look at a healthy version of the left-hander until 2024, when he pitched across three levels and finished at Double-A with impressive combined numbers (3.19 ERA, .229 BAA, 10.3 K/9), mostly as a reliever. They did not, however, protect him on the 40-man roster and the Angels took him in the Rule 5 Draft in order to give him a chance to make their big league staff. A 6-foot-2 left-hander, McDaniels likely profiles best coming out of the bullpen, which he has done for most of his pro career. He typically sits 94-95 mph with his fastball, dialing it up to 97. He can spin two different breaking balls, with his 87-89 mph slider showing glimpses of being a potential out pitch, and he’ll mix in a slower curve as well. He’s shown a propensity for missing bats (10.5 career K/9 rate) and getting ground-ball outs (2.35 GO/AO). McDaniels doesn’t have pinpoint command but is generally around the zone and that could continue to improve the further removed from TJ surgery he gets. He did make seven starts to begin the 2024 season, and while Angels GM Perry Minasian talked about how hard it is to find good left-handed relievers following the Rule 5 Draft, he didn’t rule out giving McDaniels the chance to start down the road.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: McDaniels was selected in the Rule 5 Draft by the Angels in 2024, and pitched in a handful of games before left biceps tendonitis put him on the shelf. Upon his return, he was DFA'd and returned to the Dodgers; he spent the rest of the season with Triple-A Oklahoma City. He's predominantly a sinker/slider reliever with two above-average offerings. Fringy control/command have limited the lefty’s ability to consistently crack a big league roster, and both the length of his arm swing and the moving parts in his delivery suggest that he’s brushed up against the ceiling of his ability to throw quality strikes. The stuff is good enough for all of this to work in a mid-leverage capacity. Despite coming over the top, McDaniels gets pretty good run on his two-seamer, which should foster barrel-missing utility even if he’s not consistently hitting his spots. The slider misses bats when he runs it beneath the zone, and he should be able to do that enough to play some sort of relief role, possibly yo-yoing between Triple-A and the big leagues throughout his pre-arb years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Milwaukee’s 2024 international class came with a big seven-figure name in Jorge Quintana ($1.7 million) and a future Top 100 prospect in Jesús Made. Anderson’s $60,000 bonus out of the Dominican Republic barely would have registered from an outside perspective. But Brewers evaluators had Anderson down as an early breakout candidate, and he achieved that status by leading Milwaukee Dominican Summer League prospects in homers with eight (two more than Made) while slashing .283/.403/.512 over 201 plate appearances. His .916 OPS was fifth best by a Brewers DSL prospect since 2010. Anderson has impressed Milwaukee hitting instructors with his ability to stay balanced at the plate, especially compared to other teenagers with his level of pro experience. That helps his above-average power play in games already, and there could be even more coming as he continues to fill out his 6-foot frame. Anderson walked 14.4 percent of the time against often wild DSL pitchers but has seen that approach challenged more with an aggressive jump to Single-A Carolina this season. Anderson is a solid runner at this stage and swiped 15 bags in 19 attempts in 2024. He might slow down a touch as he matures, and he's already seen time in both center and right at this early stage of his career. He’s expected to head to a corner full-time as he joins clubs with faster players up the middle, and his arm strength and power would be fine fits in right.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Anderson has bat speed, gets to lift consistently, and could grow into plus power. That’s a good start, particularly for a guy who shows signs of being able to adjust off the fastball. His swing is grooved, though, and he tends to mishit a lot of what he reaches. An aggressive approach isn't doing him any favors, as both his swing and chase numbers are pretty scary for a hitter at his level. There’s a short-side platoon ceiling here if Anderson can find a way to hunt pitches in his bat path, but it’ll require a sea change in how he goes about his business.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A former catcher, Hall redshirted his freshman year at Division II Central Missouri and moved into the Mules’ bullpen as a sophomore with rough results (9.20 ERA in 14 2/3 innings) in 2024. He was showing signs of a big breakout as a junior starter, fanning 19 of the 62 batters he faced, before suffering an elbow injury that required season-ending internal brace surgery. He showed enough in that limited look for the Mets to take him in the sixth round and he signed for below slot at $297,500. Some evaluators believe that, if healthy, Hall could have gone closer to the third round based on his talent. He showed a four-seam fastball up to 98 mph in February before getting hurt, and he threw the pitch out of a low release height, generating a good vertical approach angle. If that velocity -- he was typically closer to the mid 90s early in starts before tapering off -- and movement hold, it could be a plus pitch at maturity. Hall also flashed some good low-80s sliders and upper-70s curveballs with promising depth, and he showed he could at least turn over a decent changeup. The 6-foot-3 right-hander is still very much finding his way as a pitcher, and the elbow surgery put his collegiate development on pause. Mets officials have praised how well Hall has tackled his rehab, and coming out of the Draft, they believe he has enough promising athleticism to deliver strikes and earn starting looks. Hall could be a fun pick to click if his stuff returns to form and holds up in his first taste of the pros in 2026.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Hall is a converted catcher who redshirted while he moved to the mound. He pitched just 29.1 innings total in two seasons at Division-II Central Missouri (they're the Mules), in part because he was a reliever his first year and in part because Hall blew out after four starts in 2025. He had internal brace surgery in the late-February/early-March area and should be back at some point in the middle of 2026. 
Hall is an exciting sleeper with great pure stuff. He sat 93-95 early in outings before backing into the low-90s with riding life and a pair of breaking balls spinning in excess of 2,700 rpm on average. He's slight of build, but he's tall, athletic, repeats a short arm action, and is so new to pitching that he's likely just scratching the surface of his abilities. He's one of the more fun sleeper arms in this system and should be a priority target for teams that might talk trade with the Mets at the deadline, because he's one of the org's higher-variance players.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Lantigua signed for just shy of $1 million in 2024 and slashed .263/.397/.395 in his DSL debut season, then hit .288/.433/.399 in the 2025 FCL. He has a well-rounded offensive skill set and a projectable frame. Lantigua isn't a lanky 6-foot-3 or anything like that, but he has a near ideal baseball build at a square-shouldered 6-foot-1. His showcase tools are currently average or below (he runs in the 4.3s home-to-first), but he has feel for the zone and barrel. He buttons fastballs to all fields and crushes lefties. Lantigua doesn't have a huge ceiling, but he could be a good part-time outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lantigua was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 42 prospect in the 2024 international signing class and joined the Mets for $950,000 out of the Dominican Republic when the window opened that January. He performed well in the Dominican Summer League with a .397 OBP and 123 wRC+ over 45 games in his signing year and continued to build on that as a Florida Complex League end-of-season All-Star in 2025. He hit .288/.433/.399 with three homers, 33 walks and 29 strikeouts in 49 games as an 18-year-old in his first stateside campaign. Given his projectable 6-foot-1 frame, Lantigua was expected to be power-over-hit, but to this early point in his career, he’s been quite the opposite as his K/BB ratio last year would attest. His 14.9 percent K rate and 17 percent BB rate ranked eighth and 10th among FCL qualifiers, respectively, but that will be tested when he faces full-season arms that can pitch in the zone more easily. Lantigua also hit 55.5 percent of his batted balls on the ground. Some have noted he’s begun to look more physical this spring, and that could mean the promised power is around the corner. Oddly, Lantigua performed better against fellow righties in the FCL (.900 OPS) than lefties (.584), though the latter came in a much smaller sample. Lantigua hasn’t been an efficient baserunner to this point and went only 13-for-23 in steal attempts in the FCL last year. He’s been a primary center fielder, but if he slows down as he adds bulk (as he’s expected to), then he’ll slot into a corner. Lantigua, who is still only 19 for all of 2026, will then need the power to start playing more in games to lock down a starting MLB role in left or right.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Petit was the first selection in this past winter’s Rule 5 draft, plucked out of Detroit’s system. The ironically named (though it's pronounced like Andy Pettitte, not Yusmeiro Petit) 6-foot-8 right-hander was the Tigers’ 14th-rounder out of Charleston Southern back in 2021. He pitched his way to Triple-A Toledo in 2025, amassing a 2.44 ERA across 66.1 innings of work. When healthy, he has a pretty standard mid-90s fastball (94-97 mph, touch 98) and a plus slider. He utilizes his slider in all counts because his size creates a hittable plane on his fastball, though the addition of a second fastball type (he throws both elevated four-seamers and in-zone two-seamers) helped limit opponents’ contact quality against his heaters in 2025. Petit also creates enough sink on his changeup to keep lefties in check, so his role isn't at risk of being minimized to that of a righty specialist if he throws enough strikes (no guarantees) to profile. Unfortunately, we'll have to wait until 2027 to find out, as Petit blew out this spring and recently underwent Tommy John surgery. He'll remain with Colorado and will try the whole Rule 5 thing again next season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies are no strangers in trying to find bullpen help via the Rule 5 Draft. Anthony Molina was a 2023 selection who spent parts of the next two seasons in the big leagues. Back in 2020, they gave Jordan Sheffield a shot, and he appeared in 30 games the following season. This year, they’re hoping Petit will be their Rule 5 lightning in a bottle. While he was a starter in his last year at Charleston Southern, Petit has done nothing but relieve as a pro since the Tigers drafted him in the 14th round in 2021. After reaching Triple-A in 2025, he was left off the 40-man roster for the second straight year, and the Rockies made him the No. 1 pick in the Major League phase. Petit is a mountain of a man, standing at 6-foot-8 and 300 pounds, though he’s a good athlete, especially for his size. He can touch as high as 98 mph with his fastball, sitting around 95 and using a steep downward plane to get ground-ball outs. His 84-mph gyro slider is his out pitch, missing a lot of bats and getting a lot of chase, a breaking ball the Rockies think might work in Coors Field. He does have an upper-80s changeup that tunnels off the fastball effectively. The big right-hander has shown an ability to get hitters on both sides of the plate out and has kept his walk rate in check. His best chance of sticking with the Rockies will likely be as a bulk reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: With the aesthetic of Forrest Gump after three years and two months of running, Owens comes at hitters with a hard two-pitch mix. He sits in the mid-90s and touches 99 with a fastball that has a little natural cut. He primarily pairs it with a sharp two-plane slider that flashes plus. There’s also a split here, though he has limited feel for it and it was a tertiary offering for him last year. This all sounds like the description of a grip-'n-rip guy just trying to hit the box, but Owens is an average athlete who repeats his drop-and-drive delivery pretty well. He works the edges, and while he’ll nibble his way into a few walks, he’s also got fair feel for finding both sides of the plate, and working up and down. A hip injury pushed Owens off the 40-man last summer after he'd made his big league debut, and he’s still recuperating from offseason surgery, though he should be ready to throw in games soon. It’s a concerning enough injury that we’re rounding down on his FV grade here, though you could just as easily value him in the tier above.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Owens has had quite a journey through the Minor Leagues since signing out of high school for $547,000 as a 13th-round pick by the Braves in 2019. Atlanta traded him to Texas for outfielder J.P. Martinez just before Spring Training in 2024. The Rangers converted him from swingman to full-time reliever, then traded him to Detroit for catcher Carson Kelly. He dominated down the stretch at Double-A Erie, prompting the Tigers to add him to their 40-man roster in his second year of Rule 5 eligibility. Owens has a unique look as a 5-foot-10 pitcher with a power fastball, sitting at 96-98 mph while teasing with triple digits at times. Small in stature, Owens uses his long wingspan to his advantage, hiding the ball behind his back knee in his delivery before getting good extension upon release.
