Fontenelle has only played third with the Angels, and while he’s big and a below-average runner, he has good instincts (which help him steal some bases despite the lack of quickness) and actions, with enough arm to have a chance to stick at the hot corner. He’s played first base and even a little left field in the past, so there are some options should a move be needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hynes took a leap as the top Canadian prep pitcher in the 2025 Draft by adding four ticks of velocity last spring and performing well against professional teams, including a group of Guardians prospects. Months later, Cleveland drafted him in the second round and signed him away from his Wake Forest commitment for $950,000. He did not pitch after signing, similar to how the club has treated high school hurlers in the past. Considering how few reps he had as a teenager from Ontario heading into pro ball, Hynes has quite a good feel for his delivery and creating spin. His best pitch to date is a potentially plus slider that operates in the low 80s with plenty of horizontal movement from his low three-quarters release. Hynes' sinking fastball now touches 95 mph and figures to have another gear in it, as he has a lot of room to fill out his 6-foot-2 frame. His changeup fits his arsenal well with sink and run but has a ways to go to reach its potential. Hynes is a quality strike-thrower, and his athleticism and sound delivery portend above-average command to pair with his promising control. The Guardians are generally cautious with prep arms, so he will likely start in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, but he has the pitchability to take off pretty quickly and a solid chance to stick as a starter. While Hynes lacks the high-end traits of 2024 picks Braylon Doughty and Joey Oakie, he's a nice combination of the two.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivas earned NCAA Division II All-America accolades at Indianapolis in 2022 before transferring to Mississippi, where he was the Rebels' best starter as a junior before missing all of 2024 following Tommy John surgery. The Yankees still drafted him in the 16th round because they were intrigued by the deception of his pitches. He returned to the mound last year and recorded a 3.38 ERA with a .166 average-against and a 31 percent strikeout rate while advancing from Rookie ball to High-A. Rivas doesn't fool hitters with a riding fastball that sits at 90 mph and maxes out at 92, but he utilizes it well enough to set up a pair of baffling secondary pitches. He does an excellent job of killing spin on a low-80s changeup with splitter action that generated a 41 percent chase rate and 57 percent swing-and-miss rate in his pro debut. Hitters also consistently swung over the top of his tight low-80s slider. Though Rivas spent his first pro season as a starter, he profiles better as a tricky left-handed reliever. He has to nibble with his below-average heater and get chases with his slider and changeup, so only a third of his pitches landed in the strike zone last year. His competitive makeup also would work well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Martinez-Gomez pitched one season each at San Bernardino Valley (Calif.) JC and Temple (Texas) JC before the Cubs signed him for an under-slot $100,000 in the 10th round, using some of the savings to land since-traded Zyhir Hope with their next pick. Used primarily as a reliever as a pro, he got torched in his debut and spent most of his first two seasons in Rookie ball. He broke out in 2025 with a 1.46 ERA and 29 percent strikeout rate at two Class A stops, which may earn him a chance to show what he can do as a starter this year. The key to Martinez-Gomez's success was developing a low-80 splitter that's a weapon, as he does an excellent job on killing spin before it dives under barrels. The splitter plays well off his fastball, which parks at 93-95 mph and touches 97 with sink and armside run. He also spins a fringy slider in the low 80s. Martinez-Gomez's athleticism helps him get down the mound well and create extension in his delivery, though it hasn't helped him repeat mechanics well enough to provide regular strikes. He has a career 16 percent walk rate in pro ball before slicing that mark to 6 percent at High-A during last season's final month. If he can maintain average control, he might become a back-of-the-rotation option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds are always active players on the international market and it was no different during the 2024 international signing period. They focused much more on bats, with seven of their top bonuses – all six figures or more – going to hitters. Down the list was Torres, a six-foot right-hander who got $30,000 to sign with the organization when the period opened in January of that year. He was among the Dominican Summer League’s leaders in ERA, WHIP and batting average against, then came stateside in 2025 and was equally dominant over 38 1/3 Arizona Complex League innings. While a bit undersized, Torres is strong and stocky and his intriguing combination of feel for pitching and solid all-around stuff points to a future as a starter. He has three usable pitches, all of which are average but could be better as he progresses. His fastball sits in the 91-94 range, and he’s shown the ability to maintain his velocity throughout outings, he spins a low-80s curve very well and has good feel for an 85-87 mph fading changeup. All of his offerings play up because he’s shown a very strong feel for throwing them all for strikes, especially for his age. He’s walked just 1.9 per nine in his brief pro career heading into 2026, with the hopes of him having at least above-average command in the future. He’s yet to show he can answer the bell in a full-season rotation, but the Reds are bullish on his ability to start long term. Other organizations have definitely noticed his early success as well.

fangraphs.label: 2022updated
fangraphs.text: Pintar has a rare power/speed combination for an up-the-middle college player and crushed several piped, mediocre ASU pitchers’ fastballs during the Cougars’ trip to Phoenix a couple weekends ago. He ran very well, posting several home-to-first times in the 4.1-4.2 range during my looks, which are comfortably plus, approaching plus-plus run times. Pintar’s swing is grooved through the middle of the zone, and a shoulder injury might be contributing to issues with his arm strength, but even projecting a 40 hit tool here makes Pintar an strong early day-two prospect because the showcase tools (power and speed) are so big. He’s been added to The Board.

fangraphs.label: 2022updated
fangraphs.text: Vrieling has one of the deeper repertoires in the draft, with four distinct pitches headlined by his cutter/slider and curveball, which have distinct shape, and which Vrieling command to his glove side. He doesn't throw all that hard, only sitting 90-92 mph most of the time, but he'll reach back for the occasional 95 and his heater has carry that plays at the letters. His fastball command is notably worse than his feel for locating his breaking stuff, even though his arm action is quite short. Vrieling also has a frame built for the rigors of pro ball and might yet throw harder, though he already has back-of-the-rotation stuff, at least.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Riemer does not swing and miss. You can count on your fingers the number of times he whiffed in 2022, as he seems to find a way to put the bat on the baseball no matter where it is in the strike zone. He isn't clubbing traditional extra-base power, but he is stinging the ball in a Steven Kwan-ish way that feels like it will translate to pro ball. Riemer has played shortstop at Wright State, but he isn't a realistic fit there in the pros due to a lack of arm strength, so there might have to be more power here if he can only play second base at the next level. If he ends up with an elite hit tool, though, he'll find a way to be a big league contributor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending two years at Sacramento City Junior College, Costeiu transferred to Arkansas and showed off the ability to miss bats in a relief role in 2021. The Angels took him that summer in the seventh round and decided to stretch him out as a starter. There were some positive early returns with High-A Tri-City, but he blew out in July and needed Tommy John surgery. He missed all of the 2023 season and returned to amass 74 1/3 innings in a solid post-surgery return. One of the reasons why the Angels thought he had a chance start despite being a six-footer is because he does have a real four-pitch mix, even if he doesn’t have one offering that jumps off the page. His low-90s fastball can be effective because of good spin rates and carry up in the zone. His changeup might be his best pitch, a low-80s cambio that can get swing-and-miss and groundball outs. His upper-70s curve was his go-to when he started his career, and he’s since added a distinct slider. Costeiu was an outstanding strike-thrower in 2022 before he got hurt and he wasn’t as sharp upon his return in 2024. If this command returns, he could have a chance to start, though the size and the elbow history will have some thinking a move to the bullpen is in the offing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he played on the same Goodpasture Christian HS (Nashville) as Tigers fourth-rounder Carson Rucker in 2023, Elkins flew somewhat under the radar because he was also an all-region running back in football who didn't spend much time on the showcase circuit. Teams recognized his tools but didn't have much history with him, allowing the Dodgers to land him in the eighth round with an over-slot $407,500 bonus. After making a one-game pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, he returned there last summer and batted .285/.412/.457 with 20 steals in 57 games. Elkins has a strong 6-foot-1 frame and a quick right-handed swing that give him plus raw power with the potential for more. He has a pull-happy approach and looks to drive the ball in the air, enabling him to tap into most of his pop. He'll have to prove he can hit advanced pitching because he tied for the ACL lead with 80 strikeouts while whiffing at 35 percent clip, though he did show a willingness to work deep counts and take walks. Elkins may have the best combination of power and speed in the system. He's a plus-plus runner who's aggressive on the bases and in the outfield. Both his center-field defense and arm strength grade as at least plus, and the Dodgers have some internal 70 grades on both tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roberts went undrafted after his junior year at Utah in 2023, when he batted just .266 with three homers over 46 games, but he started to show out for Mankato in the Northwoods League that summer (.346/.476/.555), creating some momentum for himself. He built on that with a Pac-12 All-Conference nod after slashing .356/.430/.562 with seven homers in 55 games for the Utes as a senior. His 33 steals were most among Pac-12 players. The Padres selected him in the seventh round and signed him for just $10,000, but Roberts continued to show out with a .340/.414/.470 line in 24 games with Single-A Lake Elsinore in his first taste of the Minors. Roberts cuts a stunning figure in the field at 6-foot-5, 205 pounds, and he moves exceptionally well for that size, notching 60-yard dashes in the 6.5-second range. He was a perfect 14-for-14 in steal attempts during that short run in the California League, and the Padres don’t have much doubt that his speed will continue to play as he reaches higher levels. With those wheels, Roberts is a comfortable fit in center field and has just enough arm for the position, too. That said, the left-handed hitter hasn’t been a huge power threat despite his size, though San Diego officials were intrigued by the good weight he put on during in his first offseason. He struggled to make contact against sliders and changeups as a senior and will need his speed to help run high BABIPs that can make up for some of the contact issues. Roberts already enters his first full season at age 24 and doesn’t have a long runway, but his best skills could be useful in the Majors in short order.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heuer had some of the best physicality and projectable fastball velocity in the 2023 Draft, but he turned down the Guardians as a 16th-rounder to attend Texas Tech. He served as the Red Raiders' No. 1 starter and pushed his fastball to 98 mph last spring, but he also logged a 6.28 ERA as a Draft-eligible sophomore. That didn't deter the Yankees, who signed him for an over-slot $400,000 in the eighth round. Heuer operates at 93-95 mph with cut and carry on his fastball, which is effective up in the zone but gets pounded when he doesn't command it well. His mid-80s slider with sweeping action can be a solid offering when it's on, though he has trouble landing it for strikes and it sometimes flattens over the heart of the plate. His mid-80s changeup with fade and depth was his most effective offering as a sophomore, though he didn't use it much. Scouts don't love Heuer's delivery, which features a short arm action, high release point and some crossfire. He presently has fringy control and below-average command, which may make him more of a reliever than a starter in the long run. If he doesn't make it in baseball, he has his own livestock business with his brother and raised ewes that won grand champion titles at the 2020 and 2022 Georgia National Fairs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dumesnil looked like he could be a high-round Draft pick after an eye-opening sophomore season at Cal Baptist, including a .362/.440/.702 slash line with 19 homers, and an All-Star season in the Cape Cod League, hitting .311 and leading the circuit in steals (26). A difficult junior season changed his momentum, but the Tigers snagged him in the eighth round, signed him for $214,300 and immediately put him at Single-A, where he made an impact for Lakeland in the Florida State League playoffs. Strong and athletic, the 6-foot-2 Dumesnil showed the ability to hit with power in college, but his 2025 season came with struggles against spin, notably sliders, and inconsistent power. Both of those continued in Lakeland, where he hit fastballs well but not for much power while whiffing on breaking balls. He’s not a fluid runner but has enough speed and aggressiveness to swipe bases, which he did often in a small sample size for the Flying Tigers. Dumesnil’s speed does help him cover ground in the outfield and he’s shown he can be solid at all three spots defensively. Some feel he can play center long term, but others feel he’s best suited for a corner, with left being a better option because of his fringy arm strength. Even with the struggles he’s had, the Tigers will try to get him back to 2024 Cape form.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: If you’re a high-ceiling high school pitcher who hasn’t heard his name called in the top 10 rounds and think you’re headed to college, the Angels can always give you hope. On an almost annual basis, extra bonus pool money is available to take and sign some prep arms. In 2025, they targeted a pair of intriguing high school lefties, taking Talon Haley in the 12th round and Mitchell a round later. Rather than head to Texas, Mitchell signed for $872,500, heading down a baseball path despite coming from a football family that includes an uncle who quarterbacked in the Canadian Football League and a brother who was a wide receiver at Arizona. After pitching for Team USA the summer before his senior year, Mitchell got off to a good start back at school but was shut down with shoulder fatigue after a month, so building up strength will be a key. He can sit 90-92 mph with his fastball, touching 94, and the fastball plays up because of deception in his delivery and carry up in the zone. He has a good feel to spin an upper-70s curve with depth that works well off of his heater. Like with a lot of high school pitchers, he hasn’t used a changeup much, but he’s shown glimpses of a decent cambio in the low-80s with fade and sink. Mitchell is athletic on the mound, repeating his delivery well and filling up the strike zone. There’s room to add muscle to his 6-foot-3 frame, which could help all of his stuff tick up as he gets his pro career going.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2024, the Mariners signed Chia-Shi Shen out of Chinese Taipei. They hit that pitching market again in 2025, signing Lin for $460,000 when the signing period opened in January. A former two-way player who pitched well in international competition, Lin looked really good in Spring Training after signing, but then wasn’t able to make his pro debut because of a lat strain, though he did get some innings in the bridge league at the end of the year, once again raising expectations. Lin had played both the infield and outfield previously, and he brings that athleticism to the mound. The 5-foot-11 right-hander has the chance to have a full starter’s repertoire, with his splitter the standout pitch. It flashes plus and can fall off the table with excellent depth while also throwing a distinct changeup. His fastball sits around 92-93 mph, but he’s shown the ability to reach back for more, and there could be more velocity in the future. He has some feel to spin with a more traditional slider, though it’s behind the other offerings, and there’s been some talk of adding a sweeper to his mix. Lin’s athleticism helps him repeat his delivery and find the strike zone consistently. His stuff may never wow anyone, but his feel for pitching and full array of offerings gives him the chance to start, with the Mariners getting to see what he’s like in competition this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Mason Martin, a former Pirates farmhand who ranked fourth in the Minors with 35 homers in 2019, Martin also stands out with his well-above-average raw power. Signed for an over-slot $250,000 in 2023 as an 11th-rounder from a Washington high school, he struggled for two years in Rookie ball before doing more damage in Single-A last year and drawing significant trade interest from other clubs. He earned Carolina League all-star honors after leading the Single-A circuit in extra-base hits (43) and ranking second in slugging (.440) and third in homers (12) and OPS (.783). Martin can drive the ball out of the park to all fields with an impressive combination of bat speed and strength, and he hits the ball harder and farther than most Rangers farmhands. In 2025, he did a better job of attacking hittable pitches in early counts and launching them in the air to his pull side, allowing him to make better use of his pop. How much he'll be able to tap into his 25-30 homer upside at higher levels will depend on his ability to improve his swing decisions and handle secondary pitches. Though Martin stole 15 bases in as many attempts last year, he has fringy speed with good instincts on the bases. He has limited range and below-average arm strength, relegating him to left field and diminishing his value outside of the batter's box. He's adequate at first base and can fill in in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In the top 10 rounds of the 2025 Draft, the Phillies took nine pitchers, eight of them from the college ranks. The lone hitter in the group was Ferrara, a high school shortstop from Toms River East High School in New Jersey. The athletic middle infielder had shown off some tools on the summer showcase circuit and turned in a strong season in the New Jersey Shore Conference. The Phillies had some bonus pool money to play with in the ninth round when they took Ferrara, who signed for an over-slot bonus close to $600,000, or fourth-round money. The Phillies pushed the six-foot right-handed hitter to full-season Clearwater for a 15-game debut that did not go particularly well, though little should be read into thrusting an 18-year old kid from the Northeast into that level of competition. What was impressive was that even in the small sample, he was starting to make some small adjustments that should help him in the future. He wasn’t on time, launching his barrel too late, which led to poor barrel accuracy. When he got more synced up, his barrel accuracy and zone contact improved. He’s already added strength and physicality since signing, which could help him get to more impact. While Ferrara only played second base during his debut, the Phillies think his athleticism gives him the chance to stick at short. He’s an easily plus runner with decent actions defensively. He’ll continue to see time on both sides of second base, and it’s not out of the question that he gets some run out in center field at some point in the future.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Jarvis had been on the fringe of prospect lists at FanGraphs for years but his combination of below-average velocity and control (despite his fastball's other traits) kept him toward the bottom or off the list, entirely. In 2023 he had a two-tick velo spike and is now sitting 93-95 with plus-plus riding life. Jarvis' command is still not very good but his type of fastball gives him in-zone margin for error. His due north arm slot, which is largely where Jarvis' vertical ride comes from, also helps him impart depth on his breaking balls. His isn't overpowering but mixes in four average pitches and has thrown enough strikes to continue developing as a starter, especially while he has options left. Jarvis' extremely skinny build creates doubt about his ability to hold his new velo under a starter's workload and so he projects as a long-term long reliever here at FG.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Wyatt is a somewhat undersized righty with a fairly violent delivery. He dominated Connecticut high school baseball with a mid-90s heater that touched 97 and a plus slider. Wyatt looked good at the Combine despite not showing peak velo. His size and mechanical violence are bullpen indicators, or possible signs that the stuff Wyatt showed during the spring of 2023 will not sustain itself, kind of like Deivi Garcia. Despite the heightened risk beyond what's usually associated with a prep pitcher, Wyatt has a million dollar arm and breaking ball, and could have two plus pitches at peak.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Sullivan is an ultra-deceptive cross-bodied lefty with a rise/run heater. His stride direction takes him toward the first base line at an extreme angle, and this, in concert with his low three-quarters slot, makes him very deceptive; it takes hitters a few looks at him to get comfortable. He does most of his swing-and-miss damage with a low-90s fastball that averaged 90 mph across all of 2023 but was sitting more 90-94 during his postseason starts. His repertoire is fastball-heavy in the extreme at about 75% usage, which isn't sustainable in pro ball. His slider's length helps the 77-81 mph pitch play left-on-left; his changeup (80-84 mph) often has slider look due to its angle. There aren't any big league starters who look like this, and it's more likely that Sullivan is a low-leverage long man or second lefty coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners took Beilenson as a money-saving senior sign in the fifth round of the 2024 Draft, with his $25,000 under-slot bonus helping pay to sign Ryan Sloan. But Beilenson had success in college, especially once he moved to Duke after three years at Brown, saving 12 games for the Blue Devils while getting a pair of graduate degrees. While he was old for the High-A level where he began his first full season of pro ball, he pitched well enough to earn a promotion to Double-A after 20 appearances, putting him on the prospect map. Now 26, Beilenson is more a sum-of-his-parts kind of pitcher than a reliever who is going to blow hitters away. He has a foundation of three pitches but manipulates them into different shapes to give him a repertoire of as many as five. He’ll throw both a four- and a two-seam fastball, averaging around 93 mph. His best pitch is his kick-change that has splitter-like action to it. He’ll throw both a sweeper and a shorter, harder slider around 81 mph with cutter-like action. Beilenson can throw a ton of strikes with all his offerings, but it’s control over command, and he got hit more once he got to Double-A. If he can find a bit more consistency from one outing to the next, he could be knocking on the door to a big league bullpen job.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a long winding path for Mejia, who started his college career by redshirting at Arizona in 2019, then transferred to Pima Community College in 2020, but made just five starts there because of the pandemic. The right-hander went to New Mexico State after that, mostly relieving in 2021 then stepping into the rotation in 2022. He signed for $100,000 as an 11th-round pick that summer, spent all year with High-A Rome in 2023 and then had another solid, and durable, season with Double-A Mississippi in 2024. Mejia’s feel for pitching and the ability to mix his offerings to keep hitters off-balance stands out more than any of his pure stuff. His fastball averaged around 92 mph last year and maxed out at 94 mph. It doesn’t feature a ton of life, but he commands the pitch consistently. His low-80s slider is his go-to pitch, and he threw it almost as much as his heater in 2024, missing bats at a 42-percent clip. His 83-84 mph changeup is a decent third offering and he’s been working on a splitter as well. The 6-foot-3 Mejia does a nice job of repeating his delivery and has a history of throwing strikes, especially in 2022 with the Aggies and during his first pro season. His walk rate did jump a bit in 2024, but he’s posted consistently, topping 120 innings in each of his two full seasons. His ceiling is probably as a No. 5 type starter because of the lack of wow stuff, but he’s close to showing if it can work in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seven years after the Tigers took a Draft flier on a college pitcher with mixed results a year removed from Tommy John surgery (Tarik Skubal), they went a similar route with Leys, who missed the 2024 season recovering from surgery before taking the mound for the University of Maine in 2025. Leys won America East Pitcher of the Year with a 2.69 ERA and 74 strikeouts in 67 innings, better than his first two seasons with the Black Bears. The Tigers drafted him in the fourth round, five rounds earlier than Skubal, and signed him for $574,900. While Leys isn’t big for a pitcher, he has a quick, fluid delivery with a big leg kick and a three-quarters arm angle. His fastball can touch 96 mph, setting up a slider and a changeup both in the low 80s. Leys greatly improved his strike throwing and command upon his return from surgery, cutting his walk rate in almost half from his first two seasons while ticking up his strikeout rate. The Tigers have been aggressive at times starting out college pitchers in full-season ball, and could do the same with Leys, who made an impression in Spring Training. If he can hold his command while adding more swing-and-miss, he could force his way up the system quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Draft picks taken after the 10th round are automatically assigned a slot value of $150,000. When a college senior gets taken in Round 11, as Clohisy was out of St. Louis in 2024, and signs for that exact slot amount, it tends to fly under the radar. But when that senior plays his way from High-A to Double-A in his first full season and finishes third among all Minor Leaguers with 79 steals before stealing 22 more to lead the Arizona Fall League, as Clohisy did in 2025, folks tend to sit up and take notice. Clohisy’s future in the big leagues is directly connected to his legs. In 2025, regular season and AFL combined, he stole 101 bases in 120 attempts (84.2 percent success rate) in 152 games. Not only does he have great speed, he’s aggressive in using it, wreaking havoc at all times. His wheels also help him cover a ton of ground in the outfield. He can no doubt play center field, but has and will continue to get time in all three spots. That’s important because his future role would be as a fourth or fifth outfielder if it all clicks. And that will depend on how the left-handed hitter swings the bat. There is a little extra-base ability, but his job will always be to put the ball in play and get on base, and it will be interesting to see whether he can carry over the offensive success he had in Double-A and Arizona to lift him up to Atlanta.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lohman was a steady buildup at Fort Zumwalt North HS, northwest of St. Louis. He didn’t show much velocity with a fastball only in the upper 80s as a junior, and that initially made him a low priority with many figuring he was set to honor his commitment to Missouri. Instead, he turned heads with a little extra heat as a senior, along with a pair of interesting breaking balls, and he attended the MLB Draft Combine in Arizona. The Mets selected him in the eighth round and signed him for well above slot at $797,500 (late third-round money) to keep him out of the SEC. That improved velo pushed Lohman’s fastball into the 91-95 mph range, and with his size at 6-foot-4, he can create downhill plane from a high release point. He’ll work with both a mid-70s curveball and low-80s slider that have promising two-plane depth. The curveball might be a better fit for his over-the-top delivery, but both pitches have the chance to become at least average Major League quality. His low-80s splitter was a work in progress but looks like a pitch with some promise. Lohman uses short strides on the mound, rather than getting big extension, and that’s what leads to the high release. He’ll either need to improve the shape of his fastball and slider or locate them exceptionally well in pro ball to get the most out of both offerings against pro bats, but as a prep arm, he’ll be given plenty of time and space to work on both goals. There could be even more strength coming in his projectable frame, and the Mets, who have a run of pitching development success, could be the right org to get the most out of Lohman’s budding potential.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Cairone, who was signed away from a Coastal Carolina commitment for just over a million bucks, is a breakout candidate in this system. The smooth-operating southpaw has a gorgeous delivery and fairly projectable frame, and Cairone's fastball velocity has been climbing steadily throughout the last year and a half. During the summer after his junior year of high school, he was sitting about 86; post-2025 instructs (in a casual, short-outing setting), he was 91-93. Cairone (pronounced like "Tyrone", some Erykah Badu jokes were made during the completion of this prospect list) throws quality strikes with his fastball and showed similarly advanced feel for his 80-ish-mph slider.  That pitch is better in the zone than as a finisher right now. We're skeptical of the sustainability of new velocity like this when it's seen in well-rested, one- or two-inning spurts like Cairone's was in the fall, but we can't help but be excited by his overall stuff, feel, and athleticism ingredients, and are giving him fairly aggressive placement here.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Did you read the Junior Ciprian blurb and think “that sounds nice, but he’s a little too advanced for me?” Well, have I got the pitcher for you. Vasquez is another long and lean Dominican hurler. He generates some of the easiest 97s and 98s you’ll ever see, and both his raw ability to spin the ball and his feel for his change are good, particularly for the level. Complex-level bats were overwhelmed by both of them. 
Vasquez is very raw, though. While he’s made strides since his walk-the-world DSL days, he doesn't have much feel for where it’s going. He’s a hard lander, he gets off balance, and some scouts have said he’s got “darty” arm action, which you can think of as a guy who tends to aim the ball rather than really let it rip. Those issues are also limiting his ability to execute. He hasn't yet harnessed all that spin into anything more than a slurvy breaking ball, and while there’s a potential plus pitch in him, he’s a long way from finding it. The change is also inconsistent and will need reps to reach its projection. Inevitably, the range of outcomes for a teenager with a great arm is wide, and the top end of it here is a mid-rotation starter with three above average or better offerings. From my vantage, the athleticism and stroke is a little too concerning for that lofty of a projection. Arizona should keep starting Vasquez for the reps and maybe something clicks, but the overall package seems more like a reliever in the end, albeit one with upside in that role.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Redona put up video game numbers in his first DSL season — 0.86 ERA, 0.67 WHIP, 36.8% K%, 2.6% BB% in 31.1 IP — thanks almost entirely to his mature command of a deceptive riding fastball. He doesn't throw all that hard, but the pitch averages 18 inches of vertical break and Redona commands it with machine-like precision to the top half of the zone. His fastball represented 70% of Redona's pitch deployment. His silky smooth arm action helps him sell a precocious changeup, and he will show you an average breaking ball anywhere in the 77-84 mph range, but this is more a prospect with a shot to have special command than one who'll grow into elite stuff. He's a priority name to know from rookie ball even though he's much more likely to be Tom Milone than Tom Glavine.

fangraphs.label: bos2026may
fangraphs.text: Bravo popped onto the radar because of his 2025 data (he posted an 88% contact rate during his debut season), and would have based on his visual scouting look in Florida this year, albeit for entirely different reasons. On paper, Bravo looks like a slappy contact hitter with special feel for the barrel but no power (16% hard-hit rate). In person, he has a bloodthirsty low-ball swing with an epic finish in the dirt behind him. He also looks like a prospect with strikeout risk, as his front foot is often bailing down the first base line when he swings, and his scoopy bat path leaves Bravo vulnerable to elevated fastballs away from him. When he gets a ball in his wheelhouse on the inner third of the dish, his swing looks like that of a baby Darryl Strawberry. Because the BoSox FCL roster is chock full of shortstops, Bravo’s reps there have been limited, but he’s looked competent on the opportunities he’s gotten. The incongruity between Bravo’s scouting look as a hitter versus his DSL data from last season is fascinating, but not deleterious. Most of what’s happening here is positive and exciting, giving the Red Sox yet another fun young infielder to monitor.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Nikhazy only sits 88-90 or so, but his fastball has sneaky carry because of its angle and spin axis. He commands the hell out of it, as well as two above-average breaking balls. If he can throw harder, he'll break out.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: There was a run on prep pitching just before the Phillies made their second selection in the 2016 draft, the year they took Mickey Moniak first overall. Gowdy was the last pitcher of that talent tier remaining and ended up eschewing a UCLA commit to go pro. A surgery and the pandemic combined to knock out three years of Gowdy's five-year pro career. His stuff was up in 2021, looking more like his peak amateur days (low-to-mid-90s, promising slider) while profiling on the middle relief/5th starter line.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: He's old for the class and not at all projectable, but Panzini has real stuff, including a mid-90s fastball that plays at the letters and the makings of two good breaking balls.

fangraphs.label: 2022updated
fangraphs.text: Barco is a low-slot lefty with advanced command and several underlying pitch traits that give clubs hope of more upside, even though he looks like a lower-variance backend starter prospect on the surface. Barco's arm slot creates a flat approach angle, but he's not really inclined to climb the ladder and pitch at the top of the zone right now, and instead lives on the arm-side third of the plate. His slider lacks nasty, biting movement, but his arm slot makes it tough on lefty hitters, and his command of it gives it back-foot utility against righties. As a high schooler, his ultra-low spin splitter seemed like the more promising pitch, but his feel for it has regressed. He entered the 2022 spring as a high-probability 40 FV prospect who some scouts thought belonged in the 40+ tier because of pitching approach changes Barco can make in pro ball that could enable a breakout, but he ended up blowing his UCL and having Tommy John in May. The timing of his surgery is more detrimental than that of the other college pitchers, as it ups the odds that he won't (or that he'll barely) pitch in 2023. He's still a good prospect, one that teams that take interest in unique release points might be more intrigued by.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: After he started just one game as a freshman, Honeyman had a breakout sophomore year when he hit .329/.402/.506 during the NCAA season and .289/.400/.530 on Cape Cod. He followed that up with a .307/.382/.502 line as a junior. Honeyman has fantastic breaking ball recognition, modest barrel control, and good hitter's timing despite his sizable leg kick. Honeyman can bend at the waist to hammer pitches on the outer edge of the zone, and in fact he's not great at hitting pitches in other parts of the zone. Honeyman also moved to right field in 2023 but looked okay enough as a sophomore to deploy him in CF in pro ball and see how it goes. He never hit more than 6 homers in a season at BC so the power to profile in a corner may not be here.

fangraphs.label: 2024updated
fangraphs.text: Transferred from Pima Community College to Arizona and finally to Oregon State. Cross-bodied, low-slot righty with typical 6-foot-2 pitcher's frame. Secondary-heavy approach to pitching due to fastball's hittable sinking shape. Plus low-80s sweeper that he throws a ton. Feel for locating it is much better than his other pitches. Upper-80s changeup has a miss rate north of 40% but May's feel for landing it much less consistent. Lots of relief risk here due to fastball shape and lack of command. Plausible to add a cutter, which, if he can command it like his slider, would help him get closer to starting. Nomadic amateur career might also point to looming improvement once he gets to stay in one place for more than a year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers swiped Pacific Northwest prep pitchers away from Oregon State commitments in consecutive Drafts. The more recent, Swanson, was a two-sport star in Washington, the son of a high school basketball coach who was the top-ranked high school player in the state. The Tigers drafted Swanson in the ninth round and wooed him to pro ball with an above-slot $722,500 bonus. Swanson’s athleticism has allowed him to blossom as a pitcher at a later stage than others. His fastball ranged from the low-to-mid 90s in high school but is more of a power offering with carry since working with the Tigers’ pitching department to refine his delivery. His high-spin slider has a lot of movement and depth. His changeup needs work but could be the difference between starting and relieving. The Tigers drafted Swanson fully knowing he could take longer to develop but believing in the athlete and competitor. His introduction to pro ball will be delayed after he underwent Tommy John surgery ahead of the 2025 campaign, knocking him out for what would have been his first full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Following two subpar seasons at South Carolina, Milone transferred to Oregon in 2022 and transformed into a different hitter by earning first-team All-Pac-12 honors as a junior after hitting .337/.405/.545 with 12 home runs in 60 games. The A’s took note of this revelation, selecting him in the sixth round of the 2022 Draft. Since joining the organization, he has quickly climbed up the prospect radar. He spent 2024 at Double-A Midland and hit .278/.361/.441 with 15 homers, 29 doubles and 70 RBIs in 120 games. The A’s initially figured they would have to tweak Milone’s mechanics at the plate given his unconventional setup and swing, but his production thus far at every level has led them to allow him to stick with what is working for him. His power numbers have been decent to this point, and he draws a good amount of walks and has solid bat-to-ball skills to round out an overall solid approach at the plate. Defense has always been the big question mark surrounding Milone. The A’s have tried giving him looks all around the infield, and while they plan to keep him versatile, first base is likely going to be where he ends up. Regardless of position, hitting is what got him this far, and the bat is what will take him to the Majors one day if his offensive output continues as he advances through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best sleeper in the Giants' 2024 international class, Tejada signed for $147,500 out of the Dominican Republic. Known most for his power when he turned pro, he turned in a nifty all-around offensive performance in his debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. He slashed .300/.405/.488 with 19 extra-base hits, 22 walks and 13 steals in 46 games. Tejada has plenty of strength in his stocky 5-foot-11 frame and generates impressive bat speed and high exit velocities with a simple right-handed stroke. In the DSL, he showed the ability to drive balls in the air to his pull side and the possibility of 25-homer seasons in the future. Though he has a power mentality, he also displayed some feel for hitting and for managing the strike zone. Tejada makes the most of his average speed with an aggressive nature on the bases and good instincts in the outfield. He spent his pro debut in center field, yet his quickness is better suited for the corners in the long run. Though he has average to solid arm strength, he didn't record an assist in 42 games last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of Georgia's best prep pitching prospects in 2019, David slid to the Diamondbacks in the 35th round amid signability concerns and opted to attend Auburn instead. He never pitched for the Tigers during the pandemic-truncated 2020 season before bouncing from Gordon State (Ga.) JC to Northwest Florida State JC to NAIA program Southeastern (Fla.) before the Astros drafted him in 2024's 10th round as a fifth-year senior. He moved from Single-A to Double-A in his first full pro season, compiling a 3.47 ERA with 87 strikeouts in 85 2/3 innings. David's fastball parks at 95-96 mph and peaks at 98, and he maintained that velocity throughout 2025. It features carry and armside run. His tight mid-80s slider doesn't get a lot of chases but does generate a lot of in-zone swings and misses, and he can turn it into an 89-91 mph cutter on occasion. After focusing primarily on his heater and slider in college, he has worked on incorporating a low-80s curveball and an upper-80s changeup with depth but has trouble landing both for strikes. There's effort in David's delivery that has prevented him from throwing consistent strikes, so he's more of multi-inning reliever than a starter in the long run. He spent the first two months of 2025 in the rotation at Single-A Fayetteville before shifting to the bullpen. He'll pitch at age 25 this season, and the less challenging role will accelerate his timetable to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abeldt was one of college baseball's best relievers in his first two years at Texas Christian, recording a 2.81 ERA with 125 strikeouts in 99 1/3 innings and spending both summers with the U.S. collegiate national team. The Horned Frogs planned on turning him into a starter in 2025, but he blew out his elbow just before the beginning of the season and required Tommy John surgery in February. The Rangers still popped him in the fifth round and signed him for $450,000. Abeldt relies heavily on a 91-94 mph fastball that peaks at 96 and is much more effective than its ordinary velocity would indicate. His heater has riding action and plenty of deception coming out of a crossfire delivery, and it's nearly impossible to lift when he works down in the zone. He can't overpower hitters with a slider that sits around 80 mph, but it can baffle them with its sweeping action when it's on. While he doesn't use it much, Abeldt has the makings of an effective low-80s changeup with sink. He looks like a shorter, stronger version of Chris Sale with his slingy delivery, and it generates a lot of empty swings and groundballs. It remains to be seen if he can succeed as a starter, but he comes with a high floor as a quality lefty reliever once he returns to full health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gourson spent three years starting for UCLA (mostly at second base), earning a reputation as a gamer who maximized what tools he had, even earning a spot on Team USA after his sophomore campaign in 2023. He had a solid, albeit unspectacular junior season, finishing with a .909 OPS, and the Pirates took a low-risk flyer on him in the ninth round of the 2024 Draft, signing him for a touch under $190,000. After a nondescript pro debut after signing, he was one of the pleasant surprises of the Pirates' system in 2025, performing well in all facets of the game with High-A Greensboro and Double-A Altoona. Gourson earned a ticket to pro ball because of his approach at the plate, swing decisions and contact skills. There was enough bat-to-ball skill to think he had a chance, and that was apparent in 2025; he kept his strikeouts relatively low, despite a little more swing-and-miss once he got to Double-A, while also posting a walk rate north of 10 percent. What wasn’t expected was the increased impact from the left side of the plate. He gained a few miles per hour in bat speed and that resulted in a huge uptick in exit velocity, allowing for more quality contact. Gourson's instincts and aggressiveness make him an average runner or perhaps a slight tick above that as he stole 31 bags in 34 tries in 2025. He’s seen time at three infield positions -- all but shortstop -- and he should get some reps in the outfield corners as well. If he takes another step offensively, he has a utility role kind of future in the big leagues, and it’s hard to bet against him given his intangibles.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Tunink enticed scouts with his left-handed stroke and athleticism as an Illinois high schooler, his strong Notre Dame commitment clouded his signability in the 2024 Draft. The Dodgers floated him down to the eighth round and were able to land him for $412,500, the equivalent of fifth-round money. He earned Arizona Complex League All-Star honors in his pro debut last summer after finishing fourth in the Rookie circuit in wRC+ (152), slugging (.550) and OPS (.967), but he also struck out at a 30 percent rate. Tunink's bat speed, growing strength and propensity for driving the ball in the air to his pull side generate high exit velocities and plus raw power. He's not overly aggressive in terms of chasing pitches, but he has holes in his swing that lead to too many in-zone misses. Viewed as more of a hit-over-power guy as an amateur, he flipped that projection in the ACL. Tunink features at least plus speed that makes him a basestealing threat and a solid center fielder. He has below-average arm strength and didn't record an assist in 35 outfield starts last year.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: James signed for $2.5 million rather than head to Ole Miss and was assigned to Low-A Fredericksburg to start his pro career in 2026. Part of the crowded infield contingent there, he has played a mix of second base, third base and left field as of list publication. A terrific low-to-the-ground athlete, James can be slow to approach grounders and makes some plays unnecessarily close at first base. This is more an issue of polish and the speed of pro ball rather than talent, and he should still become a good infielder with time. While it was obvious that James had a power-over-hit skill set as a draft prospect, the degree to which that is true is coming into greater focus. He is pummeling pitches with power when he connects, but he's struggling to make adjustments to pro sliders. James can really run, he's strong, and he has power to both gaps. He's a fun, toolsy dev project who is probably going to take a while to mature on both sides of the ball.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Sando thrived as a junior reliever at Santa Clara and then struggled as a senior starter and spent his first full pro season in the bullpen. After an early-2025 demotion to Low-A, he pitched so well that the Reds not only elevated him back to Dayton, but also moved him into the rotation there. Sando thrived, twirling some impressive six-inning outings late in the year, and was again promoted, this time to Double-A. 
Sando is a control-over-command southpaw with a low-three-quarters delivery that helps his fastball play up. He bullies the zone with uphill fastballs and can land both his slider and changeup for strikes, but neither of those pitches is especially nasty. You could consider Sando a swingman candidate for 2027, though it's more likely he winds up as a bullpen's second or third lefty.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Mariano is a switch-hitting middle infielder who draws Ozzie Albies starter kit comparisons from his most ardent proponents. He slashed .336/.466/.580 with more walks than strikeouts in his second DSL season after adding relevant physicality between years one and two. Mariano is built like a wiry defensive back. He's undersized but is definitely bigger than his listed 5-foot-7, 140 pounds, and his gorgeous swing is actualized to get to the modest power he currently has. This isn't a super projectable hitter likely to fit at a premium position (Mariano has experience at several positions, but our sources think second base is his best fit) and grow into big power, but Mariano is a special athlete who worked hard to add meaningful strength, and he's a skilled enough hitter that he might be able to punch above his weight. He's a high priority target on the 2026 Arizona Complex circuit.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Pacheco has had early-career success as a rookie ball starter, with 1.19 WHIP in 62.1 career innings. He throws hard, with his fastball residing in the 93-96 mph range through most of 2025 as he worked four to five innings per start. Pacheco's arm action is explosive, and he generates six-and-a-half feet of extension even though he's only six feet tall. He's been able to throw strikes despite his delivery featuring a good bit of effort, and he's walked just 6.5% of opposing hitters since signing. His arm action (and ability to kill spin) allows for lots of projection on his power changeup, which currently lives in the 86-90 mph range. His breaking ball is a blunt 80-mph curveball that might morph into a harder slider/cutter with time. It'd be easier to project Pacheco as a starter if he were a bigger athlete; it's rare for righties this size to wind up in a big league rotation. But he throws hard, throws strikes, and should have at least one viable secondary weapon at peak (the changeup), which would allow him to be a reliable middle reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: De Andrade is an international prospect straight out of central casting. He has a well-rounded collection of tools hovering around average quality, he's got a relatively projectable frame, and precocious baseball feel and instincts. He is not a remarkable or especially explosive athlete right now.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Redshirt junior who was at Wake Tech and Catawba before Wilmington. Velo peaked during the postseason, where Banks was 96-99 mph at Regionals. Powerfully built 6-foot-3 with a short arm action that generates cut and ride on his fastball. Inconsistent fastball command and breaking ball shape. Sliders 85-87 with anything from cutter action to vertical drop, no consistency here, but promising amounts of movement. There's a right-tail outcome where Banks has a 70 fastball with upper-90s velo and maddening cut and a plus slider, the raw material for that is in here, but he needs a grade of command development to be anything at all. Middle relief is his most likely outcome.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tom Candiotti rode the knuckleball to a 16-year career in the Major Leagues. His son, Clark, utilizes a very different arsenal that took him on an interesting ride as a college player. Candiotti played for five schools in five years between St. Mary’s (2020), Vernon (Junior) College (2021), Grayson County Community College (2022), Wichita State (2023) and finally Arizona (2024). He was a Pac-12 All-Conference selection after posting a 3.39 ERA with 103 strikeouts in 95 2/3 innings with the Wildcats, and that helped push him to Padres with the 135th overall pick in the '24 Draft, where he signed for $80,000. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has the look of a durable starter. He added fastball velocity between his time at Wichita State and Arizona, averaging around 93 mph with the latter while touching 96. The heater can feature good carry, eliciting chase above the zone. Candiotti, however, leaned even more heavily on his 83-85 mph slider, throwing it 45 percent of the time and using it against batters from both sides. It has sharp, short movement, allowing him to wear out the gloveside half of the plate. He mixed in a 78-82 mph curveball for a different breaking look and barely used his mid-80s changeup in ’24. Candiotti did a great job of throwing strikes in each of his last two collegiate seasons, but a significant portion of that was getting batters to expand the zone. That ability will be tested against pro bats. There is a certain temptation to throw Candiotti in the bullpen because of his age -- he'll be 24 entering his first full season -- but given his late college trajectory, he could have a fighting chance to stick in future rotations, too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Etzel spent a semester at Texas A&M then played two seasons at Panola (Texas) JC, but it was actually a stint in the MLB Draft League that set him up for his professional future. He slashed .371/.463/.586 with 25 steals in 33 games there in 2022, putting himself on scouting radars a year before signing with the Orioles as a 10th-rounder out of Southern Mississippi. Baltimore sent him to the Rays as part of a three-prospect package for starter Zach Eflin in July 2024, then Tampa Bay shipped him to the Marlins for Nick Fortes a year later. Etzel’s performance dipped after a promotion to Double-A and fell off when he joined the Rays, as he batted .232 with a .692 OPS and a 35 percent strikeout rate in 36 games for Montgomery. The swing-and-miss jump was somewhat alarming, as Etzel typically makes a fair amount of contact (especially against fastballs) and already puts a lot of balls on the ground. Granted, he has the speed to make that work and added value by stealing 45 bases over 119 games last year, but it will require him to boost his slugging percentage with doubles and triples, not home runs. Despite his above-average speed, Etzel seems likely to settle in at a corner position. He played all three outfield spots at an almost exactly even rate last year and even saw time at first base in an effort to keep his bat in the lineup. He hasn't made much progress at Double-A this year, a telling sign that probably caps his ceiling as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 While Joswa Lugo received the highest bonus of any player from the Angels’ signing class at the start of the 2024 international signing period, De La Rosa received the most of any pitcher signed by the organization, getting $300,000 to get his pro career started. He did that in the Dominican Summer League and put his best foot forward out of the gate, finishing with a 2.79 ERA, .211 BAA and a 9.9 K/9 rate in a typically hitting-friendly environment. At 6-foot-4, the hope is De La Rosa can develop into an innings-eating workhorse-type starter. His fastball maxes out at 96 mph and typically sits 91-94, though the hope is more velocity will come as he matures. He has a solid 77-82 mph slider that flashes above average and could develop into an out pitch. There’s an upper-80s changeup in there, but it’s too firm and it’s behind the other two offerings. For his first time out, De La Rosa did a decent job of being in and around the strike zone. He’ll be just 18 as he comes stateside for the 2025 season and he’s a long way away, but with improved command and velocity to go along with a solid third pitch, he has a big league starter ceiling.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Very projectable righty with beautiful arm action. Naturally cutting fastball in the low 90s, could be plus at peak depending on how strong Hamilton gets. His lower half usage is not as athletically impressive as his arm action. Curveball in the 77-82 mph range is average at times, changeup tends to be below. High-variance dev project with fastball shape in the wheelhouse of many analytically oriented teams.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cohen spent five years at George Washington and was the Colonials' best starter in the final three before signing for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2022. Since missing the first half of the 2024 season with a back strain, he has been one of the most unhittable relievers in the Minors during the past two years, logging a 1.62 ERA and .155 opponent average. Though the Yankees declined to protect him on their 40-man roster this offseason, he slipped through the Rule 5 Draft and will compete for a big league bullpen job in 2026. Cohen's money pitch is a tight mid-80s slider that hitters can't lay off or catch up to when it ventures into the strike zone. His fastball is fairly ordinary, ranging from 92-94 mph and reaching 96 with nice carry at times but also below-average command that can make it vulnerable. His mid-80s changeup with fade and sink can be a solid offering at it's best. Cohen hides the ball well with an up-tempo, upright delivery with a high leg kick. While his mechanics provide deception, they also hamper his control and have resulted in a 12 percent walk rate in pro ball. He profiles more as a middle reliever than a high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Grinsell made a big leap between his sophomore and junior seasons at Oregon, lowering his ERA by a full run and cutting his walk rate in half while becoming just the sixth pitcher in Ducks history to post 200 career strikeouts. While he wasn’t overpowering, his ability to miss bats and his athleticism -- he was a very good two-way player in high school -- led the Tigers to take a sixth-round pick on him in the 2025 Draft and sign him for $297,500. Deception is the name of the game for Grinsell, who doesn’t have a dominant pitch but has a good feel for sequencing and reading hitters. His fastball sits in the low 90s but plays up thanks in part to extension and location. It also sets up an 80 mph changeup that he hides well with a similar delivery. His slider was his third pitch in college. While he fits into the Tigers’ pitching philosophy of commanding the strike zone, he could also add velocity if the club can improve his delivery. Projection can be difficult with a college pitcher, but Grinsell’s athleticism provides some potential for upside if he can find another tick or two on his fastball, which could then make his changeup that much better. He’ll need an effective breaking pitch to make it as a starter, but a good fastball-changeup combination could be the foundation for a potential crafty lefty reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round selection by the A’s in the 2024 MLB Draft out of Boston College, Leary underwhelmed a bit in his first taste of pro ball upon joining the organization. His first full season as a pro went much better, as he began the year at Single-A Stockton and earned a promotion to High-A Lansing, where he held his own over a 33-game stint. Between the two levels, Leary hit .269 with a .798 OPS in 126 games. Leary has above-average power potential which showed up in stints last season, with an ability to hit to all fields after working with the A’s to tighten up his swing. He can draw a decent amount of walks, but his 130 strikeouts last year highlight some swing-and-miss issues that will need to be corrected for him to fully take advantage of that power. Leary might be one of the better baserunners in the entire organization, evident by his 56 stolen bases in ‘25 while getting caught only eight times. Defensively, he can move around well, but his below-average arm likely limits him to left field, though the A’s plan to work with him on his quickening up his release to see if his positional versatility could expand to the other two outfield spots. The A’s are still trying to figure out just what type of player Leary might end up being, but there were some encouraging signs in his first full year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves had a compensation pick after the fourth round of the 2025 Draft after losing Max Fried to free agency. They used it to pick up Williams, a middle infielder who was coming off a solid junior season at East Carolina, finishing with 14 homers and an OPS over 1.000 before going 8-for-20 and being named to the all-tournament team at the NCAA Greenville Regional. He signed for just under $500,000, a bit under slot, becoming the earliest-drafted hitter from the Pirates program since Connor Norby was a second-rounder in 2021. Williams brought his solid approach from the left side of the plate with him during his relatively brief 28-game pro debut last summer with Single-A Augusta. He could be an average hitter in the future with solid on-base skills and strike zone control. He drew more walks than strikeouts in his last year of college, part of what helped him get to his power more, with his over-the-fence pop coming mostly to his pull side. His debut with Augusta was solid, but the Braves think the underlying data points to even better contact rates to come. A plus runner who swiped 22 bases in 25 tries last year at East Carolina, Williams could have a potentially intriguing power-speed combination in the future. Where he ends up defensively is still up in the air. He played second and third in college, and his arm might be a tad short for the hot corner. His best bet long term to stick in one spot might be as an offensive-minded player at the keystone. But he’ll likely move around some, with center field one day not out of the question for a more likely utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were two Indiana natives on the World Cup-winning US 18-and-under national team in 2022: Max Clark and Tilly. While Clark went third overall to the Tigers in the 2023 Draft, Tilly was unselected as MLB Pipeline’s No. 208 prospect in the class and headed to Auburn instead. He pitched primarily out of the bullpen in his two years in the SEC and sported a 5.48 ERA with 58 strikeouts in 46 innings as a Draft-eligible sophomore last year. The Mets took him in the seventh round and signed him for above slot at $397,500 to keep him from heading back to school. The Mets have early interest in developing Tilly as a starter because of his interesting pitch mix. His fastball sits at 92-94 mph, touching 97, and because of the average velocity, he was willing to go liberally to his secondaries in his final season on campus. Since his amateur days, Tilly has earned praise for the high spin rates on his low-80s slider, and he’s developed his mid-80s splitter into arguably an even better pitch, one with enough dip and movement to cause lefties fits. Tilly also worked in another high-spin curveball in the mid 70s with Auburn but saved it mostly for early counts. Tilly walked 13.4 percent of the batters he faced in his two years at Auburn -- a rate that would keep anyone in the bullpen early in their collegiate career -- but the Mets believe there’s untapped pitchability there, especially if they can tame some of his spinnier options. There’s a good chance Tilly would have gotten starting looks as junior anyways, and now that can happen under the eye of a New York organization that has specialized in pitching development in recent years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly was a two-sport standout who didn't stop playing football until his senior year of high school. He was on scouts' radars in southern California but headed to pitch at UC Irvine. Although Injuries interrupted his progress over his two first years with the Anteaters, a chance to move into their rotation in March of his junior year allowed him to take off. He landed in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft, and while he didn't pitch officially after signing, he got in some good work during instructs. An athletic 6-foot-5 right-hander, Kelly entered pro ball with three pitches and might now have four at his disposal. The Rockies are hoping there might be another tier of velocity to reach with his fastball, which currently sits in the 91-94 mph range, occasionally touching 96. It has some good metrics with some ride and finish to the pitch. But Kelly's really all about the spin. His upper-70s curve has 11-to-5 shape and regularly tops 3,000 rpm, and he can miss bats with his low-80s changeup as well. During instructs, he found a slider grip that works for him, giving him a fourth pitch that could be Major League average. Kelly started throwing better quality strikes when he became a starter during his junior year, and the hope is that trend continues. He has the pitch mix to start and will be given the opportunity to stick in a rotation if he can hold the zone consistently throughout his outings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De la Rosa signed with the Yankees out of the Dominican Republic for $400,000 last April, receiving the third-highest bonus given to any left-hander on the 2025 international market. He quickly stood out with his stuff and strikes during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, drawing immediate trade interest. Three months after he turned pro, the Giants acquired him in a four-prospect package in exchange for Camilo Doval. De la Rosa works with a 92-94 mph fastball that reaches 96 with significant carry as well as armside run. Both of his secondary pitches also show promise. He throws both a tight slider and a sweepier version in the low 80s, and his fading changeup is a tick harder. While De La Rosa has three legitimate pitches and posted a 7 percent walk rate in his first taste of pro ball, there are questions about his ability to remain a starter in the long run. He's undersized and works uphill with some funk in his arm action, though his delivery provides deception without costing him control. If he does land in the bullpen, he has the upside to work in a late-inning role.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Pestka was one of a couple Reds' 2023 draft-and-follow prospects who played amateur ball in 2024 before agreeing to a deal with Cincy that May; Petska was committed to Tennessee and would have pitched there in 2025 had he not agreed to a deal. Instead he pitched in Daytona for a second summer and worked 54 innings in 31 relief outings. Petska has a great curveball and good feel for locating his pitches. He isn't a great athlete, but his delivery is easy and repeatable, and he located his fastball consistently in 2025 even though he was throwing two ticks harder than in pro ball the year before. Petska's pure breaking ball quality is the kind commonly seen in big league bullpens. His curveball freezes opposing hitters and is an effective strike-one offering, preceding elevated fastballs. A new cutter rounds out a deep mix of breaking balls that should eventually facilitate a middle relief role. Consider Petska a candidate for accelerated promotion in 2026, as his 40-man platform year is already upon us.

fangraphs.label: bos2026may
fangraphs.text:
At 29, Gamboa is one of the oldest players we’ll rank this list cycle. He’s had a full baseball life already. He originally went to Fresno State out of high school, but blew out and was an elder statesman at Fresno City College when the Dodgers plucked him in the 2019 draft. He slowly climbed the ranks with L.A. and sort of developed into the pitching equivalent of Ryan Ward : talented enough for the big leagues, but stuck in Oklahoma City in an org overflowing with pitching depth. He spent most of 2025 dealing for Lotte in the KBO, a stint he parlayed into a minor league contract with Boston this past winter. He made his long overdue big league debut earlier this season, firing a scoreless inning and striking out two.

Gamboa’s rock-and-fire delivery feeds into a high overhand release. He sits in the low-to-mid-90s throughout his starts with good, if unexceptional, carry. The curve is a shapely steal-a-strike offering, while the slider is a tight and hard breaker that flashes above average. It looks like he takes something off on his secondaries, particularly his changeup, though the pitch is playing just fine in Triple-A this year. Gamboa is peppering the zone this season, which is unusual, as he’s been more of a nibbler and fringy control pitcher throughout his career.

There aren’t a ton of stretched lefties with average arm strength and a starter’s repertoire toiling in the minors. Crazy as it is to say about a 29-year-old with very little major league experience, this looks like a no. 5 starter, or at the very least a perfectly fine one-time-through guy. Gamboa’s below-average command and lack of a bat-misser may ultimately get exposed at the highest level, but there are a half-dozen clubs around the league who could justify giving him a look in their rotation tomorrow. For his sake, hopefully Gamboa can find his way into one of those organizations in short order.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Mahoney played both ways a little bit as an underclassman. He pitched out of the bullpen during most of his freshman year, then missed 2022 recovering from Tommy John, though he was still able to hit a little bit that year. He held 92-94 and touched 96-97 across 16 starts as a junior. His fastball tails, and he commands a short, mid-80s slider sitting 84-86 mph and has arm-side changeup feel. His secondaries aren't all that nasty, but Mahoney's feel for location is advanced considering his lack of college reps. There's a backend starter projection here, with a non-zero chance he's scratching the surface of more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2023 NCAA Division II player of the year after batting .408/.506/.901 with a school-record 28 homers at Point Loma Nazarene (Calif.), Christian transferred to San Diego for his Draft year. The Toreros' best power prospect since Kris Bryant, he slashed .364/.460/.828 with 26 homers to win West Coast Conference player of the year honors. He played briefly in Single-A after signing for $397,500 as a fifth-rounder. Christian's 6-foof-5, 225-pound frame gives him tremendous strength and leverage, and his right-handed stroke provides plenty of bat speed and loft. That combination results in well above-average raw power that allows him to smash balls out of any part of the ballpark. He does come with an aggressive approach and swing-and-miss concerns, especially against non-fastballs, and he struggled to produce with wood bats in college summer leagues. Christian moves well for his size, displaying fringy speed with decent instincts on the bases. After playing first base at Point Loma Nazarene, he moved to right field at San Diego and spent most of his short pro debut in left field. He has adequate range and average arm strength on the outfield corners.

fangraphs.label: 2024updated
fangraphs.text: Well-built 6-foot-4 righty with mid-90s fastball and two breaking balls. Pitched sparingly as an underclassman due to injuries and wasn't great when he did. Big velo boost in his draft year, now sitting 93-95. Higher release creates downhill dilution of his fastball but adds depth to low-80s curveball, Eagen's best breaking ball. Small school dev project with arm strength and up-pointing arrow in 2024.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bigbie hit the prospect radar in 2023 coming off an eye-opening season that vaulted him three levels and garnered comparisons to another former Tigers 19th-round Draft pick, Kerry Carpenter. Bigbie spent the 2024 season at Triple-A Toledo but struggled to carry the momentum in a frustrating season, including just four home runs in 135 games. The Tigers left him off their 40-man roster at season’s end. Bigbie climbed the Tigers' system with an all-fields approach that allowed him to stay on time for fastballs, still be aggressive on offspeed pitches and remain patient for high walk rates. That approach was tested in Triple-A. Bigbie actually improved his plate discipline, boosting his walk rate while making more consistent contact in the strike zone. But while his contact rate improved, his ground-ball rate soared, comprising more than half of his balls in play. He also oddly struggled to hit left-handed pitching. Defensively, the converted first baseman has shown steady improvement as a corner outfielder, though his arm strength limits his ability to hold runners. Bigbie is a prime example of why the Triple-A level and its more experienced pitching remains a critical step on the way up the system. He could yet be a late bloomer and break into the Majors as an extra outfielder if he can get back to spraying line drives to all fields. But at 26, this is a big year for his career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After four years at the University of San Diego, the last of which saw him homer 16 times and hit .373, Ricketts was taken in the seventh round of the 2022 Draft by the Phillies. He’s managed to play his way to the upper levels of the system in his first two years of pro ball, though injuries have hampered his development and he’s yet to top 275 at-bats in a single season. Hopes that making up for lost time in the Arizona Fall League in 2023 would serve as a springboard were dashed when he posted a .670 OPS with Double-A Reading in 2024. While Ricketts’ numbers with Reading were disappointing, he still checks off some boxes and has some traits the Phillies like. He’s a left-handed hitting catcher, always a hot commodity, and he makes a lot of contact and gets on base at a solid clip. He hasn’t impacted the ball consistently, though he’s shown some ability to drive the ball to his pull side. He’s a sneaky good athlete who runs well for a catcher. Ricketts had split time between catching and playing first base at the outset of his pro career, but he was exclusively a backstop in 2024 and the organization was pleased with the progress he made with his receiving and game-calling. He’s still working on his throwing stroke to improve his arm strength and accuracy, as he’d been prone to dropping to a lower slot at times. He probably has a ceiling as a big league backup if it clicks.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Smooth-operating southpaw with upper-80s to low-90s heat. Feel for location, quality fastball strikes. Similarly advanced slider feel in the 78-81 mph range. Better in the zone than as a finisher right now. Late-arriving arm strength, spring breakout guy with starter mechanics and feel.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery ended Patteson’s 2022 college season early at Central Florida, but the Royals were convinced enough in their scouting of him and his makeup that they still drafted him in the fifth round that year. It took Patteson time to come back from the injury and start to make an impact, but his stuff shot up in 2025. He made 13 starts in High-A with a 1.99 ERA, while holding batters to a .199 average. He finished the year with 11 appearances (eight starts) in Double-A, where he had a 4.41 ERA. Patteson’s fastball hovered around 90-92 mph over the past few years, but once he got to Double-A in ‘25, he started running it up to the mid 90s and touching 97. The velo spike, which was more about a return to his pre-TJ form, also helped his main breaking ball become more firm as a mid-80s average slider that tries to be gyro but can get a little sweepy. Patteson also throws a curveball with good depth and feel to land it for strikes. His best weapon, though, is a mid-80s changeup with plus potential. Patteson throws strikes and has a clean delivery, hiding the ball well with short arm action. Lauded for his pitchability and being a student of the game, Patteson might be a late bloomer but is really coming into his own now that he’s reached the upper levels. He needs to show more consistency at Double-A and continue to refine his secondaries, but if the stuff continues to look like what it did there in ‘25, he has back-end rotation potential. The Royals might try him in the bullpen to see whether the stuff ticks up even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After putting himself on the Draft radar with three solid years at South Florida, Boser transferred to the University of Florida and boosted his stock as a senior with an impressive season. Entering the 2025 MLB Draft on MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 list, Boser landed with the A’s as an 11th-round pick.
