Ahead of his first full season as a pro, he got his feet wet with 32 games at Single-A Stockton. Boser has an intriguing profile as a hitter. He’s got some power to all fields and showed he can do some damage with the bat in college with good bat speed and balance at the plate. There’s also a bit of swing-and-miss to his game, which he’ll have to improve to tap into that power as a pro. Boser fits the mold of a versatile utility player who can provide strong defense at multiple positions that the A’s traditionally value highly, similar to past prospects such as Jeremy Eierman and Max Schueman. He has a good, accurate arm that should allow him to get plenty of reps at shortstop, third base and second base. He also worked to improve his athleticism in college, and that shows through on the bases as a decent runner. There is a solid floor here as a productive super-utility type, and the A’s liked what they saw from him at first glance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly bounced around a bit as an amateur, going from a two-way high school standout in Northern California to starting his college career at Texas A&M. After a redshirt year, he moved to McLennan Community College and played both ways, then was on the move again, this time to Arizona State as a pitcher only. He missed a bunch of bats as a reliever, helping him land in the sixth round of the 2025 Draft, and he headed up to High-A to get his feet wet professionally. He capped things off by striking out the side to get the save that gave Everett a Northwest League championship. The 6-foot-4 Kelly is strong and physical and comes at hitters largely with a two-pitch mix and a funky delivery. His four-seam fastball topped out at 99 mph in college, and it misses bats thanks to its carry up in the zone. He backs it up with his 79-84 mph slider that can have good depth and bite to it at times, a breaking ball that could be at least above average if he can find the strike zone with it more. He had a changeup for lefties on occasion at ASU, but he might not need it, and there was some talk of him bringing a two-seamer he used to feature back into his repertoire. Kelly’s unusual mechanics come with a ton of effort and a low three-quarters arm slot and cross-body delivery. But he tends to get down the mound well and throw a decent amount of strikes. If he can be around the zone enough, especially with his slider, it’s not out of the question to see him in high-leverage relief situations in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Girton played three springs at Texas Tech but never found a regular spot in the rotation -- an injury-marred 2022 didn’t help -- and transferred to Oklahoma in '24. Ten of his 16 appearances with the Sooners were starts, but success was still limited with a 7.32 ERA, 47 strikeouts and 31 walks in 35 2/3 innings. The Mets selected him in the 10th round -- two rounds after taking OU teammate Ryan Lambert -- and signed him for below slot at $122,500. Girton dominated High-A Brooklyn in his first full season, posting a 2.59 ERA with 91 strikeouts in 76 1/3 innings, before slowing down in his final four starts with Double-A Binghamton. The 6-foot-1 right-hander pitches with bounce in his delivery and throws from a high three-quarters slot. His four-seam fastball can move in the mid 90s and acted like a downright weapon with cut-ride action at the top of the zone, getting whiffs on one-third of opponents’ swings against it across both levels in 2025. Girton works with two slider variations -- a mid-80s sweeper with a ton of horizontal break and a tighter upper-80s option that practically acts like a cutter. He has talked about adding a splitter but went to very little offspeed last season. Luckily for him, the sweeper can backfoot lefties well and helped fend off splits issues. Girton really struggled to deliver consistent strikes in school and looked to correct course midseason in ’25, only to struggle again after his move to the Eastern League. He’s already entering his age-24 season and might not have too long of a leash for starting, now that he’s seen the upper Minors, unless the control is ironed out or he finds a split/change. Even so, the fastball/sliders could put him on the fast track to Queens on their own.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Blanco is a gigantic corner outfield/1B prospect with arguably the most present raw power in the January 2022 signing group. He absolutely towers over his father, who was twice a Baseball America Top 100 prospect but spent most of his pro career in Japan. The recent track record of hitters this size is not favorable, with only Franmil Reyes really panning out, but it's exciting to watch Blanco take BP and see how loose and athletic he is for his size. He signed for $900,000 and will be an unmistakable fixture on Pittsburgh's backfields for the next couple of years.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Born in Puerto Rico and raised for a bit in the U.S., Mercedes eventually settled in the D.R., where he became a prototypical right field prospect with plus potential power and arm strength. The Twins signed him for $1.7 million in January.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Merejo was born in Florida and grew up there before moving to the Dominican Republic late in his high school career and signing for $340,000 in 2023. He followed up a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League by coming to the United States at age 18 last year. After beginning the season in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, he concluded it by batting .282/.372/.466 in the final month Single-A as one of the Carolina League's youngest players. Unlike most of the Guardians' international signings, Merejo stands out more for his power than his hitting ability. His physicality and the bat speed in his right-handed stroke produce plus raw pop, and he taps into most of it by concentrating on driving balls in the air to his pull side too. He has some feel to hit and is willing to take walks, though he'll have to tone down his approach because it leaves him vulnerable to non-fastballs. Most of Merejo's value will come from his bat. Though he stole 11 bases in 77 games last year, he's a below-average runner who's probably limited to first base. He committed 10 errors in 53 starts there in 2024 while also getting time on the outfield corners, where he displayed solid arm strength but substandard range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barnett headed to Division II Wingate as a two-way player before exploding offensively as a junior in 2024. His 26 homers were second-most for that level of collegiate baseball, while his .739 slugging percentage placed 32nd among qualifiers. He posted a .349 average and 1.138 OPS over his 59 games with the Bulldogs while also making six appearances out of the bullpen, striking out seven and walking six over five frames. The Padres took him in the 11th round in the '24 Draft and signed him for $175,000 ($25,000 of which counted toward their bonus pool). Barnett only hit and played corner outfield with Single-A Lake Elsinore after joining the organization, but he pitched in late workouts and turned more than a few heads on the mound. He ran his fastball up to 97 and averaged closer to the mid-90s. His slider sat in the upper-80s with a hard cutter-like break, and that pitch could easily be a weapon, too. The ball comes out of his 6-foot-2 frame easily, and his delivery isn’t overcomplicated. With his position-player background and athleticism, he could get to average control with the right professional instruction. As much as many in the organization prefer Barnett’s work on the mound, the Padres will still give him a chance to DH part-time to begin his first full season. His power is undeniable from the right side, but he really struggled against non-fastballs in the California League last year. Had Barnett shown this level of stuff more consistently, some believe he would have gone several rounds earlier as a pitcher alone, and that’s likely where his future lies.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hipwell played just 76 games in three seasons at Santa Clara and had little experience with wood bats in summer ball, so he was tougher to evaluate than most collegians in the 2024 Draft. He lost the final three weeks of his sophomore year and the first two months of his junior season to a suspension for performance-enhancing drugs, which he attributed to an over-the-counter supplement. Signed for $345,700 as a sixth-rounder, he batted .196/.360/.402 with five homers and 40 strikeouts in his 29-game pro debut in Single-A. Hipwell is built to hit for a power with a quick left-handed stroke with loft, a strong 6-foot-3 frame and a pull-focused mindset. He has a patient-bordering-on-passive approach that results in walks, but it also leaves him behind in counts too often and leads to strikeouts. He pounds fastballs but had a 38 percent swing-and-miss rate against non-heaters in his debut. With below-average speed, Hipwell offers little value on the bases and limited range at third base. His solid arm strength fits the hot corner, but he's an erratic defender who may have to move. He played some right field and first base with the Broncos and also dabbled at second base in the MLB Draft League.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Callahan was a career .351 hitter at St. Joseph’s and posted an OPS above 1.000 in both his sophomore and junior years with the Hawks. But questions about how he’d hold up against better competition dropped him to the 13th round in 2023, and the Tigers picked and signed him for $197,500. He’s shown flashes of dominance at virtually every stop since but has struggled with injuries, including a dislocated finger and right lower leg hematoma in 2024 and a pulled quad in 2025. He finally cracked Double-A to begin 2026 -- his age-24 season -- with positive results out of the gate. A left-handed hitter, Callahan has long shown promising raw power as a professional, and he proved that this spring in limited Grapefruit League looks with a pair of home runs hit above 105 mph and one batted ball at 112.2 mph. But an overly aggressive approach early in his career seriously put into question how much of that pop translated into game action at the upper levels. Callahan, who has gone from an open stance to one more straight-on while keeping his leg kick, has been less swing-happy to begin ’26, allowing his walk rate to double in the season’s first month and making a potential MLB future all the clearer. Standing 6-foot, the former Atlantic 10 first-teamer can get moving out of the box, and he’s proven capable of making strong throws from the grass. The Tigers have rotated him around the outfield because of both skillsets, and he could prove to be above-average defensively in a corner. Much will come down to maintaining his early swing-decision improvements, especially with Rule 5 eligibility coming up this offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros paid the two highest bonuses in their 2025 international class to a pair of players who trained together in Santo Domingo, D.R. Cuban outfielder Kevin Alvarez signed for $2 million, while Venezuelan infielder Manzueta turned pro for $847,500. The latter slashed .224/.405/.392 with 42 walks in 47 games during his pro debut as one of the youngest players (age 16) in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Manzueta stands out with his advanced feel for the barrel and his control of the strike zone. He has a sound right-handed stroke and recognizes pitches well. He won't be physically imposing and needs to add strength to his 5-foot-10 frame, but his ability to turn on pitches and square them up gives him some sneaky power that could translate into 12-15 homers per season. While Manzueta trained as a shortstop, his below-average speed and average arm strength aren't suited for the position. He played there briefly in the DSL while spending most of his time alternating between second base and third base. He profiles best at the keystone and could wind up a utilityman who derives much of his value from his on-base skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taurek redshirted his freshman year at St. Mary’s in 2023, then played sparingly the next season. He made it count in 2025, earning second-team All-West Coast Conference honors while hitting .328 with 11 homers and helping the Gaels win the WCC tournament and reach NCAA Regional play. The Mariners liked his swing enough to take a $150,000 flier on him in the 13th round of the Draft, and he went out and hit some more, posting a .336 average over 27 games with Single-A Modesto during his pro debut. The one thing that seems certain about Taurek is that he can make a lot of contact with a chance to hit at this level. He’s small and compact and so is his right-handed swing, with simple mechanics and direct to the ball action. He does not strike out much -- just 9.5 percent with the Gaels in ‘25 -- and while he’s very aggressive at the plate and doesn’t walk a ton, he also limits chase. He’s not all that projectable from a physicality standpoint, and it’s unclear whether he’ll have that much impact. Taurek is a bit of a tweener defensively. He doesn’t have enough speed to play center field regularly -- he played left exclusively at St. Mary’s, and that’s where he spent most of his time during his pro debut. But he doesn’t have enough thump to profile as an everyday guy in a corner. The right-right undersized profile is a tough one, but he’s swung the bat well enough to make him interesting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An alumnus of MLB Develops programs like the Hank Aaron Invitational and Breakthrough Series, Drake was a toolsy outfielder from Atlanta who went to the MLB Draft League to test his mettle ahead of the 2023 Draft. He performed well over a small sample there ahead of the Braves taking him in the fifth round of that July’s Draft and going over slot -- close to $750,000 -- to sign him away from his commitment to Georgia Tech. The younger brother of former NFL running back Kenyan Drake, Isaiah really struggled in his first full season of pro ball, but made some great adjustments in 2025 to perform his way from Single-A Augusta to High-A Rome in his age-19 season. The Braves knew it might take a while for things to click for Drake, and when they sent him to Augusta in 2024 to sink or swim, he sunk, hitting .163 with a 35.5 percent strikeout rate in 69 games in the Carolina League. He slashed that last year with just a 21.3 percent K rate across two levels, and his overall miss and chase rates also went down. Strong and physical, the next step in his development with his improved ability to make contact might be tapping into his considerable raw power more consistently. Drake loves to run, swiping 46 bags last year, with some scouts putting an 80 run grade on him. That helps him go get the ball in center field and he’s improved in that facet of the game as well. There’s work to be done still, but he could be a plus defender when all is said and done. This was a bit of a lottery ticket for the Braves, but if his aptitude keeps trending in this direction, they could cash in.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pitts was a “famous” high schooler in the Atlanta area at a very early age, and he actually committed to the University of South Carolina as a shortstop before he even began his high school career. By the time his Draft year came around in 2025, he had moved to the outfield and changed his college commitment to the University of South Florida. He might have had the chance to move up boards more during his senior year, but a hamstring issue slowed him considerably. After being able to work him out a couple of times and getting to know more about his makeup, the Reds rolled the dice and took him in the fifth round, going a little over slot at $575,000 to sign him. Pitts didn’t make his pro debut after signing and he was slow coming out of the spring as he continued to nurse his hamstring back to health. The Reds think this was a good upside play based on his athleticism and potential to stay up the middle. A right-handed hitter and thrower, Pitts’ carrying tool is the speed he wasn’t able to showcase much his senior year, getting 70 grades from some evaluators when he’s healthy. He’s shown off solid raw power at times and a decent feel for hitting that gives some hope he can tap into that pop consistently in the future. That plus speed is also an asset defensively, and Pitts has the athleticism to play center field at the next level, albeit with an arm that needs work. It’s a bit of a lottery ticket given that he wasn’t seen that much in 2025, but if he can get past the hamstring problems, there’s some ceiling for him to grow into.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Cutter: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 Dalena shares an alma mater of Montoursville Area (Pa.) HS with Mike Mussina and was mentored by the Hall of Fame pitcher growing up in the Keystone State. After a stint at Monmouth in 2021-22, he played both ways at Division II Shippensburg in 2023, turned toward pitching in ’24 and posted a 3.36 ERA and a 1.17 WHIP with 99 strikeouts in 83 innings as a graduate student in ’25. The Padres took him in the sixth round, making him the first Shippensburg player selected since 2018 and the highest since 1999, and signed him for $10,000. Dalena made three brief appearances for Single-A Lake Elsinore in his pro debut. The 6-foot-3 right-hander is entering his age-24 campaign in his first full season but has some upside given his limited background. He was sitting mid-90s with impressive ride up in the zone after signing, and it’s a pitch he uses to set up the rest of his repertoire. It’s likely to be a true north-south look with an upper-70s curveball that drops off the table and a low-80s slider that stands out more for its drop than sweep. The deuce has better action and got more whiffs in his final collegiate season, but finding a consistent preferred breaking pitch will be a priority in ’26. Dalena also worked with a cutter and a changeup, the latter of which he struggled to command in his brief pro look in the California League. Dalena has a history of landing multiple pitches in the zone though, and he’d come up in offseason trade talks with other clubs intrigued by his early mix. He must prove his stuff can play beyond Division II, but the quality of the arsenal could make him a quality low-money, middle-round sign.

fangraphs.label: bos2026may
fangraphs.text: Brannon is a power goof with a short, rock solid build. He’s been developed as a catcher throughout his career, though most scouts expected him to wind up at first base, which has finally come to pass this season. Perhaps not coincidentally, he’s flourished with the bat in 2026, and is hitting .317/.429/.762 (190 wRC+) with seven dingers and a career high 15.6% walk rate. He’s still striking out more than you’d like, but his swing-and-miss numbers are better overall, and down considerably against fastballs. He’s made a slight adjustment to his swing and setup this year as well. He used to step in the bucket toward third, but has now fully spread out and doesn’t have a stride at all, which seems to be helping him stay in and cover the plate. He gets low and lets it fly in a way that reminds us of Tyler White , though Brannon is primarily a middle-of-the-field shooter. Like White, he could have a productive, bat-only prime.

fangraphs.label: 2022updated
fangraphs.text: Rumors are that Kennedy, who is committed to LSU, is going to be a pretty tough sign. He's one of the younger players available in the draft and yet at a listed 205 pounds, he is more physically mature than most of his peers, even some of the ones who are a year or more older than he is. What he does bring to the table is significant fastball utility. While he has a low three-quarters slot, Kennedy's fastball still has riding life at the letters, and he can impart two-plane sweep on his breaking ball (it could stand to have more consistent depth, but the flashes are there), working to the back foot of righties while also landing his breaker in the zone against lefties, who struggle to deal with his arm slot. His delivery is simple, compact, repeatable, and easy-looking, and you can project heavily on his changeup, though he often gets underneath it and it tends to cut on him. Even though Kennedy is 17, you're not really projecting on his frame in a positive way so much as it feels possible he could have impact command at maturity, because his delivery is so effortless and the quality of his fastball strikes so advanced.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While fellow infielder Nestor Miranda was the Tigers’ headline signing of the 2024 international class, Dickson had the better introduction to pro ball after signing for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He was one of the more impressive performers for the Tigers in the Dominican Summer League and earned a spot in the DSL All-Star Game. Dickerson has a lanky, athletic build with a solid swing that becomes more formidable as he physically matures. He had a leg kick when he signed, but the Tigers worked to quiet his stance. He was pull heavy in the DSL with a high rate of ground balls and fly balls and good extra-base power without a home run, but his aggressive approach was tempered by a good eye at the plate for his age. He’s an opportunistic baserunner whose high stolen-base total in the DSL came with a good success rate. He moves well at shortstop but could move positions as he fills out. Dickson’s success in the DSL should move him to the Florida Complex League as an 18-year-old. He has the tools to become a promising prospect, but his physical maturation will have a big impact on his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Columbia, Mo., native and Missouri State product, Nivens was the Royals’ fifth round selection in the 2023 Draft, signing for just above slot at $472,500. He was slowed out of the gate in ‘24 with High-A Quad Cities, dealt with a hamstring strain in April and didn’t hit well in the first half with a .168 average through June and a high strikeout rate. He absolutely turned it on in the second half, though, and especially in August, when he hit 13 home runs alone. In all, Nivens slashed .243/.333/.475 with 20 homers and 17 doubles. Nivens clearly has power, especially pull side, and can drive the ball, but he was more aggressive in his first full season of pro ball than what he showed in college, striking out at a 26.9% clip. A lot of that was the inconsistency in his stance with a hand pump, a leg kick that can turn into a hang and a lot of moving parts that get exposed as a pro. He toned that down some in the second half and is continuing to simplify and sync up the movements to get on time, because when he does, it’s above-average power. Nivens fits best in the corner outfield with his power, and most likely left field with his below-average arm strength and average speed once he gets going. There weren’t many hitters who did what Nivens did in August 2024, and his second half surely could give him momentum as he likely heads to Double-A in ‘25. Nivens needs to stay consistent with his movements and keep hitting to reach the big leagues and stick there as a fourth-outfielder type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants drafted Heliot Ramos in the first round out of the Leadership Christian Academy (Guaynabo, P.R.) in 2017, then went back there six years later to take Ortiz in the 13th round. He impressed with his athleticism on the U.S. high school showcase circuit and continued to do so in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League the last two years. Promoted to Single-A last August, he banged up his knee running into the outfield wall in his first game, ending his 2024 season. Ortiz isn't very physical, so he focuses on making contact and getting on base. He has good feel for his right-handed swing and the strike zone and looked more comfortable against pro pitching during his second stint in the ACL. He did a better job of turning on pitches and lifting them last summer, so he could grow into 12-15 homer power once he fills out his 5-foot-11 frame. Ortiz earns plus grades for his speed, arm and center-field defense. He has the mentality and aptitude to steal bases, and the instincts enhance his range in center. His arm is stronger than most at his position, adding to his credentials as the system's best defensive outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a notable freshman year at Arizona State in which he was honorable mention All-Pac-12, the Louisiana native transferred closer to home to Mississippi. He proved to be one of the more disciplined hitters in the Southeastern Conference, and his high floor helped him go in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft, where the Guardians signed him to an above-slot $722,600 bonus. The infielder thrived during a 15-game cameo at Single-A, where he slashed .347/.459/.510 with seven steals and as many walks as strikeouts. Built strongly at 6-foot-1, 200 pounds, Hill retains a hit-over-power profile. His combination of strong swing decisions and in-zone contact enables him to run high walk rates, although he can struggle with whiffs when he does swing out of the zone, in particular on secondary pitches. He has a sound right-handed swing and consistently makes strong contact, but his habit of hitting the ball on the ground and the other way caps his power ceiling. If he is able to catch the ball out front more, he could project to hit more than 15 homers per season. Hill has below-average speed, his weakest tool in a well-rounded skillset, although he's a heady baserunner who may be able to nab double-digit bags in the big leagues. That lack of range caused him to shift from shortstop in college to third base and second, where he's currently splitting time. His average arm should be enough for either position, and he could also see time at first base (or an outfield corner) for increased defensive versatility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coming out of San Diego’s St. Augustine HS, Boles got time on the showcase circuit in 2024 and even started the High School All-American Game in his native city at Petco Park that August, picking up a pair of strikeouts in his lone frame. He had a commitment to Texas and looked likely to head to Austin as the 2025 Draft passed before the Royals selected him in the 18th round. Kansas City eventually signed the right-hander for $500,000 ($350,000 of which counted toward its Draft pool), and that was the sixth-highest bonus in the organization’s 2025 class. Already standing in at 6-foot-5, Boles is all about projection. He ran his fastball up to 94 mph in his final amateur season, and it’s easy to dream on him sitting mid-90s more regularly as he fills out that frame with strength in the pros. His low-80s slider also shows present and future promise with impressive spin and sharp movement to the glove side. He can also flash a solid mid-80s changeup to give him an offspeed pitch going the other way while his slow curveball doesn’t look like a true weapon. Boles could be all around the zone at times heading into the Draft, and tightening up his slinging delivery should be a focus on the pro side. The Royals tend to take things slowly with prep arms early in their careers, and Boles will be no exception as he’ll open his age-19 season in the Arizona Complex League with the goal of cracking Single-A Columbia at some point in 2026. He has received positive reviews from Royals officials for his willingness to take pro-level instruction, and that combined with his stuff gives him higher upside than a traditional 18th-round flier.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Benny Agbayani spent parts of five seasons in the big leagues after being a late-round Draft pick out of Hawaii Pacific University in 1993. When the Twins took his son Bruin out of the Hawaiian high school ranks in the sixth round of the 2025 Draft, he beat his dad by 24 rounds, signing with the Twins for just over $380,000. He got his feet wet with a handful of games with Single-A Fort Myers after signing. A 6-foot-2 left-handed hitter who earned Hawaii Gatorade Player of the Year honors last year, Agbayani enters pro ball with a very good feel to hit. He routinely finds the barrel with outstanding bat speed and while he’s a hit-over-power type, there is some thump, especially to his pull side, which was on display when he ripped a 106 mph triple to right-center field in the MLB Draft Combine High School Game last June. There should be extra-base impact to come in the future as well. Agbayani likes to use his above-average speed on the basepaths, but few think he has the ability to stay at shortstop -- his high school position -- not only because of a lack of range, but also because he doesn’t possess the actions or hands for the premium spot. He’ll still get reps there, but his best chance of staying on the dirt will likely be second base, though some amateur scouts thought an outfield corner will make the most sense long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It has been well documented several times on the current Angels' Top 30 that this organization likes rolling the dice on high-end high school pitchers in later rounds of the Draft. In 2025, they did it five times, acquiring a group that included LaCourse in Round 6, making him the first Michigander prep pitcher to be taken in the top 10 rounds since Brock Porter was a fourth-rounder in 2022. The Angels went about $120,000 over slot to sign the right-hander away from his commitment to Michigan State. LaCourse’s size, projection and feel for spin all stood out to the Angels scouting staff. The 6-foot-3 starter routinely hits elite spin rate levels with his slider, registering consistently north of 3,000 RPMs with what could be a true out-pitch in time. While he had touched 93-94 mph in short stints in high school, he was more around 88-92 mph with his fastball as a starter, though Angels player development staff have been pleased to see that his velocity is starting to creep up. He throws the heater with a lot of spin for good carry up in the zone to miss bats. His changeup has also improved under pro supervision in the early going. A strong athlete who played basketball in the winter and shortstop when he wasn’t pitching as a prepster, LaCourse does an excellent job of filling up the strike zone with all of his offerings. If the early gains are for real and he can continue to add strength and velocity, he could turn into an inning-eating starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Michigander during his high school days, Steensma headed to Boone, North Carolina, home to Appalachian State, for college ball. After pitching out of the bullpen as the Mountaineers' closer, racking up seven saves as a freshman in 2023, he moved into the rotation as a sophomore, finishing among the Sun Belt Conference top 10 in a host of pitching categories. An elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery in December 2024 kept him off the mound in '25, but a combination of Mariners scouts and their analytics department saw enough potential from his performance the year prior to take him in the ninth round of last July's Draft. Now healthy, he got off to a very good start during his pro debut at Single-A in 2026. A strong 6-foot-4 right-hander, Steensma has a potential four-pitch mix that gives him a chance to start. While his fastball sits 92-93 mph and touches 95, it plays up and misses bats thanks to riding life that comes as a result of the combination of good extension and low release height. His tight mid-80s slider has ticked up since his college days and could be an out pitch in time. He'll mix in an 80 mph curve, and while he does have a potentially serviceable changeup, he wasn't throwing it much at the outset of his pro career. The Mariners are bullish about Steensma because he's still learning how to mix his pitches effectively. He was throwing a ton of strikes out of the gate, with the organization thinking he could have future plus command. They don't want to put unfair expectations on him, but the Mariners have done excellent development work with formerly injured college arms taken later on Day 2 of the Draft, like sixth-rounder-turned-All-Star Bryan Woo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jarvis spent four years at the University of Alabama, serving as the Crimson Tide's regular shortstop from 2021-2023, building a resume as a gritty glove-first middle infielder without that much of an offensive profile. The Tigers gave him a chance as their 11th-round pick in 2023 and he had reached Double-A in 2025 mostly because of his defense and heady play. The Braves picked him up at last year's Trade Deadline in return for Rafael Montero, touching Triple-A before the end of the season and finishing up with a stint in the Arizona Fall League. He was a bit more productive with the bat back in Triple-A to start the 2026 season, earning his first call up to the big leagues in early May. An undersized left-handed hitting infielder, Jarvis has always displayed an ability to make contact. He walked more than he struck out in his Alabama career and he carried a strikeout rate under 14 percent in the Minors into the 2026 season while continuing to draw a fair share of walks. He's never going to have much impact at the plate, though he was showing some ability to hit the ball harder with Gwinnett prior to his first call up. While he has just average speed, he's an above-average baserunner who can swipe a base thanks to excellent instincts. Those instincts are also a huge asset on the dirt. He's a plus defender at short, with excellent actions and a slow game clock. He has all the tools to play the premium position at the highest level while also showing he's capable of playing outstanding defense at third and second as well as he tries to carve out a career as a big league utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heredia joined the Phillies in the winter of 2021, signing for $300,000, and the early returns were very positive. He played well in the Dominican Summer League in '22 and performed well enough to climb from the Florida Complex League to full-season Clearwater the following year. He struggled with his approach -- and with staying healthy -- in '24, while better production in '25 with High-A Jersey Shore was cut short by a broken pinky. He got off to a solid start, albeit with similar approach issues, with a move to Double-A in '26. A strong and athletic right-handed-hitting outfielder, Heredia has shown glimpses of using all five tools, with hard contact from the right side of the plate and the ability to get to his power. He improved his bat-to-ball skills in 2025 after having worked with Luis Arraez's hitting guy in the offseason prior, but he'll have to watch his swing-and-miss and chase rates if he wants to keep being productive. Heredia isn't a burner and isn't much of a basestealing threat, but the strong and compact outfielder runs better than you might think. He has the kind of plus arm teams like to see in right field, and he continues to get work in both outfield corners. If he can refine his approach at the plate, he might have the offensive profile to fit in one of those spots at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montgomery was well-known as an Orlando-area high schooler and slotted in at No. 34 on MLB Pipeline’s 2020 Draft rankings. The shortened Draft and his strong commitment to Florida State kept him from being drafted that year, but he never found consistent success with the Seminoles as a starter or a reliever. The Padres still took him in the 11th round in 2023 and signed him for $200,000. Montgomery needed Tommy John surgery after only three appearances with Single-A Lake Elsinore in '24, and he didn’t return to a mound in an official setting until the 2025 Arizona Fall League, where he allowed two earned runs, struck out seven and walked seven in 10 1/3 frames. He has opened his age-23 season as a starter with High-A Fort Wayne. The 6-foot-1 right-hander showcases both a four-seamer and sinker. He can sit 92-95 mph with the heat, though he’s been below that at times in the cold Midwest League this spring. The sinker has decent tail running in on righties, while the four-seam will flash promising ride, and both were significant chase pitches in the AFL. His 83-86 mph slider is back as a whiff generator in 2026, flashing enough depth to look like a potential above-average offering, while his upper-80s changeup lacks enough separation to be a serious weapon against lefties at this stage. Montgomery had control problems dating back to his first year in Tallahassee but has actually tightened up his command coming out of his TJ recovery and rehab, enough to keep getting starting looks. He’s already facing Rule 5 eligibility this upcoming offseason though, and unless there’s a significant jump in stuff in 2026, he might not be far off from seeing if the sinker-slider combo can play up as a righty-heavy option in the bullpen.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Virahonda isn't big for a catcher, but he is solidly built, and he should be able to contribute on both sides of the ball. At the plate, he’s short to the ball with a lofted swing. He’s got average bat speed or a tick better and has a knack for adjusting to spin, thanks in part to good balance and a front foot that gets down early. His approach is also coming along nicely for a teenage catcher, and I like how he shortens up a tick with two strikes. 
Defensively, Virahonda is a stout receiver with strong wrists and a splayed setup conducive to giving the umpire every chance to call the low strike. He’s got a strong arm, and his accuracy and quick release have helped him hose nearly a third of baserunners throughout his minor league career. The knock here is that he’s not especially projectable. Virahonda has enough pop to drive balls out to left, but it'd be a pleasant surprise if he grew into average power. I like Virahonda and think he’s a bit of a sleeper in this tier, but the responsible projection is that of a good backup.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
The Orioles held a mini pre-draft workout for area prospects at Lo Re's high school in Tempe (just a couple of miles down the road from Eric's lair) and ended up drafting the infielder in the fifth round, signing him away from a BYU commitment for about half a million bucks. He's a smaller player without big present bat speed, but his swing is beautiful and he had a great contact track record in high school (though he was at fewer events than some of his peers). He also takes a great infield, and he entered pro ball with an uncommon defensive versatility that the Orioles have immediately put to use, as Lo Re played four different positions during his first ever week of actual games. 
Though he doesn't swing especially hard, Lo Re's body is well-connected from the ground up. His top hand drives his swing a lot of the time, allowing him to cover the top and inner third of the strike zone. It's an offensive skill set similar to Myles Straw, though Lo Re is a better rotator and might end up with a bit more power if he can get stronger without sacrificing his mobility. Lo Re has played three infield positions and center field already in pro ball. He looked like a viable pro shortstop to the eye in high school, but it's going to take some time before anyone outside the org will have a firm grip on his fit in center field. He's only just begun playing there, and only some of the time. The infield/outfield mix is another similarity with prospect-era Myles Straw, though we feel better about Lo Re's ability to stay on the dirt. Baltimore has had recent success with six-figure high schoolers and we think Lo Re will continue that trend en route to a contact-oriented utility role.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Smith creates really tough angle on his pitches (a Brewer pattern of acquisition), will show you 95, and he executes his changeup with remarkable consistency for a 40-grade athlete. He was a high-priority senior in the 2021 draft and projects as a quick-moving reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Sales' pro debut — 94.2 innings combined between the Tigers and Nats systems (he was in the Kyle Finnegan trade), 2.85 ERA, 26% K%, 7.3% BB% — marked his second consecutive season approaching 100 innings with starter-quality strike-throwing. He has begun 2026 on the IL with a vague upper body injury that, according to a source, is related to his torso rather than his arm. Healthy Sales has two nasty breaking balls in a cutter and slider that both generated plus miss in 2025. He can throw a slower curveball into the zone and uses it more often against lefties, who had a .750 OPS against him last year. The next box Sales needs to check to continue projecting as a starter is an offspeed pitch that will help keep lefties off of his back. As his repertoire is currently constituted, he should be a good middle reliever who'll face righties as often as possible.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Of all the pitchers taken in the 2025 Rule 5 Draft, Winquest might have the best long-term chance to remain a starter. The former eighth rounder out of UT-Arlington reached Double-A in 2025 and worked 106 total innings with a 3.99 ERA. He’s a bouncy 6-foot-2, and has both starter-quality athleticism and physicality at a well-composed 205 pounds. Winquest also consistently locates his 94-97 mph fastball to the up-and-arm-side quadrant of the zone where it plays best, and then bends in several different breaking balls — cutters, curveballs and sliders — off of that pitch. He’s better at landing his breakers in the zone than he is at dotting them for chase, and he’s comfortable pitching backwards, which he may need to do against big league lefties since he lacks a changeup. 
Winquest's control gives him a good chance to stick on the Yankees' roster, and his pedigree as a minor league starter puts him in position to provide length in the event that he makes the team. He can lean on his fastball/curveball combo an inning at a time and work in the other breaking balls if he eventually returns to starting. Either way, he should be a solid, lower-ceiling contributor to a pitching staff for the next several years.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Nuel is a blazingly fast up-the-middle position player prospect from Jamaica who slashed .261/.433/.398 in his second DSL season and cut his K% from 30.3% to 20.4%. He's now hitting leadoff for the FCL team and mostly playing second base. Nuel has two catalytic qualities in his speed and selectivity. He's built like a college defensive back at a lanky 6-feet tall, and his swing is already geared for lift in the extreme. That may not suit Nuel's skill set at maturity, as it won't take advantage of his speed, but if he grows into meaningful power in his 20s, then the swing foundation to do damage is already here. 
Nuel has just started playing some center field and it might eventually be the spot where he can best make a big impact on that side of the ball. The crowded nature of Baltimore's complex position player group is going to make it tough to get a great feel for any of those guys' defensive chops this year. Instead, the biggest part of Nuel's 2026 is going to be carrying a viable contact rate through his first domestic pro season. He's a toolsy, high-variance prospect who seems to have begun to find his footing.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: At age 19, Alberto is built like Mikal Bridges and unusually twitchy for a teenager with limbs this long. He has a near ideal pitcher's frame, with a high, tapered waist and broad shoulders. He's already sitting 92-94 with some breaking ball feel. <em>(DR Instructs)<em>

fangraphs.label: 2022updated
fangraphs.text: Another Tech pitching prospect with huge arm strength and a nasty breaking ball, Birdsell's delivery is stiff and upright and he looks like a reliever on the surface. He hasn't walked an excessive number of hitters, though. Repertoire depth may still funnel him to the bullpen, but as ugly as his delivery is, Birdsell's glove-side fastball/slider control is pretty good, and both pitches are plus.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Yeager has an above-average two-pitch mix. He gained five ticks on his slider from when I first saw him in early 2024 to when I caught him again last summer. Suffice to say, that's hard to predict and he deserves a lot of credit for the transformation. His fastball ticked up a bit as well, and he now touches 99; the velo is enough to miss bats even though he doesn't get a lot of extension. His slider flashes plus and is a tight bender that appears more firm than sharp to my eye, but hitters look bad against it, and missed on more than 40% of their swings last year. The arsenal is shallow and the stuff isn't quite late-inning loud, but Yeager has enough in the holster to project as an optionable reliever. Sometimes those guys turn into long-term middle relievers.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: After a hot first half in the Cal League, Figueroa was one of the many, many prospects San Diego traded to Baltimore as part of their 2025 deadline push. He was promoted after the deal, but struggled and hit .182. He then began 2026 on a power-hitting heater putting him on pace to blow through his 2025 total. Figueroa whiffs a lot. He had a 71% contact rate last year and has been closer to 60% to start this season. But Figueroa has real thunder in his hands and enough juice to hit for power the opposite way, which he must because his swing's length causes him to spray most of his well-struck contact that way. He's a stiff-legged guy and below-average athlete, a one-tool player with enough power to carry some value despite his issues.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Coleman went undrafted after an up-and-down college career at LSU. While he split time between the bullpen and rotation in college, it’s in the latter role that he’s taken a big step forward in pro ball. Critically, his velocity climbed several ticks last summer. He now touches 97 mph from the left side, which is enough to get anybody’s attention, especially when it comes with a low release and bat-missing carry. Paired with an average slider and a fair change, Coleman has the arsenal to work in a big league bullpen. His track record of throwing strikes isn’t long, but he’s also never had quite this much stuff to attack with. The forecast here is for average control, enough to let the heater play.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: While he was a pure relief prospect, Dowd had one of the best breaking balls in the entire 2023 draft, his upper-70s curveball which features monstrous break and depth. Like many of Stanford's talented arms the last handful of years, Dowd's feel for strikes arguably regressed while he was there. He has four distinct pitches but didn't develop any velocity at Stanford, and was drafted sitting 92, same as he was in high school. A pared-down repertoire might be in order since Dowd is likely to continue to be a reliever in pro ball. His breaking ball quality is strong enough to anticipate he'll be a solid middle inning option.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Swan presents the Dodgers dev group with exciting raw material and lots of late-bloomer traits. For one, Swan throws really hard and was holding 96-98 mph velo as a starter at Middle Tennessee. He's also huge, at a broad-shouldered 6-foot-6, and is coming from a smaller program. It's feasible things might click for Swan from a command standpoint and enable him to start, but his current level of control is too raw to project him as a starter. Swan is capable of missing bats with all three of his pitches, be it his upper-90s heater, his mid-80s slider, or his low-90s changeup. He works with extreme downhill plane, so steep it might actually be good, especially for his slider's playability. Swan is a very interesting developmental pitching prospect with a wide range of potential outcomes, the most likely of which puts him in a middle inning relief role.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
The longer I do this, the more I think that the 18-year-old-or-older arms in the international market offer the best bang for your buck of any player group. Santana fits the mold as a $15,000 signee who has developed into a pretty interesting relief prospect. He’s a low-slot, almost sidearm lefty with a quick arm and a fastball that he can run into the mid-90s. His two-plane slider was above average pretty often by year’s end, and he has nascent feel for working with it both in the zone and below. If you're feeling optimistic — and let’s live a little here, we're all about projection in this space — you can dream on average control. Santana is a decent athlete with a chance to throw more strikes if he can build more stability in his lower half and finish his delivery more consistently. 
The low release is going to give his fastball a lot of utility even if he doesn’t command it very well, and the guess here is that Santana will have enough pitchability for mid-leverage work. You won't get rich betting on A-ball relievers, but there’s a lot to like here.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Bleis is a righty corner outfield power projection prospect with a whippy, low-ball swing and room for about 30 pounds on his frame.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Knapczyk was one of the stronger bat-to-ball performers in the entire 2023 draft, especially among the college ranks, but it's unclear where he fits on defense to to severe issues with arm accuracy and fielding the ball cleanly. He's just not a good defensive infielder despite playing shortstop at one of the country's bigger programs, and might have to move to the outfield as a pro. If that's the case it's going to be tough for the undersized Knapczyk to profile in a corner. He is very similar to a lot of Cleveland prospects, most recently Ernie Clement.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
The old saw about how long levered guys sometimes just need extra time to grow into their bodies can be a little frustrating because there’s not much you can do but wait and hope. It’s still early in the season, but we may be seeing that at play with Gongora. The lefty always threw strikes in college, but after a rough year in that department in 2025, he’s posted a tiny 1.97 BB/9 through his first seven starts at Double-A. He’s probably running hot and his command is still progressing — on video, it isn't unusual to see him alternate a perfectly placed breaking ball with a heater 18 inches from the target — but it’s impressive nonetheless, and his control drives a backend starter projection. 
Gongora has a classic starting pitcher’s four-pitch mix. Out of a high slot, he works with a low-to-mid-90s fastball, straight with a bit of carry. He has two functional breaking balls, a lovely 1-7 curve and a harder two-plane slider. He used his change less often than the breakers last year, but it too has good action and arm speed, and projects average. Unlike a lot of Orioles arms, Baltimore hasn’t overhauled too much with Gongora. He’s slowed the cadence in his delivery in pro ball, and to Brendan's eye he looks a little more limber. But the O’s have kept his high slot, and the tweaks to his offspeed pitches have been minor. That continuity has perhaps been helpful as he’s developed in pro ball, and it also means there’s runway ahead to play with a cutter, a split, or something else if the current mix proves hittable. As is, he’s having success at Double-A — 3.66 ERA, 40 strikeouts, two homers allowed in 32 innings across seven starts — and projects as a backend starter.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Arias is a twitchy, medium-framed outfielder who runs well enough to develop in center field. He swings pretty hard, but it requires a good bit of effort for him to do so, creating risk that he'll whiff more as he climbs. His $1.2 million deal with the Dodgers was one of the earlier handshake agreements in the class.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Gray is an athletic, projectable two-way player. He gets way down the mound and is very balanced over his lead leg as he delivers home with big extension and flat angle. He also has feel for a loopy breaking ball that lefty hitters struggle with because of Gray's length. He has some young Josh Hader traits.

fangraphs.label: 2023updated
fangraphs.text: Walters is a "fastball-only" pitcher with close to 80% heater usage in 2023, which is actually down from 2022. He was selected by Baltimore in the 2022 draft as draft-eligible sophomore but didn't sign. Back with Miami in 2023, he struck out 72 and walked just seven in 44.2 innings. His mid-90s fastball has incredible riding life, generating tons of swings and misses throughout the strike zone. It's a dominant offering that would be enough to spearhead a single-inning relief fit in pro ball. Walters had no feel for finishing his slider/curveball in college and that offering desperately needs to be developed for him to be more than a middle relief option. How good of a second pitch he develops will dictate his future role. At best, he'll show you a slider in the 86-89 mph range with two-plane movement. He has an ideal pitcher's frame, throwing from a three-quarters slot with bend at the elbow and a north/south hand position that helps create ride.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: A native of Taiwan, Huang signed for $210,000 prior to the 2025 season. From a pitchability perspective, he was as advanced as anyone you’ll find on the complex. With a well-honed motion, Huang absolutely peppered the zone with three pitches, showing touch and feel to complement plus control. The stuff is less eye-catching. He'll touch 95 but sits in the low 90s, and his secondaries project average. The underlying foundation means things could get pretty interesting if he finds a little more velo. I'm not projecting it, though, and see Huang as more of a low-leverage arm.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Cleveland seems to prioritize switch-hitting, up-the-middle players in the international market and they have yet another in Genao, who has become much more physical in the months leading up to signing. His swing is crude from both sides but he's a good athlete with a good frame.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: A leviathan corner outfield prospect with huge power, Gomez is very likely to develop at least plus raw power at peak, and he has a slight chance to enter 70-grade territory. He has already hit a ball 107 mph during live BP this spring. Whether he'll make enough contact for that to matter we'll learn once DSL play gets underway. Right now, his swing tends to work toward the opposite field gap; he's less able to pull the ball than some of the other thumpers in the 2026 class. Still, he's similar, skill-wise, to a handful of players who got about a million bucks more than Gomez's $1.25 million bonus.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Polanco was the Pirates' big recent amateur signee, earning a $2.5 million bonus. He's a big-framed, lefty-hitting outfield prospect with loose hitting actions and precocious barrel control. The reports I sourced from international personnel in advance of the 2021 signing period led to mixed reports on Polanco, with some considering him a low-ceiling corner outfield prospect with a profile driven by his hit tool, while others see a big frame and power projection with swing-and-miss risk. (International free agent signee)

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Parker's stuff has been trending up for a while and he's so projectable that it may not stop any time soon. He had one very strong inning in his first start of the spring and flashed a 70-grade curveball before falling off later in the outing. In general he fits in the $1 million high school pitcher mold.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: High-ceiling'd, high-variance lefty-hitting infielder with big time frame projection. Explosive hitting hands, broad-shouldered 6-foot-3 frame with loads of room for strength. Really exciting at first glance, but ultimately K'd quite a bit on the showcase circuit and has considerable hit tool risk. Potential for big power could make a likely below-average contact profile workable, especially if Franco can stay at shortstop. Size and mobility looked like more of third base fit last summer. Removed his name from the draft a few days prior to selection and is headed to TCU.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: Jones is in the Sam Huff mold, possessing elite power projection but just a 30-grade bat, which might be enough to profile if he can stay behind the plate.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Physical catcher/outfielder prospect with funkadelic swing that works for him. Short to the ball, often on time to pull. Prototypical size and build for either a catcher or corner outfielder. Runs well enough that center field might be an option for him in pro ball, but given how much room he has for strength, it's more likely that he ends up in a corner. Might have trouble dipping to scoop low pitches and deal with backfoot breaking balls given this sweeping, unique bat path, but posted an 89% contact rate across multiple showcase seasons. Buttons fastballs. Toosly athlete with lots of positive outcomes, be it as a well-rounded outfielder or slow-burning developmental catcher.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Power-hitting catching prospect with plus bat speed. Linebacker build, plus arm. Doesn't track pitches well, chases elevated fastballs. Risky, high-upside developmental catching prospect. Pulled name out of draft and is headed to LSU.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Grinder outfielder with above-average contact skills and below-average power. Runs well enough to develop in center field. Works the middle of the field on offense and is especially good at covering the top two thirds of the zone. Cuts swing down with two strikes. Father Chip played minor league ball for the Dodgers and D-backs, and was a career .750 OPS guy across eight seasons. Brock looks like a potential table-setting leadoff man. A lack of both present power and overt projection has him more in the third round mix.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Two-year starter at DBU, struggled with walks both years, sustained velo deep into seasons. Was parked at 96-97 in regional start at LSU and up to 100 on the season. Downhill angle hurts fastball effectiveness but helps curveball stay hidden until descent. Prototypical big league frame at 6-foot-5, loose but erratic arm action. Threw strikes with both his fastball and curveball (his most-used secondary) less than 60% of the time. Primary offspeed is 12-6 curveball with plenty of depth, also has tighter gyro slider that was emphasized more late in the year because he can actually locate it, more like a cutter in terms of usage style. Command likely relegates him to relief, but then where does his velo end up? Shot to be late-inning reliever, but needs to find another grade of command.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Four-pitch starter prospect with a bigger build and mature stuff. Will sit 92-94 mph and just about touched 97 at PG All-American. More low-90s this spring but would sometimes work nearly 100 pitches deep into games. Fastball often has natural cut. His delivery features a lot of effort and a bit of a head whack; it's pretty violent, but he still commands the baseball. Crossland's feel for locating his fastball and his mid-80s cutter/slider is advanced. He also has an average-ish 78-82 mph curveball and a changeup of highly variable quality, though every once in a while he shows you a really nasty one. Innings-eater backend projection.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Tightly wound switch-hitting second baseman. Can move the barrel around from both sides of the plate. Swing is flat and contact-oriented from the right side, features more power from the left. Requires a lot of effort to swing hard; hands fire from a dead stop. Less smooth and graceful than most big league hitters. Second base fit on defense due to arm strength. Lacks physical projection. An interesting six figure candidate for later in the draft.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Physical, switch-hitting infielder with compact swing. Tracks pitches well, lets them travel deep before unloading. Peppers the gaps from both sides of the plate. Rotates well, left swing has more loft. Excellent showcase contact performance in a limited sample. Power projection capped somewhat by present physical maturity. Slower-twitch defender who might not be an infielder at all, 2B/1B/OF mix on defense in pro ball due to insufficient arm strength for left side of infield. Closer to 19 on draft day, but not so close that he'd be a draft-eligible sophomore in two years. Upper-six-figure type.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Very projectable righty with beautiful arm action. Naturally cutting fastball in the low 90s, could be plus at peak depending on how strong Hamilton gets. His lower half usage is not as athletically impressive as his arm action. Curveball in the 77-82 mph range is average at times, changeup tends to be below. High-variance dev project with fastball shape in the wheelhouse of many analytically oriented teams.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Hamel brings plus-plus fastball/breaking ball spin, plus fastball carry, and mid-90s velocity to a high-probability relief profile. If he has a velocity spike out of the bullpen they we may be talking about a late-inning role.

fangraphs.label: 2023draft
fangraphs.text: Witt had late-first and comp round homes during his high school draft year, but teams wouldn't meet his asking price and he ended up at Texas, where he mostly pitched in a multi-inning, high-leverage relief role as a freshman, which continued on Cape Cod and with Team USA. Put in Texas' rotation as a sophomore, Witt made just two starts before his elbow blew out, which required Tommy John. He was back toward the end of the 2023 collegiate season and didn't look very good, only sitting 90 mph with scattered command. Breaking ball depth and changeup sink are still there. He's a from-scratch pro dev project who needs a delivery overhaul — this tall, cross-bodied thing he's doing post-op makes his fastball steep and very hittable. He would be a 35+ FV prospect free of context, but that breaking ball is still in there, so he gets a little bump.

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text: Kang's performance in Korea is on the upswing again after two years marred by injuries and time away to deal with anxiety. After a very strong start to his pro career, Kang broke his toe falling down a flight of stairs before the 2022 season began, then partially tore his hamstring just a few weeks after he returned. A bout with anxiety shelved him for a month in 2023, and his season ended with an oblique tear. After he hit 29 homers in his age-18 rookie season, Kang hit just 14 combined across the 2022 and 2023 campaigns before rebounding somewhat in 2024 with a .289/.360/.480 line and 26 bombs. In 2025, he again missed time with multiple injuries, including another oblique issue at the start of the year, a toe injury suffered from an accident with a glass door in a team hotel, and then an ankle issue that had him DH'ing for the rest of the year. Though Kang didn't have the enormous offensive season he no doubt hoped for as he seemingly prepared to try to come to MLB (he hired Paragon Sports as representation during the summer), he looks pretty good. Kang is arguably in the best shape of his career and is swinging very, very hard, with one of the more aggressive, entertaining swings in Asian pro ball. His big, hard-to-time leg kick and expansive approach sometimes undermine Kang's precocious bat control, and he might strike out more than is ideal for a 1B/LF/DH. Where Kang plays when he transitions to MLB is up for debate. He caught 24 games in 2024 but was too injured to do much of it in 2025. He'd be a more attractive free agent target with a clearer position. Right now, he looks like a version of Matt Stairs, a nice lefty power bat to use off the bench.

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text: This outlet is supportive of elder millennials attempting to pull off a big career change in their late-30s, but Iwasaki is trying to pull off quite the cathartic late-career climax after losing most of 2022 and all of 2023 to Tommy John surgery. The 36-year-old reliever’s success (38.1 IP of 2.11 ERA with 37 K in 2025) is defined largely by his command of a nasty high-80s splitter. Iwasaki was touching 97 mph at points this October, but his fastball has downhill plane out of a high three-quarters release, which mirrors the split but also rarely gets above barrels, and he'll also sprinkle in a low-70s show-me slow curve. A splitter can be a volatile pitch to make a living with, and Iwasaki’s command of it isn’t surgical. Even after just 10 walks in 38.1 IP this season, there’s potential for control issues just because his game is predicated on getting a lot of chases after dirted splitters without much he'd feel comfortable challenging hitters with in the zone. The version of Iwasaki that sits 95-97 can probably work the seventh inning regardless of handedness, but the floor can cave in with a stretch of poor command.

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text: Four teams nominated Sumida to be their first round pick when he was a college pitcher coming out of West Japan Tech. He ended up with the Seibu Lions and has pitched in their rotation since 2022. Sumida is an athletic, extra-small lefty with a plus changeup. His fastball sits about 89-92 and relies on some natural cut and uphill angle to sneak past hitters at the letters. Sumida can bend in a very slow curveball and will occasionally show you an upper-70s slider, but overwhelmingly, he manipulates his changeup's shape and velocity to garner his swings and misses. He's a low-variance backend starter type who has been durable and consistent.

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text: A very bouncy, athletic little righty with a consistent delivery, Ohtsu has plus command of stuff that is mostly average or below. His changeup has enough movement to miss bats in the strike zone against NPB hitters, but that might not be as true in MLB. Ohtsu also looks much more comfortable landing his 80mph-ish slurve for strikes than he does using it as a chase pitch. If he can find a chase-inducing breaking ball, he might take a leap because he has the command to weaponize it in such a way that it will outperform his raw stuff. For now, he looks like a potential backend starter in MLB thanks to his ability to work very efficiently.

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text: Ju Won is a fairly projectable switch-hitting shortstop who took a step forward on defense in 2023, and another one on offense in 2025. He still doesn't have ideal shortstop arm strength, but he looked much better in this regard than he did as a very young player. Kim has become stronger and more physical during the last couple of seasons and had a power-hitting uptick in 2025, with a career-high 15 homers. Though it's mechanically compact, Kim's hands fire from a dead stop and his bat ends to arrive a little late, causing him to inside-out the baseball from the left side. He has roughly average bat speed from both sides of the plate and is a good, young infield defender, so on our shores, he'd project as a fine utility infielder. In Korea, he'll probably be a star as he enters his physical prime. If a more fluid lefty swing can emerge, or if Ju Won adds another level of strength, it would reveal a higher ceiling than we currently think he has, and result in more foreign interest.

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text:
Stewart was among the top high school pitchers in the 2018 draft. The Braves picked him eighth overall, but flunked his post-draft medical (wrist) and tried to sign him for a reduced amount. During that stretch, the relationship between the player and the team disintegrated, and Stewart, who was committed to Mississippi State, chose not to sign. Rather than go to Starkville, he spent a year at a Florida junior college to more quickly re-enter the draft, but his stuff took a dive and so did his draft standing. He made a move to Japan with an eye on pitching there until he was granted unrestricted free agency after six years. 
Stewart initially struggled to throw strikes and spent all of 2022 in the NPB equivalent of the minors, walking nearly a batter per inning. In 2023, he finally got an extended run in the NPB big league, where he threw most of the 100 combined innings he worked between the farm club and the Hawks. He took a step forward in 2024 when he threw 120 innings and improved his peripheral stats. Stewart continues to sit 93-95 with fairly hittable downhill plane that makes it imperative that he begin commanding his fastball more consistently to the top of the zone. He could also stand to become stronger and more flexible in his lower body, anything that might help flatten the line on his fastball or help him repeat his delivery more consistently. Stewart's trademark curveball still has fantastic, bat-missing depth, and he has added a firmer, mid-80s slider and, most prominently, a splitter. All of these play down because of Stewart's poor control. Given his pro track record of strike-throwing, Stewart remains a relief prospect at this point, but he has gotten better in this area and has another year to improve before he might be in position to consider a move to MLB.

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text: Taira looked like a late-inning power reliever until 2023, when he was moved to Seibu's rotation and dealt with a regression in stuff. He began 2024 as a starter again but was shut down with forearm tightness after just a few outings. He missed several months and was put back in the bullpen when he returned, and Taira's stuff rebounded in a big way. He sat 96 and was up to 99 late in the year. Taira has a catcherly build and a violent, high-effort delivery, but his stuff (a big rise/run fastball, plus a cutter, slider and splitter) would play in a big league bullpen. Though his secondaries (especially his splitter) have generated plus chase and miss rates, they're closer to average in terms of pure quality and would likely play down due to Taira's lack of command. He's a high-variance guy with a shot to be a good bullpen's third banana.

fangraphs.label: 2026overseas
fangraphs.text: Saito tore his ACL just before the 2023 season, and his debut with Hokkaido (who got him in a trade with Hanshin the year prior) was delayed until 2024. Saito's fastball velocity was up in 2024 and he sat 96 all year. He has a very explosive arm action and can touch the upper-90s, but he needs to find a second plus pitch to work as more than a middle reliever in MLB.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Malony is a viable defensive shortstop who has posted two practically identical underclass years at Oregon, with a .968 OPS in both campaigns. He's a strapping 6-foot-1, has authoritative hitting hands, and is often on time to pull. But Malony's style has him pulling off a lot of sliders, and he doesn't always track the baseball well, so his hit tool projection here is a good bit south of what it'd be if one were to take his 2025 data at face value. A viable shortstop fit, Malony projects as a utilityman in the Zack Short mold.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: A .347/.465/.614 career hitter in two years at Maryland before transferring to Texas A&M for his draft spring, Hacopian has a ridiculous TrackMan readout (95% contact rate versus fastballs in 2025, including on Cape Cod, 57% hard-hit rate during his sophomore season with the Terps). He is less toolsy to the eye, however, as his kind of odd, high-effort swing, medium frame, and realistic 2B/3B fit on defense make him look more like a contact-oriented utilityman. Hacopian didn't really hit for power with wood on Cape Cod (he slugged .364), which is more in line with the expectations set by his look as a hitter (middling size, strength and a lot of effort needed to swing hard). He has more of a late-second or third round feel from a visual scouting standpoint, but might be someone's data darling.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Rose is a former catcher who has become a contact-oriented corner outfielder in college. Advanced bat control drives an offensive skill set that it diluted by Rose's tendency to chase. He could be a Harold Ramírez type of role player as a part-time corner outfielder.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Bogenpohl is a massive 6-foot-6 outfielder with all-fields power and surprising feel for center field. A former two-way player, he broke Ryan Howard's freshman home run record at Missouri State back in 2024 before his numbers took a bit of a dip in 2025. Bogenpohl's lever length makes his swing a tenuous bet to hit pro velocity. He's already hitting a lot of middle-middle fastballs to the opposite field because he's not on time to pull them, and Bogenpohl's 70% contact rate is in a danger zone for a college hitter.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Tinney is a monstrous 6-foot-4 catcher who had a power-hitting breakout as a sophomore at Notre Dame, where he slugged .753 before entering the transfer portal and heading to Austin. Tinney has plus pull power and, especially after conference play began in 2025, he was among the college baseball leaders in hard-hit rate. He struggled to stay with sliders on Cape Cod and struck out nearly as much as he did during the regular season in half as many games. Tinney has big hit tool risk and needs refinement on defense, especially his framing.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Grahovac is a physical 3B/OF who hit 23 homers as a freshman despite whiffing a ton. As a sophomore, he played just six games before tearing the labrum in his left shoulder, which required surgery. He's a high-variance 2026 prospect who had strikeout risk prior to the injury.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Volchko was an electric, hard-throwing high school righty from Northern California who struggled in two seasons at Stanford (he had an ERA over 6.00 as a soph) and transferred to Georgia. At his best, Volchko has a hairy mid-90s fastball, plus cutter/slider, and a firm, low-90s changeup with sink and tail. His fastball's movement does not allow that pitch to miss bats. The possibility that a change of scenery will help his stuff play better is why Volchko is speculatively ranked here.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Bowen is a muscular, physically mature corner outfield prospect who is already generating plus bat speed. His swing is a little too awkward looking to accept that his showcase contact performance (76%, average) will hold in pro ball.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Hirschkorn's coordination for an athlete his size is remarkable, and the 6-foot-7 righty is able to locate his plus-flashing slider with mature precision and consistency. These gyro sliders enjoy a little extra depth thanks to his remarkable size, as well as his feel for spotting it. The rest of Hirschkorn's repertoire is below average, and his fastball was only sitting 93 with downhill angle last summer. There may eventually be an offspeed pitch here because Hirschkorn's feel for pitching is very special for a high schooler his size. Right now, he looks more like a Jonathan Bowlan starter kit than a righty CC Sabathia or anything like that.

fangraphs.label: 2026draft
fangraphs.text: Borthwick is a gigantic righty who drives way down the mound and misses bats with a plus slider. His build and delivery are very similar to Alek Manoah's, except Borthwick isn't quite that big yet. His slider falls off the table and he locates it well, just off the corner of the plate. It will be important for him to develop a third pitch in pro ball. His build, lack of current repertoire depth, and the effort in his delivery combine to create a good bit of relief risk here.

fangraphs.label: 2024draft
fangraphs.text: Four-pitch arsenal and a medium frame. Strong athlete, drop-and-drive delivery. Advanced command with his low-90s fastball, underwhelming secondaries aside from a good slider. Also mixed in a curve and changeup. Fills up the zone with all offerings. Limited upside arm, spot starter type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holiday bounced between two Florida junior colleges in 2022 and 2023, leading JuCo pitchers with 141 strikeouts in 88 innings for Junior College World Series champion Central Florida the latter year. He moved to Oklahoma State as a junior and led the Big 12 with 128 punchouts in 113 frames. Holiday delivered a complete-game two-hitter in the postseason against Florida in the NCAA Regionals, and the Cardinals selected him in the third round that July. He signed for $800,000, a little below slot, as St. Louis’ second pick of the 2024 Draft. The 5-foot-11 right-hander may have only sat 90-93 mph (touching 95) with his fastball in college, but his impressive command of the pitch, particularly with carry up in the zone, made it closer to an average offering. His low-80s slider caused batters from both sides of the plate to expand the zone, and he could land it especially well low and to the gloveside. His mid-70s curveball was a serviceable third pitch, while his low-80s changeup was used only against lefties and with unreliable results. Holiday uses an extremely high leg kick that could rival that of Bronson Arroyo and he makes a stabbing motion with his front foot as it lands, adding some deception. At his size, he isn’t a candidate to add a ton of velocity in pro ball, so he’ll need to continue to pound the zone and throw hitters off in other ways to stick as a starter. Holiday underwent Tommy John surgery last spring and has yet to make his pro debut.

fangraphs.label: 2024draft
fangraphs.text: Snyder is a hit-over-power bat with fringy raw at present, and looks better suited range-wise for second or third base. His arm and hands are good enough to handle either position and he likely will do so at an above-average level.
